events.title: Exhibit | Centering Philippine and Filipinx American Histories: Selections from The Bancroft Library
events.description: The Bancroft Library's collections of materials relating to the Philippines span nearly 500 years. Highlights in this exhibit include a transcript of an Inquisitorial trial from 1646, a prayer book written in the Cebuano language, and UC Berkeley Filipino student publications from 1905 to the present. The exhibit also features selections from the personal papers of acclaimed author Jessica Hagedorn, including typewritten drafts of her novels, poetry, song lyrics, and a screenplay, as well as childhood drawings and writings.Bancroft's renowned Latin American collections offer up intriguing examples of documents produced by the Spanish Empire as it exploited the islands' natural, cultural, and human resources. Examples include the transcript of the Inquisitorial trial of two women accused of being spiritual mediums, a manuscript written in the Jawi script, which is based on Arabic script promising religious freedom to the Muslim residents of the island of Mindanao, and materials regarding the trade between Manila and Mexico.The personal papers and published works of UC Berkeley professors Bernard Moses (1846-1931) and David Barrows (1873-1954) document their early involvement with American colonialism in the Philippines, especially their work in redesigning the Filipino education system. In the aftermath of a brutal war, Americans viewed education as a tool for pacifying a conquered population. Documentation of these professors' white supremacist views is contrasted with the work of Filipinx and Asian American scholars who use their words to critique colonialism and its racist underpinnings.Educational opportunities have brought students from the Philippines, and later Filipinx American students, to Berkeley since the early 20th century. The exhibit includes examples of four student publications — two published in the first two decades of the 1900s and two more contemporary examples — that provide evidence of these students' political engagement and their determination to make their voices heard.Selections from the personal papers of acclaimed author and performance artist Jessica Hagedorn are also on display, including examples of her novels, plays, poetry, song lyrics, a screenplay, childhood drawings, and writings. Hagedorn employs a kaleidoscope of pop culture references, songs, images, and quotes from historical figures, and a galaxy of characters representing various cultures, classes, genders, races, and nationalities in her depictions of the Philippines and Filipinx America.Open hours may vary. Please view the The Bancroft Library hours (https://www.lib.berkeley.edu/visit/bancroft) page for the most up-to-date information.

events.title: Exhibit | De y para el pueblo / For and by the People: Revolutionary Mexican Prints
events.description: The exhibit features highlights from The Bancroft Library's extensive collection of prints. The show examines how a Mexico City-based artists collective, the Taller de Gráfica Popular (Workshop for Popular Graphic Art), built an artistic legacy, tracing its roots from José Guadalupe Posada's portrayals of everyday Mexican life, to its enduring influence on artists on both sides of the U.S.-Mexico border today.

events.title: Exhibit | Divestment Now! Student Activism and the Anti-Apartheid Movement at UC Berkeley
events.location: The Rowell Exhibition Cases, Doe Library, 2nd floor
events.description: In 1985, UC Berkeley students, with support from faculty, staff, and labor unions, transformed the campus into the heart of a powerful anti-apartheid divestment campaign. They organized rallies, teach-ins, and shantytown encampments to protest the university's financial ties to companies profiting from South Africa's system of racial segregation. Divestment Now! Student Activism and the Anti-Apartheid Movement at UC Berkeley highlights a movement that mobilized thousands, politicized a new generation, and laid the groundwork for ongoing struggles for racial and economic justice.

events.title: Exhibition: "Hidden Layers: AI Infrastructures and Hallucinations"
events.location: Worth Ryder Art Gallery, Anthropology & Art Building, Rm 116
events.description: The Department of German and the Department of Art Practice are excited to announce the opening of Hidden Layers: AI Infrastructures and Hallucinations, curated by Antonio Somaini with Hannes Bajohr and Sonja Thiel, in dialogue with the France–Berkeley research initiative The Latent Spaces of Culture, and on display at the Worth Ryder Art Gallery. This exhibition examines some of the concealed dimensions of contemporary AI culture — the planetary infrastructures of extraction and computation, the often invisible human labor, the latent vector spaces within which culture is compressed and processed, and the models' hallucinations. Hidden Layers tackles these phenomena from two different perspectives: AI Infrastructures and AI Hallucinations. Featuring works by Nouf Aljowaysir; Gašper and Nina Beguš & Metahaven; Grégory Chatonsky; Kate Crawford & Vladan Joler; Asma Kazmi & Jill Miller; Andrea Khôra; Occitane Lacurie & Barnabé Sauvage; Greg Niemeyer; and Mario Santamaria & Alex Saum-Pascual. The project is a collaboration between the Department of German and the Worth Ryder Art Gallery at the Department of Art Practice.Exhibition Dates: September 3 - October 3, 2026Opening Reception: Thursday, September 3, 4-6:30pm, Worth Ryder Art Gallery RSVP here (https://docs.google.com/forms/d/e/1FAIpQLSd_OOMe7YQHw3CYbSr673UCSlQ0f4mn4lZ7g46KhRUTRpC5qQ/viewform?usp=dialog)Artist Talk, Gregory Chatonsky: Thursday, September 3, 6:30-8:00pm, AAPB 285 RSVP here (https://docs.google.com/forms/d/e/1FAIpQLSd_OOMe7YQHw3CYbSr673UCSlQ0f4mn4lZ7g46KhRUTRpC5qQ/viewform?usp=dialog)Related programming:Film Program: September 9, 7 pm, BAMPFAWorkshop on Latent Spaces of Culture: September 9, 2pm-4pm; September 10/11, 9:30 am-4pm on both days, 470 Stephens Additional events and more details to be announced. Times subject to change, please also check the campus calendar. This exhibition is supported by the France-Berkeley Fund of the Institute of European Studies, the Department of German and the Department of Art Practice, together with the Berkeley Center for New Media, the Berkeley Institute for Data Science (BIDS), Department of Rhetoric; Antikythera, the Pamela P. Fong and Family Distinguished Chair in China Studies, the Division of Arts & Humanities, the Townsend Center for the Humanities and the School of Information, the Technology Network of the Berkeley Economy and Society Initiative (BESI); and the Berkeley Art, Law, and Finance Project, hosted by the Berkeley Center for Law and Business at Berkeley Law. In conjunction with the exhibition, additional programming is developed in collaboration with Berkeley Art Museum and Pacific Film Archive (BAMPFA) and the Institute for Contemporary Art San Jose.

events.title: Exploration of Forms: Movement as Creative Practice, a three-part workshop with Randee Paufve
events.description: About Exploration of Forms: Exploration of Forms is a public workshop series that centers embodiment, transformation, and creativity. All workshops are free for students. Guests are encouraged to make a donation of $25 at the door, but no one will be turned away for lack of funds.Signups are available here: https://tdps.link/explorationAbout This Workshop:This workshop series investigates movement not as a set of skills to acquire, but as a creative and expressive practice to inhabit and sustain. Drawing on modern/contemporary and jazz dance techniques and performance practices, each session builds on the last — offering dancers a framework for thinking about their relationship to technique, expression, and the long arc of a life in movement.September 6th - Session 1:Technique as a Tool for Expression - What is technique for? This session uses rigorous contemporary movement — warmup, floor progressions, combinations — as a lens for examining how technical training shapes (and can liberate) individual expression. Dancers are invited to bring their bodies and their questions. September 13th - Session 2:Performance Presence and the Moving Body - How does a dancer inhabit a moment rather than execute it? This session explores performance technique not as a set of presentational skills but as a practice of attention — to space, to music, to other bodies, and to the intelligence moving through your own. September 20th - Session 3: Sustaining a Creative Practice - What keeps us dancing? This session addresses the longer questions beneath the work: how dancers build and maintain a creative practice over time, how they stay curious, how they metabolize influences, and how they find their own movement voice. Includes movement work alongside structured reflection. About the Teacher: Randee Paufve is a choreographer, dancer, teacher, and Artistic Director of Paufve Dance. A 2019 Fulbright Scholar and recipient of the Isadora Duncan Dance Award for Outstanding Individual Performance, she has been featured on NPR's All Things Considered and honored with the inaugural Della Davidson Prize for Innovations in Dance-Theater. Her work has been presented nationally at ODC Theater, SFMOMA, the Mondavi Center, On the Boards, and the Portland Institute for Contemporary Art, and internationally in India, Austria, and Portugal. She has taught on the faculties of UC Davis, CSU Sacramento, St. Mary's College of California, University of San Francisco and Lewis and Clark College, and Shawl-Anderson Dance Center. Accessibility: If you require an accommodation for effective communication or information about campus mobility access features in order to fully participate in this event, please contact us with as much advance notice as possible and at least 7–10 days in advance of the event.

events.title: BAMPFA Exhibition: Private Frontiers: Media Legacies of the Cold War
events.description: On display from Sep 9 - Dec 13, 2026 | 11 am - 7 p.m. Bookended by the end of World War II in 1945 and the fall of the Berlin Wall in 1989, the Cold War was a transformative period in global history, marking both the end of the twentieth century and the waning of modernism. Though earlier historians defined the Cold War as the noncombative contest between the capitalist United States and the communist Soviet Union, recent interventions by scholars, artists, and writers have stressed that this period was also defined by the struggles for decolonization and national liberation movements across Asia and globally. Undeniable to the history of the Cold War is the crucial role that culture played in shaping perceptions of individuals, nations, and the global order, circulated through media such as international magazines, photographs, and television.Private Frontiers presents new and recent work in photography, video, and installation by contemporary artists who critically engage the Cold War as a prism for understanding today's media-saturated world. Through their methodologically-driven practices, artists Naeem Mohaiemen, Prajakta Potnis, TJ Shin, and Tiffany Sia draw on a range of references—including historical archives, news broadcasts, pop songs, and game theory—to critically examine media as a crucial arena in which politics was articulated and contested in the second half of the twentieth century. By looking carefully at how art and politics were entwined in the media of the past, these artists offer a way for us to carefully engage with the politics and art of our contemporary moment. Curated by Tausif Noor (https://arthistory.berkeley.edu/people/tausif-noor), Assistant Curator, and Atreyee Gupta (https://arthistory.berkeley.edu/people/atreyee-gupta), Associate Professor, Department of History of Art, UC Berkeley, in conjunction with the undergraduate class HA37: Contemporary Art + Architecture from Asia, c. 1945–Present. events.title: Photography Installation: Remembering the Future: Nuclear Testing, Rising Seas, and The Marshall Islands
events.description: At Giannini Hall, 36 photographs selected from the recently published Remembering the Future: Nuclear Testing, Rising Seas, and The Marshall Islands (Radius Books, © 2026) by Mark Klett and William L. Fox extend the two men's decades-long collaboration tracing the nuclear history of the American West and the broader Pacific sphere. Installed along the building's main hallway, the images move between the physical remains of nuclear testing—bunkers, craters, camera towers reclaimed by jungle—and the everyday textures of Marshallese life: canoe building, weaving, seawalls raised by hand. Paired with archival images from the testing era and drawn from Fox's field notes and essays, the photo essay holds both histories at once: the violence of nuclear history, and the resilience of a culture that continues to inhabit these islands. An artist and curator-led tour with Mark Klett and William L. Fox will take place on September 23 at 4 PM. —Mark Klett is a photographer interested in the intersection of places, history and time. His background includes working as a geologist before turning to photography. Klett has received fellowships from the Guggenheim Foundation, the Pollock-Krasner Foundation, the National Endowment for the Arts, and the Japan/US Friendship Commission. His work has been exhibited and published widely in the United States and internationally, and is held in over eighty museum collections worldwide. He is the author/co-author of twenty books. Klett is Regents' Professor Emeritus at Arizona State University where he taught for forty years. —Presented by the UC Berkeley Environmental Arts and Humanities Initiative in partnership with the Rausser College of Natural Resources.The Kōmij Mour Ijin / Our Life Is Here expedition was organized by Kathy Jetn̄il-Kijiner, Michael Light, and David Buckland, and supported by Stellar Blue Fund and Cape Farewell. Special thanks to independent curators of UC Berkeley Kōmij Mour Ijin / Our Life Is Here exhibitions Amy Kisch and Svea Lin Soll. Kõmij Mour Ijin / Our Life Is Here at UC Berkeley is made possible with support from the Stellar Blue Fund, Cape Farewell, and the Kramlich Art Foundation. —Image Credit: "The concrete bunker destroyed by the 15-megaton Bravo explosion"2023. Mounted archival digital print, 36 x 48 inches each. Titles and dates as published in Remembering the Future. Courtesy of the artist.

events.title: BCNM Undergraduate Research Symposium
events.description: BCNM is pleased to present its first ever Undergraduate Research Symposium, organized and hosted by New Media Working Group coordinators Alexis Wood and Chloé Mauvais. It will take place on Monday, September 14, 2026, from 9am to 1pm in Jarvis Auditorium at the Grimes Engineering Center. Apply to be a presenter today! (https://airtable.com/app4eJHCOwKNbJ6Bl/pag2GIgRvnCUrNx4B/form) (Deadline September 2) Register for the symposium as an observer! (https://forms.gle/4MqxMGBMzrdohfBe8) (Register by September 9 if you will be attending lunch) Save the event to your bCal here (https://calendar.google.com/calendar/event?action=TEMPLATE&tmeid=MTFpNWFnMm8wcmRtaThpZWY5cmhzdDQ0dmQgZDV1NWVrN2o4aXBvZDBvOGlxNDE1ZTFhdnNAZw&tmsrc=d5u5ek7j8ipod0o8iq415e1avs%40group.calendar.google.com)! The Berkeley Center for New Media (BCNM) invites our undergraduate students to submit presentation proposals for the 2026 BCNM Undergraduate Research Symposium. The symposium offers students an opportunity to share original research, creative projects, and works in progress with an audience of fellow students, graduate researchers, faculty, and members of the broader BCNM community. In addition to student presentations, the event will include a networking lunch and a panel on graduate school and career pathways. Selected presenters will gain experience communicating their work to an interdisciplinary audience, receive guidance as they prepare their presentations, and connect with people working at the intersections of new media, technology, design, the arts, and the humanities. All students, staff, and faculty are welcome and encouraged to attend the symposium as observers. What kinds of projects are eligible? We welcome research and creative work related to BCNM's core areas of inquiry, including media transition and emergence, critical thinking and making, and technological equity and justice. Possible topics and formats include, but are not limited to: - Social media, online communities, and digital culture - Games, interactive media, virtual reality, and immersive storytelling - Digital art, design, performance, and creative technologies - Critical approaches to data, mapping, archives, or visualization - Technology, identity, accessibility, equity, or social justice - The social and cultural effects of emerging technologies - Making, prototyping, or practice-based research - Artificial intelligence, algorithms, and digital platforms Projects may come from coursework, independent research, honors theses, internships, creative practice, or collaborative work. Both completed projects and substantial works in progress are welcome. Students enrolled in the BCNM Certificate Program, or intending to enroll in the program, will be given a strong preference.Presentation format Presentations should be approximately 10–15 minutes long and will be followed by a brief audience Q&A. Presentations may include slides, demonstrations, videos, and/or performances. Selected presenters will be required to attend a virtual pre-symposium preparation meeting on Zoom the week prior to the symposium. During this session, participants will confirm their topic, presentation length, technical needs, and format and will receive guidance on preparing an engaging presentation for an interdisciplinary audience.Symposium schedule 9:00–10:00 a.m. | Coffee and Welcome Raw Thrills Lounge and Lobby 10:00–11:00 a.m. | Undergraduate Presentations and Q&A Jarvis Auditorium 11:00 a.m.–12:00 p.m. | Networking Lunch Raw Thrills Lounge and Lobby Participants will join guided conversations with students, faculty, graduate researchers, and other members of the BCNM community. 12:00–1:00 p.m. | Graduate School and Career Panel Jarvis Auditorium Panelists will discuss graduate study, professional pathways, and opportunities for students interested in new media and related fields.How to apply Please submit a brief proposal through this form (https://airtable.com/app4eJHCOwKNbJ6Bl/pag2GIgRvnCUrNx4B/form). You will be asked for the following information: - Your name, major, year, and a short bio - A working title for your presentation - A short description of your project and its connection to new media - Your preferred presentation format and any anticipated technical needs - The name of any collaborators or supervisors, if applicable The deadline to submit proposals is September 2, 2026.Attending as an observer All students, staff, and faculty are welcome and encouraged to attend the symposium as observers. Register for the symposium as a non-presenter (https://forms.gle/4MqxMGBMzrdohfBe8)! Please register by September 9 if you plan on attending the lunch portion of the day.Contact Questions about the symposium or application? Contact New Media Working Group coordinators Chloé Mauvais (chloe.mauvais [​at​] berkeley.edu (https://bcnm.berkeley.edu/events/109/special-events/6656/bcnm-undergraduate-research-symposium#)) and Alexis Wood (aew78 [​at​] berkeley.edu (https://bcnm.berkeley.edu/events/109/special-events/6656/bcnm-undergraduate-research-symposium#)). Questions about BCNM? Contact Associate Director Aaron Fai (afai [​at​] berkeley.edu (https://bcnm.berkeley.edu/events/109/special-events/6656/bcnm-undergraduate-research-symposium#)).

events.title: Probabilistic Operator Algebra Seminar: Entropy and large deviations for random unitary representations
events.location: to attend via Zoom email David Jekel (daj@math.ku.dk) remote on-line talk
events.description: Speaker: Tim Austin, University of WarwickThis talk will be an introduction to "almost periodic entropy". This quantity is defined for positive definite functions on a countable group, or more generally for positive functionals on a separable C*-algebra. It is an analog of Lewis Bowen's "sofic entropy" from ergodic theory. This analogy extends to many of its properties but some important differences also emerge. I will not assume any prior knowledge about sofic entropy. After setting up the basic definition, I will focus on the special case of finitely generated free groups, about which the most is known. For free groups, results include a large deviations principle in a fairly strong topology for uniformly random representations. This, in turn, offers a new proof of the Collins-Male theorem on strong convergence of independent tuples of random unitary matrices, and a large deviations principle for operator norms to accompany that theorem.

events.title: CSLS Speaker Series: "The Distribution of Federally-Insured Mortgages: 1935-1975, Evidence from Local Land Records"
events.organizer: Center for the Study of Law and Society
events.description: featuring Omer Ali, Assistant Professor of Economics, University of PittsburghAbstract: This project develops a novel dataset of federally-insured mortgages from 1935 to 1975 by digitizing local land records from county recorders of deeds across a geographically diverse set of U.S. counties. Despite the Federal Housing Administration (FHA) and Veterans Administration (VA) programs accounting for up to 50% of all mortgages for some years during this period, systematic borrower-level data has been unavailable due to a lack of federal records and decentralized county recording systems. Using a new pipeline that deploys large language models to digitize scanned mortgages, we identify and extract information from FHA-insured and VA-guaranteed mortgages, geolocate properties, and link borrowers to full-count Census data from 1940 and 1950. This produces the first comprehensive address- and borrower-level dataset beyond 1940. We investigate the share of Black borrowers among FHA and VA mortgage recipients, characterize the spatial distribution of mortgages across neighborhoods that vary in racial composition and HOLC ratings, and examine the demographic and socioeconomic characteristics of borrowers. The analysis enhances our understanding of how federal housing policy shaped metropolitan development and racial inequality during the New Deal and Civil Rights eras. (Joint with Jacob Faber, Andreas Ferrara, Jonathan Rose, Thomas Storrs, Katherine Thomas, Gabrielle Toborg, Randall Walsh, and Wenfei Xu)

events.title: Condensed Matter Seminar with Eli Yablonovitch: Can Physics Expedite Artificial Intelligence?
events.description: Can Physics Expedite Artificial Intelligence? Abstract: Artificial Intelligence (AI) requires intensive optimization calculations, which now demands nuclear power for the data centers. Logic functions, storage, and data communications each consume ~1pJ/bit, about 6 orders of magnitude higher than the Landauer Limit. This gives rise to 25MW in a Data Center versus the 25Watts of the human brain. This 6 order of magnitude shortfall is owing to the transistor being a flawed switch. Overcoming this shortfall should be deemed a "Grand Challenge of Condensed Matter Physics". New approaches are beginning to emerge in the context of Artificial Intelligence.

events.title: Seminar 271, Development: Michelle Layvant - "Committed to Education: School Fees, Vouchers, and the Timing of Cash Transfers"
events.description: Abstract: Primary-school dropout remains widespread across Sub-Saharan Africa, with school fees a major barrier to completion. In an experiment with 2,000 parents and children in Eastern Uganda, we study whether time-inconsistent preferences help explain why school fees go unpaid. Before randomization, we elicit each parent's willingness to pay for two restrictions on an unconditional cash transfer: delaying the cash until the fee date, and, holding timing fixed, earmarking it as a voucher of equal monetary value paid directly to the school. We find positive willingness to pay for both restrictions. We then randomize parents to the three transfers or a control group. Both cash transfers modestly increase fee payment, with no additional effect from delaying cash until fees are due. In contrast, the voucher sharply increases fee payment and is the only transfer to reduce within-term dropout, cutting it by more than half. All transfers increase school attendance. We interpret parents' choices through a quasi-hyperbolic discounting model in which demand for these restrictions reveals that parents are at least partially sophisticated about their own time inconsistency.

events.title: Towards breaking the curses of dimensionality in dynamic programming (Nir Halman, Bar-Ilan University)
events.description: Title: Towards breaking the curses of dimensionality in dynamic programmingAbstract:The term "curse of dimensionality", coined by Richard Bellman in 1957, refers to various phenomena that arise when analyzing dynamic programs in high dimensional spaces that do not occur in low dimensional settings. This term was later on adopted in other domains, such as machine learning and data mining, to describe somewhat similar effects. While these phenomena do make problems harder, they sometimes leave the door open for approximation schemes. In this talk I'll survey a few classes of multidimensional Dynamic Programs that do admit approximation schemes, and mention a few promising future directions to characterize more such classes.Bio: Nir Halman is an associate professor at the faculty of Engineering, Bar-Ilan University. He received his Ph.D. degree in Mathematics from Tel Aviv University. His research interests focus on mathematical optimization in general, and in particular – on designing efficient (approximation) algorithms for subclasses of mathematical programming problems.

events.title: Dissertation Talk: Verifying Secure Execution for Systems with Untrusted Components
events.description: The question of trust lies at the center of modern systems: they rely on complex components that may be compromised by an adversary. Even when one component cannot be trusted, trust in the system's behavior naturally falls apart. Techniques that enable verification of expected behavior address this challenge. To this end, we introduce new techniques for efficiently verifying secure execution across a variety of systems, from cryptographic systems to AI agents. First, we present Whisper, a system for large-scale private telemetry in the two-server setting that achieves orders of magnitude reduction in server-to-server communication when verifying that measurements are individually well-formed. After that, we look at the problem of verifiable private information retrieval, where a client privately fetches information from a remote server while verifying that the server does not cheat. We present a new protocol that reduces the client's storage by orders of magnitude for standard database sizes and a deployment mode to practically bring this technology to millions of devices. Towards the end, we transition to the world of AI agents. We present Pincer, a system that augments agents with a digital twin that verifies their actions against automatically learned user preferences.

events.title: Future Visions: Photography in Nabokov's Invitation to a Beheading
events.description: Future Visions: Photography in Nabokov's Invitation to a Beheading While critics have long noted the overt theatricality of the surreal dystopia in Vladimir Nabokov's Invitation to a Beheading (Priglashenie na kazn', 1935–36), photography plays a no less central role in the novel. The trial and anticipated execution of the condemned man Cincinnatus C. are sensationalized in the photo-illustrated press, and the executioner is himself an amateur photographer. Given photography's negative association with the novel's totalitarian regime, it has typically been dismissed as "bad" art. This talk aims to unsettle this reductive view by showing how the executioner's so-called "photohoroscope" in fact shares certain representational techniques with the narrative, as well as how an encounter with photography launches Cincinnatus's development as a writer. In this talk, the photographic objects on prominent display are taken as an invitation to examine the novel's own aesthetic form.

events.title: Analysis and PDE Seminar: A conditional Lagrangian clock barrier at the $C^{1,\frac13}$ threshold for axisymmetric Euler without swirl
events.description: Speaker: Ovidiu-Neculai Avadanei, CaltechWe consider axisymmetric no-swirl solutions to the three-dimensional incompressible Euler equations, with initial velocity in $C^{1,\alpha }\cap L^2$, where $\alpha \in \left [\frac 13,1ight )$. In a major breakthrough, Shkoller introduced a clock-and-driver framework that he used in order to prove finite-time type I blow-up below the $C^{1,\frac 13}$ threshold. Motivated by this, we define Lagrangian classes of coherent initial data and conditional solutions for which the same mechanism yields a supercritical-critical barrier to blow-up when $\alpha \geq \frac 13$. When $\alpha \frac 13$, the aforementioned barrier is genuinely depleted, whereas at the critical endpoint $\alpha =\frac 13$, we obtain an exponential bound preventing blow-up. In the general case, we formulate a matrix-clock criterion in terms of the smallest singular value of the deformation gradient and show that, under cusp-tail, Dini coherence, near-field compatibility, and bounded transverse-distortion hypotheses, this singular value cannot collapse in finite time. In the on-axis case, the criterion reduces to the scalar clock inequality $\displaystyle \dot J(t)\gtrsim -B(t)J(t)-CJ(t)^{3\alpha }$, which rules out Shkoller-type clock collapse for $\alpha \geq \frac 13$. These results do not enlarge the known Lorentz-space global regularity classes. Rather, they in particular identify the supercritical Lagrangian obstruction dual to Shkoller's subcritical blow-up mechanism in the case $\alpha \frac 13$.

events.title: Physics Colloquium with Aaron Manalaysay: Who ordered that? An anomalous event in the LUX-ZEPLIN dark matter search
events.description: Who ordered that? An anomalous event in the LUX-ZEPLIN dark matter search The LUX-ZEPLIN experiment (LZ) employs the world's most sensitive detector looking for dark matter in the form of Weakly Interacting Massive Particles (WIMPs). Seven tonnes of ultra-pure liquid xenon (LXe) are instrumented to detect scintillation and ionization signals from incoming particles, along with two veto detectors to tag background signals. Though typical WIMP searches focus on low-energy interactions of O(10 keV), there are viable, generic models in which these low-energy scatters are suppressed, leaving higher energy O(=100 keV) recoils as the dominant signal from a WIMP scatter. Additionally, background rates are greatly reduced at these high energies. Analyzing 220 live days of data, we observe one event that is consistent with a 250 keV nuclear recoil, in significant tension with our background models. I will discuss these recent results, what we have learned so far, and what we plan to do going forward.

events.title: 2026 Annual Distinguished Lecture in Astronomy: "The Universe In Us"
events.description: Abstract: Where did the building blocks of life come from? The answer lies in the hearts of distant stars and incredibly powerful explosions such as supernovae, which help spread fundamental elements to galaxies far and wide, where they can spark new life. The talk explores how hundreds of millions of celestial events have forged the elements that make up the Solar System, Earth, and us. Travel deep inside a giant star nearing the end of its life and witness the collision of stellar corpses. From the oxygen we breathe to the iron in our blood, the silicon in Earth's mantle to the uranium that warms our planet's core and helps give our planet its protective magnetic field, we owe it all to the stars! About the Speaker: Enrico Ramirez-Ruiz was born in Mexico, studied physics at the Universidad Nacional Autónoma de México, and pursued his PhD at Cambridge University. He was the John Bahcall Fellow at the Institute for Advanced Study at Princeton before joining the faculty at UC Santa Cruz, where he is a professor of astrophysics and astronomy and holds the Vera Rubin Presidential Chair.

events.title: Construction Inspection of Traffic Signals
events.description: Description Traffic signal construction is a critical component of roadway infrastructure that demands precision, adherence to standards, and proactive oversight. For inspectors, construction managers, and traffic engineers, success depends not only on understanding how systems are built but also on recognizing when installation deviates from plans, specifications, or best practices. Minor issues such as improper wiring, inadequate grounding, or ineffective traffic control can introduce safety risks, trigger costly rework, and increase agency liability. This intensive online course is designed to prepare participants for what they will encounter in the field when overseeing traffic signal construction. While the course does not focus on signal design, it provides essential exposure to design elements from an inspector's and owner's perspective. It is intended to help participants understand how design intent is translated into constructed systems and how to verify that the work is completed correctly, safely, and in compliance with Caltrans Standard Plans and Specifications. Participants can expect practical, field-oriented instructions on inspecting and evaluating key signal system components, including conductors and cables, signal heads, controller cabinets, grounding systems, and pedestrian and vehicle detection technologies. The course also emphasizes plan interpretation at a level appropriate for oversight roles. Participants will learn what to look for in the plans, how to identify inconsistencies, and how to apply sufficient technical understanding to assess compliance without performing design work. In addition, the course addresses coordination with contractors, construction documentation, and communication practices that support CIP delivery and protect agencies throughout project implementation. Through real-world case studies, participants will gain insight into common construction challenges, effective inspection strategies, and documentation approaches that stand up to scrutiny. Led by experienced industry professionals, this course equips inspectors, construction managers, and traffic engineers with the practical knowledge and judgment needed to confidently oversee traffic signal construction by bridging the gap between design intent and successful field execution. Topics IncludeSignal Plan Interpretation & Pre-Construction Activities Reading and understanding traffic signal plans Site assessments and preparatory inspections Electrical and Structural Installation Electrical service installation procedures Standards for pedestals, posts, and mounting hardware Bonding and grounding requirements Conduit and Cabling Systems Conduit installation and layout Cable splicing and termination Pull box installation and accessibility Traffic Signal Components Installation of signal heads, brackets, and supporting appurtenances Vehicle and pedestrian detector systems Pedestrian Safety & Americans with Disability Act (ADA) Signal controller cabinet assembly and configuration Construction Close-Out & Asset Management Maintenance considerations during and after construction Salvage and reuse of components Integration of new technology and smart signal components What You Will Learn By attending this class, participants will gain a comprehensive understanding of the full lifecycle of traffic signal construction-from interpreting signal plans and preparing for construction, to installing electrical systems, conduit, and signal components. Attendees will learn industry best practices for ensuring proper bonding, grounding, and splicing, as well as techniques for setting up signal heads, controllers, and detection systems. The course also covers maintenance strategies, salvage procedures, and the integration of modern signal technologies. Through this training, attendees will be equipped with the practical knowledge and field-based insights necessary to effectively inspect, manage, and support the delivery of safe and compliant traffic signal projects. Who Should Attend Ideal for traffic signal technicians, engineering inspectors, electrical contractors, junior engineers, and traffic signal engineers involved in the design, oversight, or inspection of signal infrastructure projects.

events.title: Organic Chemistry Seminar
events.description: Jeffrey Seeman, Visiting Research Scientist, University of RichmondWas Plagiarism Involved in the Woodward-Hoffmann Rules? In 1981, Roald Hoffmann and Kenichi Fukui shared the Nobel Prize in Chemistry "for their theories, developed independently, concerning the course of chemical reactions". Had R. B. Woodward (1917 – 1979) lived two years longer, he would surely have received his second Nobel Prize in Chemistry for his contributions to the Woodward-Hoffmann rules. In the March 29, 2004, issue of Chemical & Engineering News, E. J. Corey wrote in his Priestley Medal Address, "On May 4, 1964, I suggested to my colleague R. B. Woodward a simple explanation involving the symmetry of the perturbed (HOMO) molecular orbitals for the stereoselective cyclobutene/1,3-butadiene and 1,3,5-hexatriene/cyclohexadiene conversions that provided the basis for the further development of these ideas into what became known as the Woodward-Hoffmann rules." Letters between Corey and Hoffmann in 1981 and 1984 and other relevant information will be shown and discussed. This seminar will focus on responsible conduct of science and the practice of science in today's complex and fast moving scientific, academic, and political environments.The Organic Seminar Series is sponsored by the William G. Dauben lecture fund

events.title: Canadian Studies Student Research Showcase
events.description: Learn about the research Canadian Studies funds through our Edward E. Hildebrand Graduate Research Fellowships (https://canada.berkeley.edu/grants-and-awards/edward-e-hildebrand-graduate-research-fellowship), as recipients present overviews of their projects.Refusing Bifurcation: Mobility, Kinship and Chinese-Indigenous Families in the Pacific Northwest Borderlands Jessica Jiang, PhD candidate, Department of Ethnic Studies In the late-nineteenth-century Pacific Northwest, colonial and transpacific migration routes overlapped and often conflicted with longstanding Indigenous geographies. This talk traces several mixed Chinese-Indigenous families on the Columbia/Interior Plateau across generations, showing how these larger forces shaped their lives and movements. These families found themselves in the crosshairs of both US and Canadian policies that sought to control the movement of Chinese and Indigenous people; however, they also found creative ways to navigate and circumvent these restrictions. Drawing on both Chinese and Indigenous knowledge, practices, and relationships, mixed-descent individuals used their dual heritage to negotiate different kinship traditions, maintain their families, and protect their connections to their homelands.The Gang Exception: Eroding Propensity Rules in Canadian Criminal LawReakash Walters, PhD candidate, UC Berkeley Law The Gang Exception demonstrates how evidence law is applied differently for race and class marginalized accused than for other accused persons. The methodology of the article pairs a systematic content analysis of reported Canadian criminal cases with a content analysis of trial transcripts involving accused with serious charges. Admissibility decisions involving gang-related charges are compared with a separate group of non-gang cases that turn on the admissibility of bad character or propensity evidence arising from a similar set of serious charges. This design helps isolate what might be particular to how courts reason about the admissibility of gang-affiliation evidence. The article argues that the reasoning through which gang affiliation evidence is admitted departs from the principled application of the propensity framework set out in R v Handy: the probative value and prejudicial effect inquiry the rule demands is often thinned or left unstated. Further, courts engage in a unique form of reasoning not present in the comparator cases to justify admission of gang-affiliation evidence. This research further illustrates how the organizational mechanisms that shape criminal legal institutions affect systemic inequality.

events.description: Abstract: The first two entries of the IRF of firm-level prices to firm-level marginal cost shocks are numerically sufficient to recover the generalized Phillips curve Jacobian in a wide class of pricing models. events.title: Seminar 221 Industrial Organization: Felix Montag "Mergers and the Demand for Protectionism"
events.description: Abstract: Current enforcement practice does not consider how mergers alter the merging parties' incentives to petition for trade protection. I document mergers between domestic producers across jurisdictions that are followed by tariff petitions. I develop a model to characterize the trade-policy channel of mergers. Theoretically, a domestic merger raises the profitability of tariffs when offshoring is unavailable; once offshoring is possible, the effect becomes ambiguous. I apply this framework to a merger between domestic producers in the U.S. appliance industry. Empirically, I find that when import competition is weak, the merging parties prefer to lower their own costs through offshoring; when import competition is strong, the merger makes it more profitable for them to raise their foreign rivals' costs through tariffs. The resulting consumer harm is comparable in magnitude to the direct market-power effect. A hypothetical cross-border merger reduces the profitability of tariffs in this market.

events.title: Space Physics Seminars: Shaosui Xu - UC Berkeley SSL
events.description: Title: Miniature Dungey-like cycle and discrete aurora at MarsAbstract: With its non-uniform distribution of crustal magnetic fields, Mars exhibits complex and highly variable auroral patterns related to both planetary rotation and solar wind conditions. Using in situ electron, ion, and magnetic field data from the Mars Atmospheric and Volatile EvolutioN (MAVEN) mission, we show that auroral processes associated with these small-scale crustal magnetic fields can be understood in terms of a miniature cycle of magnetic flux and plasma circulations that resemble a miniature version of what occurs at the Earth. However, at Earth, this Dungey cycle, named after its discoverer, operates in the presence of a global intrinsic dipole field with a strength approximately 100 times stronger and spatial scales roughly 20 times larger. From a universal perspective, the current finding adds an entry to the zoo of auroral concepts that enriches our understanding of the diversity of (exo)planetary plasma and our understanding of how planets interact with their space environments. (If time allows) We will also touch briefly on how we use the Knight relation to explain the auroral electron behaviors at Mars, in comparison to Earth and Jupiter.Bio: Dr. Xu got her PhD in Space Sciences and Scientific Computing from the University of Michigan in 2015. She is currently an associate researcher at the Space Sciences Laboratory at the University of California, Berkeley. Dr. Xu is the Deputy PI of the ESCAPADE mission and the deputy lead for the MAVEN/SWEA instrument. Her primary research interest is the interaction of the solar wind with Earth and planetary space environments, mainly Mars, the Moon, and Venus. She specializes in space plasma data analysis and energetic electron transport modeling. events.title: Seminar 218, Psychology and Economics JMP Practice: Lucio Wasserman "Shrinkflation: What Happens When Package Sizes Change?"
events.description: Abstract: Package size is a central characteristic in consumer goods, and changes in size have implications for consumer demand, welfare, policy, and firm behavior. This paper first develops a method to identify size changes at scale. We apply it to retail scanner data and show that size reductions are considerably more common than increases. Next, we estimate the dynamic demand response to size changes using an event study approach. The demand response to size increases is immediate and stable over time. In contrast, after size decreases, demand has a sluggish response: the size elasticity is smaller in the short term than in the medium term. An incentivized shopping experiment shows that individuals deviate from optimal behavior by responding less to size than to price, and provides evidence of attention as a mechanism. With the experiment, we test policy interventions, showing that displaying unit prices and making sizes more prominent can reduce welfare losses. On the other hand, size change labels generate a bias in the opposite direction, causing individuals to over-respond to sizes and thus generating only moderate reductions in welfare losses. We explain the empirical results with a dynamic demand model that allows for inattention, paired with a supply model in which firms strategically advertise size increases but not reductions, and derive sufficient statistics for the consumer-surplus effects of inattention and related policies. In the short term, the consumer surplus losses from inattention after a median size reduction are equivalent to the consumer share of deadweight loss from a tax that increases the price by 6%. Paper Link:https://drive.google.com/file/d/1_dmfFkjdc4QwcMT6gSoWWerCMXLU5spC/view (https://drive.google.com/file/d/1_dmfFkjdc4QwcMT6gSoWWerCMXLU5spC/view)

events.title: Topology Seminar: Equivalent exotic surfaces in small 4-manifolds
events.description: Speaker: Danny Ruberman, BrandeisTwo S, S' in a 4-manifold are said to be exotic if they are topologically isotopic, but not smoothly isotopic. By the isotopy extension theorem, smoothly isotopic surfaces are smoothly equivalent, ie related by a self-diffeomorphism of the ambient manifold. We give a number of constructions of pairs of surfaces that are topologically isotopic, smoothly equivalent, but not smoothly isotopic. The method shows that they are not even Torelli equivalent (ie related by a diffeomorphism that indues the identity on all homology groups). The ambient manifolds are small: $CP^2 # (S^2 \times S^2)$ and $(S^2 \times S^2) # (S^2 \times S^2)$. We find related examples with boundary; these live in even smaller manifolds, such as a punctured $S^2 \times S^2$. This is joint work with Dave Auckly, Hokuto Konno, Anubhav Mukherjee, and Masaki Taniguchi.

events.title: Harmonic Analysis and Differential Equations Student Seminar: A conditional Lagrangian clock barrier at the $C^{1,\frac13}$ threshold for axisymmetric Euler without swirl
events.description: Speaker: Ovidiu Avadanei, CaltechWe consider axisymmetric no-swirl solutions to the three-dimensional incompressible Euler equations, with initial velocity in $C^{1,\alpha }\cap L^2$, where $\alpha \in \left [\frac 13,1ight )$. In a major breakthrough, Shkoller introduced a clock-and-driver framework that he used in order to prove finite-time type I blow-up below the $C^{1,\frac 13}$ threshold. Motivated by this, we define Lagrangian classes of coherent initial data and conditional solutions for which the same mechanism yields a supercritical-critical barrier to blow-up when $\alpha \geq \frac 13$. When $\alpha \frac 13$, the aforementioned barrier is genuinely depleted, whereas at the critical endpoint $\alpha =\frac 13$, we obtain an exponential bound preventing blow-up. In the general case, we formulate a matrix-clock criterion in terms of the smallest singular value of the deformation gradient and show that, under cusp-tail, Dini coherence, near-field compatibility, and bounded transverse-distortion hypotheses, this singular value cannot collapse in finite time. In the on-axis case, the criterion reduces to the scalar clock inequality $\displaystyle \dot J(t)\gtrsim -B(t)J(t)-CJ(t)^{3\alpha }$, which rules out Shkoller-type clock collapse for $\alpha \geq \frac 13$. These results do not enlarge the known Lorentz-space global regularity classes. Rather, they in particular identify the supercritical Lagrangian obstruction dual to Shkoller's subcritical blow-up mechanism in the case $\alpha \frac 13$.This talk is an extended version of yesterday's Analysis and PDE Seminar, in the sense that it will contain additional details.

events.title: Physical Chemistry Seminar
events.description: Robert Baker, Timashev Professorship in Chemical Physics, Ohio State UniversityElucidating Charge, Spin, and Solvation Dynamics at Electrochemical InterfacesNearly all energy conversion and information processing technologies rely on charge and spin transport in systems that are far from equilibrium. The goal to understand and control these processes motivates the need to develop methods to probe the underlying electron dynamics in functional materials on the relevant scales of time and space. To meet this challenge, we utilize high harmonic generation to produce extreme ultraviolet (XUV) light with femtosecond to attosecond pulse durations. Like X-ray absorption, XUV spectroscopy is element specific, providing chemical details of individual elements in complex materials. To extend this technique to study electron dynamics at surfaces, we have pioneered XUV reflection as a surface sensitive analog of XUV absorption. This method now enables direct observation of interfacial charge and spin transport with surface sensitivity, ultrafast time resolution, and unprecedented chemical specificity. This talk will present recent measurements using linearly and circularly polarized XUV light, which show how spin polarized electron transport increases water splitting efficiency in yttrium iron garnet (Y3Fe5O12) by more than an order of magnitude compared to widely studied hematite (α-Fe2O3) through the formation of spin-locked magnon-polarons and how angular momentum exchange between electrons and chiral phonons generates ultrafast spin polarization in chiral semiconductors. Finally, this talk will describe nonlinear vibrational spectroscopy of interfacial electric fields, which mediate charge transfer kinetics during electrochemical catalysis, and show how together these spectroscopic methods provide a detailed understanding of the molecular features of interfaces that govern non-equilibrium reaction dynamics.The Physical Seminar Series is sponsored by the George C. Pimentel lecture fund

events.title: Seminar 237 - Macroeconomics/Monetary Economics: "Skewed Business Cycles"
events.description: Abstract: Using Census and Compustat firm panel data, we show that the skewness of four measures — the growth rate of sales, employment, productivity, and firm value — is robustly procyclical. All four display a fat left tail of large negative outcomes during recessions and a compressed right tail. This holds across US industries and over 60 countries. Using a firm dynamics model with adjustment costs, risk aversion, and financial frictions solved in general equilibrium, we analyze the impact of first-, second-, and third-moment shocks. A second- moment shock generates a sharp downturn followed by a rapid recovery, whereas concentrating the same total variance in the left tail—a negative third-moment shock—produces a persistent recession matching the depth and slow recovery observed in US data. Modeling recessions as a combination of negative first- moment, positive second-moment, and negative third-moment shocks is critical to match both the cross-sectional moments of firm growth and the aggregate response to recessions.

events.title: Knowing better, doing better? Lessons for police reform from a developmental science law enforcement training program
events.organizer: Institute for the Study of Societal Issues
events.description: Youth commonly encounter police in their daily lives, and one of every four arrests in the United States is of a person under the age of 25. Compared to adults, interactions between youth and police more often lead to use of force and physical and emotional harm—harms that disproportionately burden the economically poor and Black youth who come into contact with police at relatively high rates. Debates over the proper role of police in managing young people have existed for over a century, yet there is little consensus as to what the ideal relationship between youth and law enforcement should be, systematic efforts to alter these relationships have had limited or even perverse results, and contemporary phenomena (e.g., social media, teen "takeovers," and changing parenting approaches) bring new challenges to youth-police relations and reform efforts. This talk brings together developmental science, historical sociology, anti-carceral perspectives, and primary research to make sense of "what works" (and doesn't work) in implementing police reform for youth. To do so, Jacobs and co-investigator Murray will draw on diverse data sources, including interviews (n = 26) and surveys with police (n = 111), and non-participant observation of police training (154 hours) in a California county, sharing preliminary findings from an ongoing, mixed methods, multi-site and multi-year impact and implementation study of a law enforcement training program that seeks to improve police-youth interactions. Implications for scholarship and intervention will be discussed.Leah Jacobs, PhD, is an Associate Professor in the School of Social Work at the University of Pittsburgh, where she leads the Anti-carceral Social Work Research Lab and the Public Social Work Research Collaborative. Her scholarship is at the intersection of social welfare, criminal legal, and community mental health policy and intervention. In these areas, she studies social problems and responses to them, with particular attention to the disproportionate involvement of Black and economically poor Americans, and people diagnosed with serious mental illnesses, in carceral and coercive systems. Her current work focuses on the relationship between social work and policing, and on life-affirming alternatives to carceral and coercive interventions, especially those that prevent system involvement and build capacity among members of minoritized groups. She holds a BS in Psychology from Northeastern University, an MA in Urban and Environmental Policy and Planning/Child Development from Tufts University, and an MSW/PhD in Social Welfare from UC Berkeley, where she was a Graduate Fellow at the Institute for the Study of Societal Issues.

events.title: (Screening) Shankar's Fairies
events.description: Set in Lucknow in 1962, Shankar's Fairies (2021) revolves around the unlikely friendship between a young girl from a privileged household and Shankar, a village man employed as the family's servant. Through their bond and the magical stories he tells her, the film gently explores class, social hierarchy, childhood, and the inequalities of post-independence India. Directed by Irfana Majumdar, the film is based on the childhood memories of her mother, historian and anthropologist Nita Kumar (https://www.cmc.edu/academic/faculty/profile/nita-kumar), who wrote the screenplay and produced the film. Screening with Nita Kumar (https://www.cmc.edu/academic/faculty/profile/nita-kumar) present. Director: Irfana Majumdar Screenwriter: Nita Kumar Language:In Hindi with English subtitles. Year: 2021 Running Time: 93 minutes Event moderated by Paola Bacchetta (https://gws.berkeley.edu/people/paola-bacchetta), Professor and the Chair of the Department of Gender and Women's Studies. ———���–DATE: Thu, September 24, 2026 TIME: 5-7 pm PST VENUE: 10 Stephens Hall —————- SYNOPSIS Against the backdrop of a newly liberated India, a young girl slowly comes to realize the power dynamic between her wealthy family and the man who serves them. Set in 1962 during the India-China war, Shankar's Fairies follows Anjana, a child who has been born into unfettered privilege. She befriends her family's servant, a middle-aged father named Shankar who, while tending to the house's tasks, shares stories that paint a distinct picture of their culture and heritage. Her view of Shankar's position in her home is unquestioned at first, but after his own daughter becomes ill, Anjana begins to contemplate her country's entrenched class hierarchy. Shankar's Fairies is the first narrative feature from director Irfana Majumdar, and is written by Majumdar's mother Nita Kumar, based on her own experiences as a child and the close bond she shared with her family's servant (also named Shankar). ABOUT THE SPEAKERNita Kumar (https://www.cmc.edu/academic/faculty/profile/nita-kumar) is Brown Professor Emerita of South Asian History at Claremont McKenna College, California. She is the author of The Artisans of Banaras (Princeton, 1988), Friends, Brothers and Informants (Berkeley, 1992), Lessons from Schools (Sage, 2001), The Politics of Gender, Community and Modernity (Oxford, 2007), Women, Gender and History in India (Routledge, 2023), editor of Women as Subjects (Virginia, 1994), translator of Mai (Kali for Women, 2000) and Udhar ke Log (Niyogi, 2023), co-editor of Food, Faith and Gender in South Asia (Bloomsbury, 2020), and has published assorted essays, blogs, plays and scripted the movie Shankar's Fairies. She runs the organisation NIRMAN that works for children, families, education, and the arts, and the school Vidyashram the Southpoint, in Varanasi, India, a progressive, "Changemaker School.". events.title: Frank Bösch | The "New Jews": (Post-)Soviet Migration and the Reinvention of Jewishness in Germany since 1990
events.description: Jewish communities in East and West Germany were small and aging in the late 1980s. Only about 400 Jews remained in the Jewish communities of the GDR. This changed dramatically after 1990. Over the subsequent 15 years, about 220,000 Jews and their relatives emigrated from the former Soviet Union to Germany. Frank Bösch's presentation analyzes how the country that perpetrated the Holocaust became one of the foremost destinations for Jewish migration, alongside Israel and the United States, becoming the leading destination in the early 2000s. Based on extensive archival research and interviews, the presentation shows how German officials shaped this exceptional immigration program by granting work permits and social security benefits, and how migrants with Soviet backgrounds experienced life in Germany and reshaped their identities. The talk also examines the agency of those seeking to leave the Soviet Union, exploring the strategies they used to emigrate to Germany and how they circumvented bureaucratic rules. The migration process also generated many conflicts, including with established German Jewish communities, which led to new hybrid identities. At least in the 1990s, expectations on all sides remained unfulfilled. Jewish migration thus became a story of broken expectations. Frank Bösch is Professor of Twentieth-Century European History at the University of Potsdam and Director of the Leibniz Centre for Contemporary History Potsdam (ZZF), a leading research institute in Germany. He is the author of numerous influential books, including several bestsellers. His most recent book examines Germany's relations with autocracies (Deals mit Diktaturen, 2024). Previous publications have explored topics such as the history of the Christian Democratic Party (Die Adenauer CDU, 2001), the changing influence of media (Mass Media and Historical Change, 2015), and global turning points in the late 1970s (Zeitenwende 1979, 2019). He is currently writing a book on Jewish migration from the Soviet Union to Germany between 1970 and 2005, tentatively titled The New Jews in Germany. The Gerda Henkel Lecture Tours were established in 2018 by the Pacific Office of the German Historical Institute Washington in cooperation with the Gerda Henkel Foundation. Each year, the series brings leading German historians to the West Coast to present their latest research and to engage in conversations with diverse academic and public audiences across North America.

events.title: Josette Melchor // Newtemporary: Designing in the Space Between New and Next
events.description: The Jacobs Institute for Design Innovation welcomes Josette Melchor, founder and cultural strategist working across art, technology, cities, and responsible AI. As the founder of Gray Area and now Newtemporary — and a board member of the Burning Man Project — Josette has spent her career shaping experiences that connect emerging technologies with civic life, cultural infrastructure, and public imagination. Her work moves fluidly across spatial strategy, immersive media, curation, and systems thinking, always with an eye toward how culture and technology evolve together. ​In this talk, Josette will explore the idea behind Newtemporary, the notion that everything from culture to place to technology is always in transition. events.title: Bake Sale for Nepal
events.description: In August, following a glacial collapse, landslides caused catastrophic flash flooding along the Trishuli River, displacing communities and destroying local infrastructure, including hydroelectric power stations, which account for 10% of Nepal's power capacity. This event is co-sponsored by the Climate Migration and Displacement Project (CMDP), South Asian Law Student Association (SALSA), Environmental Conservation Outreach (ECO), the International Law Society, the Journal of International Law (BJIL), Native American Law Students Association (NALSA) and Ecology Law Quarterly (ELQ).

events.title: Berkeley Book Chat with Debarati Sanyal
events.description: Arts of the Border (Fordham, 2025) investigates the consequences of unfolding catastrophes across the world and the displacement they continue to produce. Through recent narratives and media representations of the refugee "crisis" at Europe's edges, it tells a new story about those on the move, the technologies unleashed on them at borders, the racialized and colonial histories that inform these technologies, and the artistry with which migrants and allies bear witness to displacement. The book reorients us toward the creativity and movement of migrants themselves — their "arts of the border" — as well as toward the political force of the arts that represent them, whether in literature, documentary film, or art installations.Debarati Sanyal (French) proposes kino-aesthetics as a framework for capture and fugitivity at borders. From kino (to set in motion) and aesthetics (relating to sensory perception), kino-aesthetics conveys the force of bodies in motion and the image in its circulation. Sanyal examines the simultaneity of capture and escape at thresholds of illegalization, from airport detention zones to Calais's "jungle" and the Euro-African border at Ceuta and Melilla. What emerges throughout these case studies is a portrayal of border violence in its racial and colonial forms as well as an archive of refusal, fugitivity, and un-bordered imagining. Sanyal is joined by Damon Young (Film & Media and French). After a brief discussion, they respond to questions from the audience.

events.title: Bioengineering Seminar: Single Cells in Context: A Dyad View that Bridges Single-Cell and Spatial Biology
events.description: Abstract: Single-cell sequencing has revolutionized cell atlases, but it is inherently context-poor: it catalogs cell states after dissociation, while many of the most important biological programs are relational: triggered by contact, proximity, or short-range signaling between specific partners. In this talk, I will present a dyad-centered framework and enabling technologies that treat cell–cell interactions as a measurable layer between single-cell and spatial biology. The central idea is simple: a cell's induced transcriptomic change in response to a partner cell is itself a quantitative readout of the partner's function. If one cell activates, suppresses, kills, rescues, or instructs another, the responder's state encodes information about what the first cell did, often more directly than measuring the first cell's basal transcriptome alone. I will describe our Lab-on-a-Particle platform, which creates millions of standardized microscale assay environments compatible with conventional workflows and downstream sequencing. Using Nanovials, cavity-containing hydrogel microparticles with selectively functionalized interiors, we can capture secreted proteins and binding events while keeping cells viable—enabling secretion-encoded functional screening followed by recovery for single-cell RNA-seq and targeted sequence identification. Building on this, I will introduce Cell-Cell-seq, which uses nanovials to co-compartmentalize defined cell pairs and couple dyad-specific functional measurements with transcriptomic profiling of a composite induced dyad-level transcriptome. By comparing paired interactions to matched single-cell controls, we can isolate interaction-induced programs, infer directionality, and map how heterogeneous immune and tumor populations engage. Together, these approaches provide a scalable route to connect function, interaction context, and molecular identity, offering a practical bridge from dissociated single-cell genomics toward the contextual logic needed for predictive multicellular biology and therapeutic discovery.

events.title: Charting Your Path in a Changing World: Using Creativity & Innovation to Shape What's Next (2026 Fall NOW Encore Series)
events.description: 2026 NOW Encore Series (https://hr.berkeley.edu/development/career-development/workshops) In a time of ongoing change across higher education and public service, the ability to anticipate, adapt, and move forward with intention has become essential. This highly engaging 75-minute virtual session invites UC Berkeley staff to explore how their creative and innovative capacities can help them chart a meaningful, resilient path - regardless of role, function, or career stage. Participants will explore how to shift from prediction to anticipation, using future-forward thinking to expand possibilities while remaining grounded in UC's mission. The session emphasizes change agility in practice: recognizing signals that it may be time to pivot, letting go of perfection in favor of progress, and using learning, not failure, as feedback. Through real-world examples, guided reflection, and practical application, participants will identify small, intentional actions that build readiness and momentum, even amid uncertainty.Learning Outcomes: –Differentiate between prediction and anticipation and use anticipation as a practical, future-forward approach for navigating complexity and uncertainty in their work. –Recognize signals that indicate when to adapt or pivot, reframing change and learning as sources of insight that strengthen change agility rather than as disruption or failure. –Apply creative and innovative thinking to take one meaningful next action, making progress without waiting for perfect conditions while remaining aligned with UC's mission.Registrants will be sent a Zoom link and bCal invite as the virtual workshop date draws near.

events.title: CTML Seminar Series: Jonas Knecht (CTML Visiting Researcher)
events.description: This week's seminar brings another thought-provoking discussion! Join us on September 16th to hear from Jonas Knecht (https://ctml.berkeley.edu/people/jonas-knecht), co-founder and co-CTO of Knit Health and CTML Visiting Researcher, presenting his talk on "Deep Causal Behavioral Policy Learning." The seminar will take place at 12:00 PM in Berkeley Way West, 5th Floor, Room 5401. Abstract: This talk introduces deep causal behavioral policy learning (DC-BPL), a framework that combines large clinical behavior models trained on electronic health records with causal inference to learn provider-specific behavioral policies. We apply the method to an empirical comparison of early- and late-shift providers, using DC-BPL to characterise how clinical action paths differ across shift timing and to estimate the downstream consequences for patients. The example illustrates how learned behavioral policies make tacit clinical knowledge, and its variation under real-world conditions, measurable at scale. Bio: Jonas Knecht is a co-founder and co-CTO of Knit Health, where he leads the AI team building clinical world models (Med-BEAM), a class of model trained on large scale clinical even sequences that learns the tacit knowledge embedded in real-world clinical practice. He is a Visiting Researcher at the Center for Targeted Machine Learning and Causal Inference (CTML) and a Research Fellow at the Center for Healthcare Marketplace Innovation (CHMI) at UC Berkeley. His research combines deep learning, causal inference and behavioral economics. Knit Health grew out of this work and is the vehicle for taking it into hospital settings. Previously he was a PhD student at UC Berkeley working with Maya Petersen and Jonathan Kolstad as well as a pre-doctoral research fellow at the University of Chicago's Center for Applied AI under Sendhil Mullainathan.

events.title: Demography Brown Bag Seminar with Joshua Goldstein and Niklas van der Wagt: "Population Momentum of Replacement-level Migration"
events.description: Joshua R. Goldstein is Maxine J. Elliott Professor of Demography in the Department of Demography at the University of California, Berkeley. He is currently director of the Berkeley Population Center and the Berkeley Formal Demography Workshops and Graduate Advisor in the Department. At Berkeley, he has served as chair of the Department of Demography and the Graduate Group in Sociology and Demography from 2013-2018. He was previously director of the Max Planck Institute for Demographic Research in Rostock, Germany (2006-2013) and a Professor of Sociology and Public Affairs and and Faculty Associate of the Office of Population Research at Princeton University (1996-2006). Niklas van der Wagt is a second-year PhD student in the sociology and demography program. He double-majored in physics and sociology at UCLA, and afterward worked on agent-based models of cellular populations at the Biodynamics Lab at UCSD. He is currently working on incorporating immigration into mathematical models for population momentum, as well as describing uncertainty in fertility decisions. Niklas is also interested in population ethics and the biopolitics of quantification.

events.title: IPSR Colloquium: Ariana Castro, Matthew Elliott, and Nathalia Carvalho
events.location: Room 1102 Berkeley Way West, 2121 Berkeley Way, Berkeley, CA 94704, USA
events.description: Matthew V. ElliottPostdoctoral ScholarDepartment of PsychologyUniversity of California, BerkeleyExperiential and Physiological Measures of Emotion Distancing in Self-Injurious Thoughts and Behaviors.Self-injurious thoughts and behaviors (SITBs) are often motivated by efforts to alleviate distressing emotions, yet the distinct roles of emotion reactivity and regulation are difficult to disentangle. We examined these processes during an emotion distancing task using multimodal measures of subjective emotional experience, autonomic physiology (pupillometry and skin conductance), and functional MRI, and tested their associations with suicidal ideation, nonsuicidal self-injury, and suicide attempts. Emotion reactivity showed limited associations with SITBs across subjective, peripheral physiological, and neural measures. In contrast, regulation-related pupillary and posterior cingulate cortex responses were associated with suicidal ideation, recurrent nonsuicidal self-injury, and lifetime suicide attempt burden, although patterns varied across clinical outcomes. Overall, findings more consistently implicated difficulties with emotion regulation than heightened reactivity and highlighted sensitive physiological measures that may point to specific neural systems for further study.Dr. Matthew Elliott is a postdoctoral scholar in Clinical Science at the University of California, Berkeley, working under the mentorship of Prof. Sheri Johnson. Prior to his postdoc, he completed his PhD in Clinical Science at UC Berkeley and his predoctoral clinical internship through the UC San Diego/VA San Diego Psychology Internship Training Program. His research investigates how challenges to emotional and circadian regulation contribute to vulnerability for mania, impulsivity, and self-injury. Dr. Elliott's work integrates careful clinical characterization, experimental methods, and peripheral and central physiological measures to better understand mechanisms of clinical risk.Ariana Andrea Castro LeonPostdoctoral Research FellowDepartment of PsychologyUniversity of California, BerkeleyEmotion and Reasoning in Mania: Effects of Internal and External Emotion on Analogical ReasoningEmotion changes how people process information, including during analogical reasoning, a process involved in learning across domains and, ultimately, meaning making. Previous research indicates that external emotional information enhances analogical reasoning when it is task-relevant and impairs it when it is task-irrelevant. Internal emotional states amplify some of these effects. The present research examined whether the effects of external and internal emotion on analogical reasoning vary as a function of hypomanic traits. Results may inform our understanding of how emotion influences thinking processes relevant to bipolar disorder.Dr. Castro is a Postdoctoral Research Fellow in the UC Berkeley CALM Program. The goal of her research is to inform models of how and why psychopathology emerges, with a focus on the role of emotional processes. Her work has developed along two interconnected lines of research. First, she examines how emotion influences analogical reasoning, a process through which people identify patterns and form beliefs about themselves, the world, and the future. Second, she studies broader emotion-cognition dynamics across different forms of psychopathology (e.g., how contentment may differentiate internalizing symptoms). She is currently examining the role of analogical reasoning in mania within the CALM Program. She is also expanding the scope of her research by studying motivation, emotion related impulsivity, and suicidality.Nathalia CarvalhoPostdoctoral ScholarDepartment of PsychologyUC Berkeley;Assistant Professor at Pontifical Catholic University of Rio de Janeiro, Psychology DepartmentThe Effects of Individual and Shared Awe on Romantic Relationship QualityAwe is a complex emotional response characterized by feelings of wonder, perceived vastness, and a need for cognitive accommodation. It is often accompanied by a diminished sense of self and a heightened sense of connection to something larger than oneself. Previous research suggests that awe can promote prosocial behavior, in part by reducing self-focus and increasing orientation toward others. Despite these interpersonal consequences, relatively little research has examined awe's role within close relationships. The main goal of the present study was therefore to examine whether experiencing awe individually or with a romantic partner is associated with romantic relationship quality, and whether shared awe is associated with greater relationship quality than individual awe. We also examined whether these associations vary as a function of theoretically relevant relationship processes, particularly self-expansion and inclusion of the other in the self.Nathalia Carvalho earned her PhD in Psychology from Pontifical Catholic University of Rio de Janeiro, in Brazil, in 2024. She is currently an assistant professor at the same university and earned an unpaid leave in 2026 to work as a postdoctoral researcher at the University of California, Berkeley.

Nathalia Carvalho earned her PhD in Psychology from Pontifical Catholic University of Rio de Janeiro, in Brazil, in 2024. events.title: Who Should Train Tomorrow's Archaeologists? Cultural Resource Management, Universities, and the Future of Archaeological Education
events.description: This talk will take place in person at the ARF and on Zoom.Register for online attendance here. (https://bit.ly/ARFtalks-2627) Abstract: Cultural resource management (CRM) archaeologists in the United States have been asking university professors to adequately prepare archaeology students for careers in CRM for over 60 years. Academia has been slow to respond despite the reality that over 90 percent of archeologists work in CRM or for government agencies, and the funding for CRM archaeology vastly outstrips funding for academic archaeology. This talk explores one archaeologist's opinion on the industry's plan to build programs designed to prepare young archaeologists for careers in CRM. What would this program look like? How would it work? What is the industry's capability to carry through on this plan? How can universities respond? I also highlight examples of existing programs that use ongoing public-private collaborations to prepare students for careers in CRM archaeology.
