events.title: Probability Seminar: Victor Ginsburg "Temperature chaos in polymers"
events.description: Abstract: Polymers in disordered media are examples of random Gibbs measures on paths traversing a random environment. Such disordered systems often exhibit intricate energy landscapes rich with multiple valleys corresponding to metastable states. This generic property makes a system fragile and extremely sensitive to perturbations. Namely, a slight variation in external parameters such as the disorder or the temperature causes a profound change in the system, a phenomenon known as chaos. In experimental studies of chaos, temperature is the prototypical control parameter as it is easier to vary than the disorder. However, on the mathematical side, studying disorder chaos is easier as perturbing the disorder amounts to infusing the system with extra independent randomness. In this talk we will report the first progress in understanding temperature chaos in the Kardar–Parisi–Zhang universality class, with the Continuum Directed Random Polymer being the model of study. Time permitting, we will also touch upon an application of our techniques to noise sensitivity in the Directed Landscape, and outline a connection between temperature and disorder chaos. This is joint work with Shirshendu Ganguly and Zoe Himwich.

events.title: Argyris Kriezis: The Invisible Threat: GNSS Jamming and Spoofing in Today’s World
events.description: Events Add to Calendar iCal / Outlook Global Navigation Satellite Systems (GNSS) are critical infrastructure for civilian and military navigation and timing, but their weak signal strength at the Earth’s surface makes them highly vulnerable to radio frequency interference (RFI) including jamming, which blocks signals outright, and spoofing, which feeds receivers false position and timing data. GNSS interference has been recorded for years, but since the outbreak of conflicts in Ukraine, Israel, and Iran, such events have grown in number, strength, and duration. Because GNSS signals serve both civilian and military users, disruptions intended for military targets often spill over, disrupting civilian infrastructure hundreds of kilometers from active conflict zones. This seminar presents research from a collaboration between the Stanford GPS Lab and other universities to detect, characterize, and geolocate sources of GNSS interference affecting civilian infrastructure worldwide. By examining these events, Argyris Kriezis assesses the sophistication, impact, and scope of such attacks. Because interference often originates across borders or in regions where direct mitigation is difficult, the work focuses on developing early-warning technologies that can alert authorities in time to eliminate the source or mitigate its effects on critical civilian and military systems.

events.title: CLIMB + Neyman Seminar with Daniela Witten: Testing hypothesis via orthogonalization
events.description: Please join us for a joint CLIMB + Neyman Seminar with Daniela Witten Testing hypothesis via orthogonalization Abstract Classical hypothesis testing frameworks break down in contemporary settings in which null hypotheses are increasingly abstract, the same data are used to both generate and test hypotheses, and minimal assumptions about the underlying data are made. In this work, we propose a new framework for conducting valid hypothesis tests in broad contexts. We propose to add and subtract external noise generated from a symmetric shift-family to our data, X, to partition it into two pieces, X1 and X2. We provide a generic strategy for orthogonalizing X2 against X1 under the null hypothesis H0, then show that testing whether the orthogonalization was successful provides a valid test of H0 under mild assumptions. Remarkably, this framework extends naturally to the post-selection inference setting with minimal modifications: we simply select a hypothesis on X1, then perform orthogonalization under the selected null. As our approach neither requires pre-specification of the selection mechanism, nor is restricted to a small class of data-generating distributions, it dramatically expands the settings for which valid post-selection inference can be conducted. We showcase the flexibility of our proposal in a number of case studies. This is joint work with Ameer Dharamshi (McGill University) and Runjia Zou (University of Washington). Bio Daniela Witten is a professor of Statistics and Biostatistics at University of Washington, and the Dorothy Gilford Endowed Chair in Mathematical Statistics. She develops statistical machine learning methods for high-dimensional data, with a focus on unsupervised learning. She has received a number of awards for her research in statistical machine learning: most notably the Spiegelman Award from the American Public Health Association for a (bio)statistician under age 40, and the Presidents' Award from the Committee of Presidents of Statistical Societies for a statistician under age 41. Daniela is a co-author of the textbook "Introduction to Statistical Learning", and has served as Joint Editor of Journal of the Royal Statistical Society, Series B. CLIMB Voleon Seminars are organized by the Center for the Theoretical Foundations of Learning, Inference, Information, Intelligence, Mathematics, and Microeconomics at Berkeley (CLIMB (https://climb.berkeley.edu/)), and are generously supported by the Voleon Group. CLIMB addresses new conceptual and mathematical challenges arising at the interface between technology, science, and society.If you require an accommodation for effective communication or information about campus mobility access features in order to fully participate in this event, please contact Naomi Yamasaki at climb-support@eecs.berkeley.edu or 510-710-8488 with as much advance notice as possible and at least 7-10 days before the event.

events.title: EECS Colloquium | Marin: An Open Lab For Frontier AI
events.description: I will present Marin, a project that aims to develop frontier language models entirely in the open from scratch. Experiments and discussions all happen in the open on GitHub and Discord, opening up the process knowledge that is missing from open-weight (and even open-source) model releases. I argue that open development is a better way of doing science that improves on preregistration, reproducibility, and peer review. I will then discuss the design decisions around data, architectures, optimizers, and scaling laws for training our latest multi-hundred billion parameter mixture of experts model. Percy Liang is a Professor of Computer Science at Stanford University, co-founder of Together AI, Simile AI, and Marin, which aims to build frontier models fully in the open. He has made a number of contributions in AI, including the SQuAD question answering dataset, the HELM benchmarking framework, generative agents, prefix tuning, and coining the term "foundation models". His awards include the Presidential Early Career Award for Scientists and Engineers (2019), IJCAI Computers and Thought Award (2016), an NSF CAREER Award (2016), a Sloan Research Fellowship (2015), a Microsoft Research Faculty Fellowship (2014), and paper awards at ACL, EMNLP, ICML, COLT, ISMIR, CHI, UIST, and RSS.

events.title: Combinatorics Seminar: Braid Group Presentations and Triangulations of the Permutahedron
events.description: Speaker: Colin Defant, Harvard UniversityFor each finite Coxeter group W and each standard Coxeter element of W, we construct a regular triangulation of the W-permutahedron. Our proof relies on the theory of total linear stability for Dynkin quivers. We also explore several notable combinatorial properties of these triangulations that relate the Bruhat order, the noncrossing partition lattice, and Cambrian congruences. Each triangulation gives an explicit mechanism for relating two different presentations of the corresponding braid group (the standard Artin presentation and Bessis's dual presentation). This is joint work with Melissa Sherman-Bennett and Nathan Williams.

Knowing your numbers is one of the best ways to evaluate your health by identifying your risk and providing motivation for managing your health. Even if you feel great and look healthy, you may not know what's going on inside. Many diseases are "silent" and affect your health long before you feel anything wrong. Know Your Numbers is a voluntary, fasting health screening including total cholesterol, HDL, LDL, and triglycerides, glucose, and blood pressure. Receive your confidential results (seen only by Be Well at Work - Program staff) and resources for follow-up immediately. Plan for 20-30 minutes to complete the screening. events.title: Gasper Begus: Understanding humans, animals, and machines
events.description: The dual quests – to understand intelligence as it arises in biology and to build it in machines of our own making – have been with us for nearly a century. While neuroscience and psychology seek to characterize intelligence in terms of underlying neural mechanisms and emergent behavior, we still lack a set of principles that can account for how the interactions of many neurons within a brain give rise to intelligent behavior. Meanwhile, modern AI is following a largely empirical path to create a new technology without scientific foundation. While the resulting algorithms exhibit intriguing behavior, the working principles are unknown, usage risks are incalculable, and the path to further development is unclear. The premise of this seminar is that the current century will see the emergence of a new scientific discipline – the Science of Intelligence – that seeks to elucidate universal principles that govern intelligent systems, be they biological or machine, and that this will provide both much needed insight in neuroscience and a solid foundation for technological development. The seminar will meet weekly, featuring speakers from across campus and elsewhere, who will share their views on the open questions, topics of study and debate, and relevant disciplines that a science of intelligence will encompass. Thursday, September 17, 2026 Time: 11:00am Location: 101 Weill hall Speaker: Gašper Beguš Affiliation: UC Berkeley (https://vcresearch.berkeley.edu/faculty/gasper-begus)

events.title: Heather Christofk: Metabolic Regulation of Cell State
events.description: Our research focuses on the relationship between metabolism and cell state. We began by studying how metabolism changes during different cell state transitions – during malignant transformation, stem cell differentiation, and virus infection. However, our work has suggested a more bidirectional relationship between metabolism and cell state, whereby metabolism is not only altered during cell state transitions, but metabolic changes can also drive them. Here, I will present examples of our recent and ongoing work in three different areas of study: tissue stem cell metabolism, developmental metabolism, and cancer metabolism. I will highlight efforts to translate our findings to the clinic, new tools and methodologies we are developing to better study cell type-specific metabolism in vivo, and new questions we are answering focused on the impact of metabolism on cell state transitions in varied biological contexts.Division(s): MTx (Molecular Therapeutics)

events.title: REI Colloquium: Banished Citizens: A History of the Mexican American Women Who Endured Repatriation
events.description: From 1921 to 1944, approximately one million ethnic Mexicans living in the United States were removed across the border to Mexico. What officials called "repatriation" was in fact banishment: 60 percent of those expelled were US citizens, mainly working-class women and children whose husbands and fathers were Mexican immigrants. Drawing on transnational archival sources, oral histories, and private collections, Banished Citizens illuminates the lasting effects of coerced mass removal on three generations of ethnic Mexicans. Ramírez argues that banishment served interests on both sides of the border. In the United States, the government accused ethnic Mexicans of dependence on social services to justify removal, thereby scapegoating them for post-World War I and Depression-era economic woes. In Mexico, meanwhile, officials welcomed returnees for their potential to bolster the labor force. In the process, all Mexicans in the United States—citizens and undocumented immigrants alike—were cast as financially burdensome and culturally foreign. Shedding particular light on the experiences of banished women expelled under claims of their likelihood to become a public charge and links to the outdated coverture doctrine, Ramírez demonstrates that US-citizen women and children were targeted as a strategy to banish entire mixed-status families. Nonetheless, banished women courageously and resiliently fought for decades to reclaim their US citizenship and return to their native country. Nevertheless, banishment often interrupted their ability to pass on US citizenship to their children, robbed their families of generational wealth, and drastically slowed upward mobility. Today, their descendants continue to confront and resist the impact of these injustices-and are breaking the silence to ensure that this history is not forgotten. This is an accessible event. If you have accessibility needs and need reasonable accommodations to participate they will be provided. For more information, and to make a request, please contact Ezra Bristow at ezrabristow@berkeley.edu

events.title: A pelagic paradox: the rise and fall of large animals with shells in the pelagic realm
events.description: In contrast to the benthos, where mineralized exoskeletons have proliferated and become increasing well protected over time, the pelagic realm shows first an increase, then a post-Cretaceous decline in large animals with shells. The pelagic realm therefore diverged from the benthos after the Cretaceous, and also shows a divergence within the realm between large and small organisms with respect to mineralization. This example illustrates a widespread phenomenon of phenotypic obsolescence through time.

events.title: The Once and Future World Order: Why Global Civilization Will Survive the Decline of the West
events.description: The Once and Future World Order: Why Global Civilization Will Survive the Decline of the West Thursday, September 17, 2026 12:30 ��� 2 pm *Lunchtime talk* Institute of International Studies 223 Philosophy HallREGISTER (https://forms.gle/k1UvS6pJUuwKDPXR7) The Institute of International Studies (http://iis.berkeley.edu/) & the Goldman School of Public Policy (http://gspp.berkeley.edu/) are pleased to welcome Prof. Amitav Acharya (https://www.american.edu/sis/faculty/aacharya.cfm) for a public talk at IIS. Since the dawn of the twenty-first century, the West has been in crisis. Social unrest, political polarization, and the rise of other great powers—especially China—threaten to unravel today's Western-led world order. Many fear this would lead to global chaos. But the West has never had a monopoly on order. Surveying five thousand years of global history, political scientist Amitav Acharya reveals that world order—the political architecture enabling cooperation and peace among nations—existed long before the rise of the West. Moving from ancient Sumer, India, Greece, and Mesoamerica, through medieval caliphates and Eurasian empires into the present, Acharya shows that humanitarian values, economic interdependence, and rules of inter-state conduct emerged across the globe over millennia. History suggests order will endure even as the West retreats. In fact, the end of Western dominance offers us the opportunity to build a better world, where non-Western nations find more voice, power, and prosperity. Instead of fearing the future, the West should learn from history and cooperate with the Rest to forge a more equitable order.

events.title: Aakanksha Singhvi: Glial functions in neural health and Parkinson's neurodegeneration
events.description: Glia make up about half the cells of the human brain and impact all aspects of neural circuit form, function and aging. We helped establish C. elegans as a powerful model to study glia in vivo at scale, from single-cell to whole-brain resolution, genes to behavior. I will summarize our prior work in developing the complete molecular atlas of C. elegans glia (first for a metazoan), finding novel regulators of glia-neuron aging, and discovering glial pruning in C. elegans. I will then focus on recent molecular insights into glial roles in Parkinson's disease, and our translational validation of these in human and murine cell-culture models and by human epidemiology studies.

events.description: Join us for a screening of a GAAVANI (https://www.gaavani.com/) film that marks a significant moment in Sikh history. For the first time in 556 years since the founding of the Sikh faith, 31 women travel across northern India to sing Kirtan in all 31 primary musical raags of the Guru Granth Sahib at sacred sites. This film captures breathtaking cinematography, soul-stirring soundscapes, while exploring how these women serve as vital carriers of wisdom, faith and strength - bringing 556 years of legacy into a sharp, contemporary and lived focus. The screening will be followed by a conversation with film producer, Navpreet Kaur. The event will be moderated by Puninder Singh (https://southasia.berkeley.edu/people/puninder-singh), the Community Lecturer in Sikh Studies at UC Berkeley. ————–DATE: Thu, September 17, 2026 TIME: 5-7 pm PST VENUE: 10 Stephens Hall REGISTRATION: The event is FREE but a reservation is required. Please reserve your seat HERE (http://www.eventbrite.com/e/1994097467204/?discount=GAAVANI) —————-SYNOPSIS:GAAVANI: Her Journey Home (https://www.gaavani.com/) follows a diverse group of 31 women—teachers, students, mothers, and community members—as they journey across northern India to perform Kirtan in the 31 primary raags of the Guru Granth Sahib. From the busy streets of Delhi to historic shrines in Amritsar and beyond, the film captures both the challenges and triumphs of this groundbreaking effort. The film explores the relationship between practice, music, gender, and lived spiritual experience. Featuring insights from scholars and speakers such as Dr. Gurnam Singh and Jessi Kaur, GAAVANI (https://www.gaavani.com/) reflects on the "female orientation" of the soul in Sikh philosophy and highlights the deep spiritual significance of sung devotion. The film also honors the role of male mentors and allies who supported this movement, presenting a vision of a community in which women and men are empowered to participate fully in the Guru's Shabad. As a legacy project, GAAVANI (https://www.gaavani.com/) seeks to inspire Sikh children and adults to discover their own musical connection to Gurbani Kirtan and to help ensure that this sacred art form continues to thrive for future generations. Running time 47 minutes. See the trailer HERE (https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=pyeqlAeNi9Q) About the Producer: Navpreet Kaur is a dedicated community leader and media producer based in the San Francisco Bay Area. As a key founder of GAAVANI (https://www.gaavani.com/), she has spearheaded global and local initiatives to raise the female voice in Gurbani Kirtan. With a background in project leadership and a passion for deep personal discovery, Navpreet coordinated the historic 31-women Kirtan tour of northern India and served as the visionary and driving force behind the film production. Her work focuses on bridging Sikh spiritual wisdom and traditions with modern and meaningful community, educational and media platforms.About the moderator:Puninder Singh (https://southasia.berkeley.edu/people/puninder-singh) completed his PhD in Linguistic Anthropology at the University of Michigan in 2024. events.title: Dante's Body: Imagination, Politics, Eschatology
events.description: Over the centuries, Dante's Commedia has left readers with indelible mental images of horrifically tortured bodies. The obvious paradox that there should be no bodies there for the torturing has done little to detract from the poem's imaginative vividness, since the two key literary and religious traditions on which the Commedia rests, classical antiquity and the Bible, both allowed for physical pain in the afterlife. Yet Dante goes to unnecessary lengths to provide theological and philosophical explanations for the existence of "aerial bodies" that could realistically sustain such experiences. Dante's quest for realism on this matter has fascinated scholars, most notably for its direct engagement with the heated debate that, in those same years, divided universities, theological schools, and the whole Church over the person's afterlife existence and beatific fulfillment. In my lecture, I will focus on Dante's striking commitment to human embodiment as essential to defining the person at a time when both theological and ecclesiastical authorities were increasingly shifting toward equating person with soul. The talk will examine how Dante places the body at the center of his theories of imagination, as the epistemological link between the spiritual and the material; of politics, as a natural dimension of the embodied person; and of eschatology, as a social enjoyment made possible by the resurrected bodies. In our time of disembodied intelligences, Dante's voice reaches us from another time when embodiment was "in crisis" and interrogates us on whether there can – or should – be humanity and intelligence without sentient bodies.

events.description: In this virtual conversation, UC Berkeley Professors Wesley Holliday and Kent Puckett will explore voting, choice theory and democracy from two complementary perspectives. This virtual lecture kicks off a new year-long series exploring the idea that the systems and records we often perceive as neutral are shaped by human choices, values, and power. Through conversations about voting systems, archival practices, and historical accounts, the talks examine who decides what is recorded, preserved, remembered, and ultimately understood as history or fact. From the structures that determine how votes become representation to the archives that determine which cultures and voices remain visible or invisible, the series invites us to question the seemingly neutral systems that shape what we know — and whose perspectives become part of the record. Each virtual lecture will feature two faculty experts who will each share a 10-minute "TED-style" talk about their research and then discuss the topics together with a moderator. The final 10 minutes will feature audience Q&A.

events.title: 21st Annual Colloquium on Scholarship in Employment and Labor Law (COSELL)
events.description: What is COSELL?In the mid 2000s, three workplace law professors Joe Slater, Scott Moss, and Paul Secunda developed the idea of having an informal meeting to workshop ideas for research in the areas of employment and labor law. They ended up naming their initiative the Colloquium on Scholarship in Employment and Labor Law, COSELL. ​ Since 2006, COSELL has brought together dozens of scholars each year to present, hear, and provide feedback on research and scholarship in labor law, employment law, and related areas, such as litigation or ADR. COSELL embraces a range of methodologies and theoretical approaches including critical legal studies and empirical approaches (among others). The conference has been held in law schools across the country, from UCLA to Northwestern to Seton Hall Law. COSELL aims to be open to all: there is no charge to attend; it rotates among schools that volunteer to host and sponsor; and presentations can be made by not only professors, but also practitioners and aspiring professors and scholars. COSELL is where the recipients are announced for two awards: the Paul Steven Miller Award to a senior scholar who has shown outstanding academic and public contributions to the field of labor and employment scholarship, and the Michael J. Zimmer Award to a rising scholar who values workplace justice and community, and who has made significant contributions to the field of labor and employment law scholarship. COSELL is an informal organization supported by the COSELL Legacy Committee. The current committee consists of Rachel Arnow-Richman (Florida), Doron Dorfman (Seton Hall), Catherine Fisk (UC Berkeley), Ann Juliano (Villanova), and Nicole Porter (William and Mary). COSELL 2026 will take place on Friday, September 18 (9:00am��6:00pm) and Saturday, September 19 (9:00am–12:30pm) at Berkeley Law in Berkeley, CA. The COSELL Legacy Committee

events.title: A Roundtable on the History of the Far-Right in the US
events.description: Over the past decade, the far right has moved from the margins of American politics to its center. In turn, the topic now transcends the margins of historical scholarship to become a thriving field of inquiry. This roundtable brings together contributors to the Journal of Right-Wing Studies' two-part special issue, "The Far Right in US History (https://jrws.berkeley.edu/issues)," to discuss recent discoveries in the field. Drawing on work that spans conservative Catholic political thought, maternal activism on the right, the transnational circulation of white supremacist violence, Klan electoral politics, American monarchism, and the deep roots of Christian nationalism, panelists will consider what is gained by treating the far right as a subject of history rather than a contemporary aberration, and what remains stubbornly hard to study. How do historians define the "far right?" When does the radical become ordinary? And what do the archives allow us to see about movements with few formal records? Please join Professors Olivier Burtin (Université de Picardie Jules Verne) and Kathryn Olmsted (UC Davis), our distinguished guest editors, as they moderate a discussion on topics in the special issue. Authors and Discussants: -Mary Byrne (Rutgers) - "Moms for Liberty and the Legacy of White Maternalist Activism: Gendered Power and Cultural Organizing in Far-Right Movements" -Faith Lazar (Yale) - "If a Bomb Goes Off in the Woods: Preemptive Counterterrorism and the FBI Sting that Triggered Ruby Ridge" -Kyle Burke (University of South Florida) - "'A Planet-Wide Race War': The Global Circulation of White Supremacist Violence in the Late Twentieth Century" -Chelsea Ebin (Drew) - "Mapping the Influence of Conservative Catholic Political Thought on the American Right" Part 1 of the special issue is available and open access; Look for Part 2, out soon!

events.title: BETR/EECS Solid State Technologies Seminar: Prof. Gitti Frey, Technion - Israel Institute of Technology | A Blend Strategy for Multifunctional Organic Transistors
events.description: Abstract: Organic electrochemical transistors (OECTs) are essential components in bioelectronics, energy storage, mechanical actuation, and sensing, leveraging organic mixed ionic-electronic conductors (OMIECs) to modify bulk channel conductivity via the electrochemical insertion or extraction of ions from an electrolyte. We introduce a novel device architecture based on blending p-type and n-type OMIECs, a strategy that enables significantly improved performance and expanded functionality. By precisely engineering the blend's microstructure through adjustments in composition and thermal annealing, we gain control over phase separation dynamics, crystallinity, and domain morphology. This careful control is crucial for optimizing the rates of ionic and electronic transport, as well as the ionic-electronic coupling efficiency. Utilizing this approach, we successfully fabricated fully charge-balanced ambipolar OECTs, which can efficiently modulate both anion and cation flux within a single device structure. Furthermore, we extended this blending methodology to achieve a dual-operation capability, combining organic semiconductors (OSCs) and OMIECs to create transistors that can seamlessly switch between functioning as an OECT and an Electrolyte-Gated Organic Field-Effect Transistor (EGOFET). The ability to manage phase separation at the nanoscale facilitates a smooth and tunable transition between these two operational modes. Our findings establish a new paradigm for engineering highly tunable, multifunctional organic transistors with enhanced coupling, providing a compelling platform for the next generation of advanced sensing and bioelectronic technologies. Bio: Dr. Gitti Frey received her Ph.D. from the Department of Materials and Interfaces at the Weizmann Institute in 1999. She spent the following three years as a Marie Curie Postdoc Fellow in the Optoelectronics Group of the Cavendish Laboratory, Department of Physics, Cambridge, UK. Since September 2002 she is in the Department of Materials Science & Engineering at the Technion, leading the Hybrid Materials and Devices Research Group. In 2009/2010 she spent a sabbatical year as Visiting Professor in the Department of Physics, Colorado School of Mines, Golden CO, and as Visiting Scientist in The National Renewable Energy Lab (NREL), Golden CO, USA. In 2017, she was a Visiting Professor in the Department of Chemistry and Biochemistry and the Center for Organic Photonics and Electronics (COPE) in Georgia Tech, Atlanta GA.

events.title: Irregular Labor Supply and Coordination in the Workplace: Experimental Evidence from India | Shreya Chandra
events.description: Job Market PresentationAbstract This paper studies how irregular labor supply affects the organization of production in the context of a large apparel manufacturing cluster in India. Production is organized as batch processing lines, where tasks are performed sequentially to produce the finished product. In the status quo, workers choose their own work timings, resulting in significant dispersion in arrival times at the firm. I conduct an experiment with 96 small factories comprising 600 workers, where all workers in treatment firms are incentivized to arrive at work by the owner's preferred start time for a period of 4-weeks. Workers are paid a daily bonus equivalent to 20% of average earnings if they arrive on or before the start time. Incentives increase timely arrival in treatment firms by 43% relative to control firms. These changes are driven by workers who were consistently late to arrive at the firm at baseline. As a result, there is meaningful improvement in coordination of worker arrival times – dispersion in arrival times decreases by 17%. Individual worker output increase for all workers in treatment firms, not only those who changed their arrival times as a result of the incentive. I show that these positive spillovers are generated through gains along the production line from improved coordination. Weekly firm output increases by 29% and delays in order-completion fall by 13 percentage points.

events.title: Music Studies Colloquium: Cesar Favila (UCLA)
events.description: The Franciscan Missionary Voice in Late-Colonial New SpainCesar Favila (UCLA) Throughout the eighteenth and nineteenth centuries, the Franciscan Order in New Spain published small books containing missionary songs for convincing nominal Catholics to confess their sins and amend their lives. While musicologists and historians have focused on the effectiveness of missionary music in the conversion of Indigenous people with no prior knowledge of Christianity, the musical implications of the Franciscan missions of spiritual renewal to the "faithful" in the centuries that followed the conquest of New Spain remain understudied. This talk explores the contents of these songbooks and the broader missionary context, revealing a Franciscan awareness of the effectiveness of song, aurality, orality, and voice to understand divine presence and to convey the Church's post-Tridentine sacramental and reconciliatory messages that aimed at maintaining a faithful citizenry in Spanish territories. This talk also demonstrates how this missionary process provided for the Franciscans to imitate Christ through voice and reveals the voice as a medium for sacramental expression. A reception will follow.

events.title: GIANTS RISING Film Screening in the Redwood Grove
events.description: A very special outdoor film screening amongst the redwoods! Experience the award-winning documentary film GIANTS RISING (https://www.giantsrising.com/) under towering redwood trees, with featured redwood researcher Dr. Todd Dawson.Movie-goers can enjoy special pre-movie after-hours in the UC Botanical Garden (5:00-6:30pm), exploring our collections of plants from around the world, including all three of the world's redwoods–California's giant sequoias, coast redwoods, and the dawn redwoods of Asia. Bring a picnic dinner to enjoy before the movie!Then head to our historic Redwood Grove outdoor amphitheater for an inspiring talk about these iconic trees with UC Berkeley professor of Integrative Biology Dr. Todd Dawson. Redwood Grove Gate opens just before 6:30pm. Film projection begins at sundown, approx. 7:00pm.Don't miss this perfect film experience celebrating redwoods on screen and in person! ABOUT THE MOVIEGIANTS RISING (https://www.giantsrising.com/)The secrets and superpowers of the redwoods Lisa Landers | USA, 2024 | 82 minutes Language: English (minimal Yurok)GIANTS RISING takes you on an unparalleled adventure through the towering majesty of California's redwood forests, crafting a narrative that's rich and as deep as the woods it explores. The film stands out in the documentary genre, breaking the mold with its heartfelt homage to these ancient sentinels […] The blend of scientific exploration and emotional, artistic depth paints a vivid picture of the redwoods, positioning them as natural marvels and central figures in our environmental dialogue." A journey into the heart of America's most iconic forests, GIANTS RISING explores the secrets, superpowers and saga of the redwoods— the tallest and some of the oldest living beings on Earth. It's an epic tale that reveals the wonders of these majestic trees and our dramatic, ever-evolving relationship with them. Living links to the past, redwoods also hold powers that may play a role in our future, including their ability to withstand fire and capture carbon, to offer clues about resilience, and even to enhance our own well-being. Through the voices of biologists, artists, Native communities and others, we discover the redwoods' scientific marvels and our deep cultural ties to them. It's a story that offers insights about the value of our interconnections, and the promise of solutions that will help us ALL rise up to face the challenges that lay ahead. "GIANTS RISINGis a powerful educational tool—stunningly filmed, deeply rooted in science, and highly engaging. I've witnessed firsthand how this expertly woven tapestry of stories captivates both students and lifelong learners, while sparking critical conversations about our relationship to redwoods, to all forests, and to the natural world." - Dr. Todd Dawson, Professor of Environmental Science at the University of California, Berkeley

events.title: 21st Annual Colloquium on Scholarship in Employment and Labor Law (COSELL)
events.organizer: Colloquium on Scholarship in Employment and Labor Law
events.location: Goldberg, Warren, MoFo, Donor Lobby, Steinhart
events.description: What is COSELL? In the mid 2000s, three workplace law professors Joe Slater, Scott Moss, and Paul Secunda developed the idea of having an informal meeting to workshop ideas for research in the areas of employment and labor law. They ended up naming their initiative the Colloquium on Scholarship in Employment and Labor Law, COSELL. ​ Since 2006, COSELL has brought together dozens of scholars each year to present, hear, and provide feedback on research and scholarship in labor law, employment law, and related areas, such as litigation or ADR. COSELL embraces a range of methodologies and theoretical approaches including critical legal studies and empirical approaches (among others). The conference has been held in law schools across the country, from UCLA to Northwestern to Seton Hall Law. COSELL aims to be open to all: there is no charge to attend; it rotates among schools that volunteer to host and sponsor; and presentations can be made by not only professors, but also practitioners and aspiring professors and scholars. COSELL is where the recipients are announced for two awards: the Paul Steven Miller Award to a senior scholar who has shown outstanding academic and public contributions to the field of labor and employment scholarship, and the Michael J. Zimmer Award to a rising scholar who values workplace justice and community, and who has made significant contributions to the field of labor and employment law scholarship. COSELL is an informal organization supported by the COSELL Legacy Committee. The current committee consists of Rachel Arnow-Richman (Florida), Doron Dorfman (Seton Hall), Catherine Fisk (UC Berkeley), Ann Juliano (Villanova), and Nicole Porter (William and Mary). COSELL 2026 will take place on Friday, September 18 (9:00am–6:00pm) and Saturday, September 19 (9:00am–12:30pm) at Berkeley Law in Berkeley, CA. The COSELL Legacy Committee

events.description: Saad Amira (al-Quds Bard College) and Samar Awaad (independent researcher and culinary artist) will be in conversation with Sherine Ebadi (PhD Candidate, UC Berkeley Geography) on decolonial research, oral history, artistic collaborations, and public scholarship. Their talks will take place on-site at the multimedia exhibition, "Jerusalem Through the Seams of Memory" which features the stories of four Jerusalemite elders, and their experiences of movement and severed connections during the time of the Nakba. The event will also feature music, Palestinian poets, and a tour of the SUMUD Mural in Uptown, Oakland led by the muralists and organizers. Refreshments will be served and a taco truck with food for purchase will be on-site. Find out more about the exhibit at bit.ly/SeamsofMemoryExhibit (http://bit.ly/SeamsofMemoryExhibit). Samar Awaad is a chef, storyteller, culinary artist, and researcher, where she specializes in Palestinian food culture. She founded Qam7 Wa Zeit (http://www.qam7wzeit.com), a participatory initiative sharing her culinary research while advocating for food sovereignty and documenting the links between cuisine, memory, and the Nakba. Her research interests include food pathways, political ecology, settler colonialism, and gender in Palestine with a deep commitment to preserving Palestinian culture and heritage. She currently serves as Treasurer on the Board of the Khalil Sakakini Cultural Center in Ramallah. She is a member of global and local storytelling and research initiatives, including the Endangered Palestinian Memories Initiative. She holds a contemporary culinary diploma, an MPH from Emory University, and a B.Sc. from the University of San Francisco. Find her on Social Media: Instagram: @Samar.Awaad (http://instagram.com/Samar.Awaad), and @Qam7_wa_zeit (http://instagram.com/Qam7_wa_zeit). Facebook: Qam7 wa Zeit (https://www.facebook.com/qam7wazeit). Website: www.qam7wzeit.com (http://www.qam7wzeit.com) Saad Amira is an academic and curator who leads the Urban Studies and Spatial Practices Bachelor degree program at Al Quds Bard College in Palestine. His work lies at the intersection of oral history, critical geography, settler colonialism, and political ecology. Amira is the founder and director of the "Endangered Palestinian Memories" initiative (www.palmemories.com (http://www.palmemories.com)), through which he has documented 150 oral testimonies, archived and digitized dozens of family albums and personal archives, and utilized interactive storytelling to present this colorful work. Sherine Ebadi is a PhD candidate in the Department of Geography at UC Berkeley. Her research looks at immigration governance through the lens of legal geography to explore how visa programs are regulated relation to conflicts and war. Ebadi's work focuses on the lived experiences of migration and displacement of Afghan and Iraqi translators for the US military, and the social and psychological aftermaths of serving with the US military in exchange for the promise of US citizenship. Find out more (https://geography.berkeley.edu/sherine-ebadi).

events.title: Film Screening: Contempt
events.description: In Italy, Fritz Lang is shooting The Odyssey for an American producer (Jack Palance). Fritz mourns classical culture but will settle for swords and sandals; like The Odyssey, Contempt is about man against circumstances, and such is the circumstance of cinema. The screenwriter, Paul (Michel Piccoli), meanwhile, becomes lost in Rome, and during his odyssey, his wife, Camille (Brigitte Bardot), enters into a crisis of contempt. Contempt becomes very much Camille/Penelope's story as, on Paul's return, their marriage is dissected. With its colors and compositions, its ruins, its vistas, and especially its movement, Contempt is epic, but it is an epic stripped bare by its director.

events.title: Film Screening: The Hole
events.description: In Taipei there are only seven days in the year 2000, the rain just keeps pouring, a mysterious plague makes people act like roaches, quarantine zones are everywhere, and even the most alienated urbanite dreams dance numbers from 1950s Hong Kong films. Such is the end of the millennium as pictured by Tsai Ming-liang in this part-musical, part-sci-fi exploration of modern isolation, environmental catastrophe, and the failure of communication. The film's apocalyptic Blade Runneratmosphere fits surprisingly well with Tsai's auteurist vision of societal and emotional collapse, as does its pathetically realistic musical numbers, inspired by the films of popular 1950s songstress Grace Chang.

events.title: Film Screening: Bellissima
events.description: "What is acting after all?" Maddalena (Anna Magnani) rhetorically asks before the mirror in Luchino Visconti's melodrama of mother love and misplaced ambition. Magnani's extraordinary performance is its own answer. As a working-class mother desperate to get her young daughter a shot at stardom through a Cinecittà casting call, Magnani turns what might have been a simplistic caricature of a domineering stage mother into a fully rendered character, both hilarious and tragically human. Visconti's direction similarly refuses to distinguish between satire and sincerity; even while it mocks the business of moviemaking, Bellissima is an exquisite example of the filmmaker's craft.

events.title: Film Screening: The Last Waltz
events.description: Martin Scorsese grew up listening to seminal rock DJ Alan Freed, and from Mean Streets onward, his movies have been driven by the power of rock and roll. His love of music is innate and instinctual, so when The Band decided to hang it up after seventeen years on the road, they chose Scorsese to film their farewell concert at Winterland Ballroom on Thanksgiving 1976. The film intercuts the glorious music from one of the all-time great concert lineups with interviews with members of The Band as they talk about their lives and music. The Last Waltz is an elegiac masterpiece that captures a special moment in music history.

events.title: Photography Installation: MEJENKWAAD
events.description: An outdoor installation organized by photographer Michael Light, presented at Memorial Glade at the heart of the UC Berkeley campus. Featuring film stills from the Kōmij Mour Ijin / Our Life Is Here expedition, the installation centers around poet, activist, and artist, Kathy Jetn̄il-Kijiner's embodiment of the Mejenkwaad: a demon from traditional Marshallese legends, said to eat babies, swallow canoes, and terrorize villages in precolonial times. Today, the Mejenkwaad is a powerful figure that bears witness to the impacts of colonialism and nuclear testing and the damage they have caused to landscapes and communities of the Marshall Islands. Jetn̄il-Kijiner is the climate envoy for the Marshall Islands Ministry of Environment and co-founder of the Jo-Jikum youth climate nonprofit. Michael Light is a Bay Area artist and co-leader, with Jetn̄il-Kijiner and David Buckland of Cape Farewell, of the Kōmij Mour Ijin / Our Life Is Here endeavor. He first visited the Marshall Islands in 2003, after globally publishing 100 SUNS, his seminal visual meditation on nuclear detonations. UC Berkeley commissioned Light to do a week-long installation of SUNS at the Glade in 2005, in celebration of the San Francisco premiere of John Adams' opera Dr. Atomic about J. Robert Oppenheimer. Twenty-one years later, Light is thrilled to now be able to bring Marshallese voices to the same UC Berkeley space in response to the violation of U.S. nuclear testing—and Berkeley's direct role in it. Light would like to acknowledge all those artists who collaborated to make the conjuring and performance of the Mejenkwaad a reality on Bikini Island in addition to Jetn̄il-Kijiner, especially extreme vocalist Carmina Escobar, painter Solomon Enos, and filmmakers Brock Scott and Jordan Dozzi. A self-guided walking tour leads visitors through the site-specific installation.Guided Walking Tour with Michael Light September 22, 2026, 6:30-7:30pm — Michael Light is a San Francisco-based photographer focused on the environment and how contemporary American culture relates to it. He has exhibited globally, and his work has been collected by the San Francisco Museum of Modern Art, the Getty Research Institute, the Los Angeles County Museum of Art, the New York Public Library, the Brooklyn Museum, the Victoria & Albert Museum in London, and the Centre Pompidou in Paris, among others. For the last twenty-three years, Light has aerially photographed over settled and unsettled areas of American space, pursuing themes of mapping, vertigo, human impact on the land, and various aspects of geologic time and the sublime. A private pilot and Guggenheim Fellow in photography, he is currently working on an extended aerial survey of the arid Western states with Radius Books, publishing monographs in 2009, 2011, 2015 and 2019. Light is also known for his globally published archival works. His first, FULL MOON (1999), used lunar geological survey imagery made by the Apollo astronauts to show the moon both as a sublime desert and an embattled point of first human contact. 100 SUNS (2003), focused on the politics and landscape meanings of military photographs of U.S. atmospheric nuclear detonations from 1945 to 1962. In 2005, UC Berkeley Department of Journalism commissioned an installation of 100 SUNS on the Memorial Glade in front of Doe Library in celebration of the premiere of composer John Adam's opera "Dr. Atomic," about J. Robert Oppenheimer. In 2023, in collaboration with David Buckland of the UK artist's climate group Cape Farewell and poet and Marshallese climate activist Kathy Jetnil-Kijiner, Light organized and led the Komij Mour Ijin/Our Life Is Here pilgrimage which brought 30 international and Oceanian creatives to five Marshallese atolls in contemplation of climate change, the US nuclear testing legacy, and cultural resistance. It is an honor to help bring Marshallese voices to UC Berkeley, and specifically to the same site previously occupied by nuclear detonations, 21 years later.

events.title: Probabilistic Operator Algebra Seminar: On the $II_1$ factors of Fuchsian Groups
events.location: To attend via Zoom email David Jekel (djekel@uottawa.ca) remote online talk
events.description: Speaker: Dimitri Shlyakhtenko, UCLAWe show that von Neumann algebras of fundamental groups of closed orientable surfaces of genus $g\geq 2$ are free group factors on $2g-1$ generators. The key technical ingredient involves a proof that the element $w=ABA^{-1}B^{-1}$ of the free group $F_2=\langle A,Bangle $ is freely complemented in the group factor: $L(F_2)=W^*(w)*W^*(v)$ for some Haar unitary $v\in L(F_2)$ that is freely independent from $w$. Combined with previous results, we conclude that for an arbitrary finitely generated torsion-free non-elementary discrete subgroup $\Gamma \subset PSL_2(R)$, $L(\Gamma )$ is a free group factor settling a conjecture of de la Harpe and Voiculescu.This result was obtained using OpenAI's ChatGPT Pro 6.0

events.title: Vivien Schmidt | The Power of Ideas and Discourse in Political Analysis—and its applications to Europe
events.description: Vivien Schmidt's new book, The Power of Ideas and Discourse in Political Analysis: A Discursive Institutionalist Perspective (Oxford 2026) provides a sweeping appraisal of how ideas and discourse are used by policymakers and everyday citizens to understand the world, communicate with one another, and mobilize for collective action. It illustrates using examples of scholarly work on capitalism and democracy, international diplomacy and human rights, environmental, economic, and social policy, conservativism, neoliberalism, socialism, and populism. In so doing, the book also provides a discursive institutionalist perspective on the (constructivist) nature of meaning, the dynamics of change and the exercise of power. At a time of major political upheaval, with populism and authoritarianism on the rise, understanding agents' ideas and discourse is even more essential today than ever. The talk will illustrate with examples from the European Union and Europe more generally, both in terms of substantive issues and methodological approaches.Vivien A. Schmidt is Jean Monnet Professor of European Integration, Professor Emerita of International Relations and Political Science, and Founding Director of the Center for the Study of Europe at Boston University. She is Visiting Fellow at the European University Institute and Honorary Professor at LUISS University. Recent books include The Power of Ideas and Discourse in Political Analysis: A Discursive Institutionalist Perspective (Oxford 2026) and the award-winning Europe's Crisis of Legitimacy: Governing by Rules and Ruling by Numbers in the Eurozone (Oxford 2020). Schmidt is a member of the American Academy of Arts and Sciences, a Chevalier in the French Legion of Honor, and a recipient of the Lifetime Achievement Award of the European Union Studies Association, an Honorary Doctorate from the Free University of Brussels, and a Guggenheim Foundation Fellowship. If you require an accommodation for effective communication (ASL interpreting/CART captioning, alternative media formats, etc.) or information about campus mobility access features in order to fully participate in this event, please contact ies@berkeley.edu with as much advance notice as possible and at least 7-10 days before the event.

events.description: This workshop brings together scholars in public administration, political science, and public policy to examine governance and policy in Japan and East Asia from a variety of perspectives. A central aim of the workshop is to foster dialogue across different areas of research. Rather than limiting discussion to highly specialized debates within each field, presenters will introduce the broader questions that motivate their research, share their approaches and findings with scholars working on different topics, and discuss their wider implications. English and Japanese will be used flexibly throughout the workshop, allowing participants to exchange ideas in either language and encouraging open and accessible discussion across disciplinary and linguistic boundaries. events.title: Polly Fordyce: "Using microfluidics for high-throughput and quantitative biophysics and biochemistry"
events.description: Macromolecular interactions drive all biological processes: proteins bind DNA and RNA to regulate transcription and translation, dense networks of protein-protein interactions convey cellular signals, and enzyme-substrate interactions allow all of the chemical transformations essential for metabolism and signaling. The strength of these interactions predicts the timing and identity of downstream responses; therefore, quantitative biophysical and biochemical measurements are critical to decipher these networks, predict how they are disrupted in disease, and manipulate them for therapeutic purposes. Here, I will discuss the development of and results from several new microfluidic platforms that make it possible to acquire quantitative biochemical and biophysical data in vitro for thousands to millions of sequence variants in parallel.

events.title: Provincializing National Literatures: Soviet Literary Universalism and Georgian Alternatives
events.description: How can a literary system celebrate cultural diversity while quietly organizing it into a hierarchy? This talk explores that contradiction through the Soviet project of "multinational literature." At its center is the six-volume History of Multinational Soviet Literature (1970��1974), which presented the literatures of the USSR as equal parts of a common whole while positioning Russian literature as the privileged route to universality. Georgia reveals both the power and the limits of this model. Through Georgii Lomidze, Akaki Bakradze, and Guram Dochanashvili, the talk traces three competing visions of literary belonging: imperial integration, national self-assertion, and a transnational republic of readers. At stake is a larger question: Who gets to define the universal—and what happens to literatures forced to reach it through an imperial center?Zaal Andronikashvili is Professor of Cultural Studies at Ilia State University in Tbilisi and a Research Fellow at the Leibniz Center for Literary and Cultural Research (ZfL) in Berlin. A literary scholar and cultural historian, he works on empire, modernity and the cultural histories of the Soviet and post-Soviet worlds, with a particular focus on Georgia and the South Caucasus. His research rethinks European and global cultural history from the perspective of regions conventionally treated as peripheral, asking how imperial and national frameworks shape literary and cultural fomations. He has published widely in German, English, and Georgian.

events.description: Mike Bollong, Associate Professor, Scripps ResearchChemical approaches to regenerative organ repair Despite perceived organismal complexity, mammals possess relatively poor regenerative potential compared to certain lesser species of Animalia (e.g., amphibians). Indeed, there are many human disease states where an insufficient regenerative response limits organ repair and is determining of disease etiology (e.g., heart failure, T1D, IPF). To overcome these limitations, we have ongoing programs aimed at identifying novel small molecules, drug targets, and repurposed drugs which control the context-specific cell growth and differentiation pathways limiting regenerative potential in a given tissue or cell type. events.title: Lara Fabian (UCLA), "The Caspian Corridor and the Making of a Connected Eurasia"
events.description: In this talk, I explore what happened when expanding empires from Iran and the Mediterranean world met the "circumcaspian system"—a constellation of patterns of mobility, exchange, and interaction that played out around the Caspian Sea over millennia. This framework helps us to see the processes that brought supra-regional powers into ever deeper contact with the diverse communities of the Caspian Sea territories. Moreover, it calls our attention to the network standards that developed as a result of imperial expansion. These norms made sociopolitical actors in the space increasingly legible to one another, facilitating increased cooperation as well as competition. To illustrate this process, I draw on multi-scalar archaeological and historical evidence concerning the eastern Caucasus beginning with the expansion of the Achaemenid Empire into this space and continuing through periods of intense Roman and Parthian interest in the space. The vectors of contact and exchange explored help us understand the shape of regional networks operating in the Caspian zone at different scales and within different social strata, and in doing so allow us to re-integrate the eastern Caucasus into broader patterns that crosscut the Iranian, Steppe, and Mediterranean worlds. But I moreover argue for the importance of the Caspian Sea as a corridor—an oft-overlooked north-south axis of connectivity—in the development of Eurasia in the second half of the first millennium BCE.

events.title: Student Faculty Macro Lunch: "House Prices and Quantities Around the World"
events.description: Abstract: We establish several first-order facts using house price and quantity data for middle- and high-income countries. First, housing units and rooms per person rise with per capita income and then asymptote so that additional increases in income are uncorrelated with housing quantities. Second, growth in housing units is strongly correlated with population growth at all income levels. Third, real house prices and housing expenditure shares rise in near-constant proportion with per capita income. A model with non-homothetic demand for home space, homothetic demand for housing quality, and upward-sloping supply of the unit-quality housing bundle can explain these relationships. A standard model where unit-supply is increasingly inelastic does not match the facts.

events.title: Black Critical Theory Initiative: Cecilio M. Cooper
events.location: 820 Social Sciences Building, the Social Sciences Matrix
events.description: "'Seeing Hints of a Trans Fella': Holotypic Black Feminisms, Stereoscopic Transantagonisms" Impelled by Hortense Spillers' and Sylvia Wynter's interventions, the 'black female', 'black woman', 'black femme', 'black feminine,' 'black girl', 'black mother', 'bulldagger', and so on have become valorized topics of gender analysis while also being intermittently leveraged to camouflage collusion with negrophobic antitrans retrenchment. Suffering deemed intrinsic to both structural emplotment beneath these specific racial headings and the sex-gender binary writ large has long been narrated as stemming from black experiences with coercive masculinization. This talk not only critically appraises black transmasculinity's aporetic function for cis-aspirant parsings of black female/woman from black male/man. Via psychosexual questions about aesthetics, taxonomy, and visuality, it likewise contends with the ways black transmasculinity and black trans manhood have been deployed as foils to ideal trans(gender) subjectivity.Cecilio M. Cooper's first monograph examines the occulted roles blackness and darkness play throughout the visual cultures of alchemy and demonology while the second contends with depictions of black transmasculinity across art and media. They have held postdoctoral fellowships in History of Science at the Science History Institute's Beckman Center for the History of Chemistry and in History of Art at the University of Michigan-Ann Arbor. Their research has also been previously supported by Long-Term fellowships from the Folger Shakespeare Library, National Endowment for the Humanities, and American Antiquarian Society. Alongside their scholarship and criticism, Cooper's creative practice draws from performance, moving image, and sculpture. They completed a PhD with distinction in Black Studies and a Graduate Certificate in Critical Theory from Northwestern University as well as an MA in Performance Studies with a Designated Emphasis in Feminist Theory & Research from the University of California-Davis.

events.title: Physical Chemistry Seminar
events.description: Jin Qian, Staff Scientist, Lawrence Berkeley National Laboratory,Development and Application of Digital Twin & Real-Space KS-DFTThe concept of a Digital Twin originated in industry as a "digital copy of a physical asset." We aim to build a virtual laboratory infrastructure to address challenges in data acquisition, control, analysis, and model-driven interpretation, with a focus on X-ray Photon Science and its potential applications in chemical conversions. This approach enables a bidirectional feedback loop between theory and experiment. I will outline our key challenges and milestones, including: 1) developing quantum chemistry methods to improve XPS binding energy (BE) accuracy, 2) recognizing the universality of chemical reaction networks (CRNs) across systems like heterogeneous catalysis, and 3) introducing our user-friendly Digital Twin for Chemical Sciences (DTCS) v.01 software package, which we welcome collaboration and feedback on. The second part of my talk addresses a major bottleneck in developing and applying Digital Twin, which is the computational limits of conventional KS-DFT with a maximum cell size of a couple hundred atoms. We employed a combination of the real space finite-difference formulation and Chebyshev filtering (CheFSI) technique to solve the Kohn–Sham equation and implemented this approach in a multi-processor, parallel environment. We derived, implemented, and achieved a ~0.15 eV desirable accuracy of ab-initio X-ray Photoelectron Spectroscopy binding energy predictions within the theoretical framework of real-space Kohn–Sham Density Functional Theory (real-space KS-DFT). Our work provides key advantages for calculating accurate core–electron binding energies of exascale systems with 10,000 atoms, hence bridging the knowledge gap between molecules to nanosystems of energy priorities.

events.title: Seminar 237 - Macroeconomics/Monetary Economics: "Reference-Dependent Utility over Prices and the Welfare Cost of Inflation"
events.description: Abstract: Survey evidence documents anger and perceived unfairness among consumers facing rising prices. I study a mechanism through which these reactions can generate welfare losses by embedding reference-dependent demand in a New Keynesian model. When posted prices exceed reference prices formed from past purchases, the same physical consumption bundle delivers less utility. This generates a first-order welfare cost of inflation absent from standard models. I calibrate the parameters governing these losses using an online survey of 1,323 U.S. consumers, with hypothetical shopping scenarios that vary reference prices while holding posted prices fixed. For cost-push shocks scaled to generate peak quarterly inflation of 1% in both models, welfare losses with reference dependence are three to five times as large as in the standard New Keynesian model. To quantify this cost during the recent inflation surge, I build a heterogeneous-agent model with reference dependence in frequently purchased goods and household expenditure shares on these goods that vary with income. Calibrated to match U.S. macroeconomic dynamics during 2021–2023, the model implies an average household welfare loss of 4.6% of one year's consumption, with reference dependence accounting for 17% of the total.

events.title: A Book is Born: The Pleasure of Texting
events.description: Lynne Huffer (Emory) and Mario Telò (Berkeley) had long admired one another's work, but always at a distance. The two met in person for the first time in fall 2025, when Huffer visited the Bay Area. A Saturday trip to the San Francisco Museum of Modern Art sparked the first of what would become thousands of texting exchanges, ranging from reflections on the banalities of daily life to sustained philosophical conversations. This text chain eventually became the basis for their coauthored book, The Pleasure of Texting: Sapphic Writing and Reading at the Edge of the World, forthcoming from Duke University Press.The Pleasure of Texting explores what it means to think across different intellectual, academic, and personal experiences. The authors' collaboration takes the form of a poetic riffing in which intellectual difference becomes generative. The rhythms of digital communication — with its waiting, gaps, and moments of connection — become part of the writing itself. The result is not a fusion of two voices but a juxtapositional form in which the authors play off of one another. In conversation with their editor, Ryan Kendall (Duke UP), Huffer and Telò explore the capacity of texting as a new model of collaborative writing, in which quotidian, obsessive texting is shaped into paragraphs, chapters, and eventually a book.

events.title: Ariel Tang | Scripting Silence: Animals Political and Unpolitical in Charlotte Beradt's Dreamscape
events.description: This talk features the implicit dialogue between the German-Jewish journalist Charlotte Beradt (1907-1986) and her fellow émigré, Hannah Arendt, regarding the boundaries between humans and animals, as well as the ethical limits of anthropocentrism during political crises. Beradt's Third Reich of Dreams, a catalogue of dreams compiled between 1933 and 1939 on the basis of dreams retold by more than fifty Germans living under totalitarian rule, prompts her readers to re-evaluate the unique traits of physiological activities such as dreaming—as opposed to discursive reasoning—in safeguarding the humane promise of politics. While conventional pictures of human nature often fall prey to naturalistic or essentialist tendencies, the vital dialogue between Beradt and Arendt helps to resuscitate the unmistakable normative value of anthropological evidence, the substance of which often escapes the immediate capture of language and yet preserves the hope for political renewal lost in effable experience. Ariel Tang is a Postdoctoral Fellow in the Department of Political Science at Stanford University. Her research focuses on Enlightenment political thought and its legacies, with special attention to questions related to knowledge institutions, education, and the interactions between culture and nature. Her current book manuscript traces an entangled history of the idea of Bildung and the rise of the modern research university. She received her bachelor's degree in Philosophy from Barnard College, Columbia University, and her PhD in Political Science from Yale University. events.title: MEJENKWAAD - Guided Walking Tour with Photographer Michael Light
events.description: Please join us for a guided walking tour of MEJENKWAAD with photographer Michael Light. An outdoor installation organized by photographer Michael Light, presented at Memorial Glade at the heart of the UC Berkeley campus. Featuring film stills from the Kōmij Mour Ijin / Our Life Is Here expedition, the installation centers around poet, activist, and artist, Kathy Jetn̄il-Kijiner's embodiment of the Mejenkwaad: a demon from traditional Marshallese legends, said to eat babies, swallow canoes, and terrorize villages in precolonial times. Today, the Mejenkwaad is a powerful figure that bears witness to the impacts of colonialism and nuclear testing and the damage they have caused to landscapes and communities of the Marshall Islands. Jetn̄il-Kijiner is the climate envoy for the Marshall Islands Ministry of Environment and co-founder of the Jo-Jikum youth climate nonprofit. Michael Light is a Bay Area artist and co-leader, with Jetn̄il-Kijiner and David Buckland of Cape Farewell, of the Kōmij Mour Ijin / Our Life Is Here endeavor. He first visited the Marshall Islands in 2003, after globally publishing 100 SUNS, his seminal visual meditation on nuclear detonations. UC Berkeley commissioned Light to do a week-long installation of SUNS at the Glade in 2005, in celebration of the San Francisco premiere of John Adams' opera Dr. Atomic about J. Robert Oppenheimer. Twenty-one years later, Light is thrilled to now be able to bring Marshallese voices to the same UC Berkeley space in response to the violation of U.S. nuclear testing—and Berkeley's direct role in it. Light would like to acknowledge all those artists who collaborated to make the conjuring and performance of the Mejenkwaad a reality on Bikini Island in addition to Jetn̄il-Kijiner, especially extreme vocalist Carmina Escobar, painter Solomon Enos, and filmmakers Brock Scott and Jordan Dozzi.

events.title: Melanie Mitchell: Conceptions of Intelligence in AI and in Cognitive Science: How They Differ and Why It Matters
events.description: The dual quests – to understand intelligence as it arises in biology and to build it in machines of our own making – have been with us for nearly a century. While neuroscience and psychology seek to characterize intelligence in terms of underlying neural mechanisms and emergent behavior, we still lack a set of principles that can account for how the interactions of many neurons within a brain give rise to intelligent behavior. Meanwhile, modern AI is following a largely empirical path to create a new technology without scientific foundation. While the resulting algorithms exhibit intriguing behavior, the working principles are unknown, usage risks are incalculable, and the path to further development is unclear. The premise of this seminar is that the current century will see the emergence of a new scientific discipline – the Science of Intelligence – that seeks to elucidate universal principles that govern intelligent systems, be they biological or machine, and that this will provide both much needed insight in neuroscience and a solid foundation for technological development. The seminar will meet weekly, featuring speakers from across campus and elsewhere, who will share their views on the open questions, topics of study and debate, and relevant disciplines that a science of intelligence will encompass. events.title: PMB Seminar with Lila Fishman | The genomics of multi-trait adaptation to Yellowstone's geothermal soil mosaic in monkeyflowers
events.description: Environmental mosaics can generate strong divergent selection on plant traits even in the face of cross- habitat gene flow, leading to microgeographic local adaptation and (perhaps) incipient speciation. Here, we use yellow monkeyflower adaptation to the fine-scaled yet physically-extreme mosaic of soil conditions in the geyser basins of Yellowstone National Park to explore fundamental questions about the genomic and molecular mechanisms of adaptation to extreme conditions. For two traits with simple genetic bases (trichome density and minimum critical photoperiod for flowering), candidate variants in predictable molecular pathways underlie dramatic phenotypic divergence over a 100m scale gradient. In contrast, a novel multi-gene locus (out6 supergene) co-ordinates plant architecture and phenological traits underlying a unique-to-Yellowstone thermal annual strategy. The out6 locus draws on both old (but novel relative to known life-history polymorphisms) standing variation and recent introgression to confer adaptation to extreme thermal soils, and contains several strong functional candidates. Finally, although Yellowstone thermal annuals are highly specialized to the unique niche created by winter snowmelt on hot soils, thus escaping summer's deadly heat and drought, they have also evolved remarkable xylem drought/heat resistance. Together, these instances of extreme local adaptation provide a composite picture of how different plant traits and pathways evolve in response to novel environments.

events.title: J. David Creswell | Allostatic Lift: When Stress Makes Us Stronger
events.location: Berkeley Way West (2121 Berkeley Way), Room 1102
events.description: Institute of Personality and Social Research ColloquiumJ. David Creswell, William S. Dietrich II Professor in Psychology and Neuroscience, Carnegie Mellon UniversityAllostatic Lift: When Stress Makes Us Stronger Most of us treat stress as something to avoid, but that isn't the whole story. We seek stress out on roller coasters, in hard exercise workouts, and increasingly in wellness pursuits like cold plunges and saunas. This talk asks when stress flips from harmful to helpful, and what it takes to shift from allostatic load to allostatic lift. Drawing on physiology, toxicology, and psychology, I'll describe how low doses of intermittent stress, paired with real recovery, can improve a wide range of adaptive outcomes. Contemporary theories on resilience emphasize bouncing back to where we started. I'll make the case for a different possibility: that stress under the right conditions doesn't return us to baseline, it lifts us above it. Dr. David Creswell is the William Dietrich II Professor of Psychology and Neuroscience at Carnegie Mellon University. As director of the Health and Human Performance Laboratory, his work focuses on understanding what makes people resilient under stress. His work focuses on basic and translational studies of stress management strategies and interventions in healthy and patient populations. David received four early career awards for his scientific contributions, from the American Psychological Association, the American Psychosomatic Society, the Association for Psychological Science, and the Social Personality Health Network.If you require an accommodation for effective communication (ASL interpreting/CART captioning, alternative media formats, etc.) or information about campus mobility access features in order to fully participate in this event, please contact Ore Carmi [Tel: 510-642-5050; Email: orecarmi@berkeley.edu] with as much advance notice as possible and at least 7-10 days in advance of the event.

events.title: Discrimination as Exploitation – Talk with Prof. Diana Reddy
events.organizer: The Law and Political Economy Society (LPE Soc)
events.description: Prof. Diana Reddy will present an anti-discrimination paradigm for the bad jobs economy. Sixty years after Title VII became law, Black, Latino, and other workers of color are dramatically overrepresented in gig, contingent, and sub-minimum-wage work, and women still predominate in the forty lowest-paying occupations in the American economy. Most scholarship on the failures of antidiscrimination law focuses either on the evolving nature of prejudice or on judicial erosion of pro-plaintiff doctrines. However, Reddy argues that discrimination law fails the workers who need it most because it remains premised on an increasingly outdated understanding of where, why, and how labor market discrimination predominates. Join us for lunch as Prof. Reddy presents her most recent work. RSVP here.

events.title: Sappho and Critical Theory
events.description: Taking inspiration from the Sapphic collages of Lynne Huffer on display at the Townsend Center through May 2027, this symposium gathers together scholars working at the intersection of philosophy, literature, and creative practice. Speakers reflect on the ways in which Sappho and the Sapphic tradition have contributed in subterranean ways to counterintuitive modes of thinking — and thus to the radical work of critical theory, broadly defined. Because so little of her work survives intact, Sappho has long been particularly available for reinterpretation. Engaging with this rich field of possibility, panelists ask: can we see Sappho as a philosopher or critical theorist who preemptively contests the all-male tradition that brackets her in the domain of ancient poetry? Can we approach her oeuvre as a practice of feminist and transfeminist production that problematizes the very distinction between poetry and philosophy? How does an approach that emphasizes the discontinuous and fragmentary state of the archive change our perceptions of Sappho — such as her traditional association with Victorian and post-Victorian models of white lesbianism? How can a fresh return to Sappho help us navigate a moment in which gender is increasingly entangled with fear, anxiety, and political contestation? Following the symposium, audience members are invited to the Townsend Center for a reception to celebrate the opening of the exhibition, Thinking with Sappho: Lynne Huffer and the Art of Collage. Participants:Judith Butler, UC BerkeleyPenelope Deutscher, Northwestern UniversityLynne Huffer, Emory UniversityRanjana Khanna, Duke UniversitySalar Mamemi, UC BerkeleyVictoria Rimell, University of WarwickMario Telò, UC Berkeley
