events.title: Geography Colloquia Series - The Futures of Black Internationalism and Global South Solidarity
events.description: This project examines the international dimensions of Black radicalism and the prospects and complications of multilateral solidarity in the 21st century. 2025 and 2026 have seen the acceleration of draconian immigration policies and the reinforced legitimacy and expansion of police and prison institutions in the U.S. These developments have demonstrated how the carceral state and western imperialism operate as collaborative forces. The fates of racialized communities in the U.S. and oppressed communities throughout the Global South are therefore deeply interconnected. This project engages participant-observer methods that involve delegations of Los Angeles youth activists in immersive traveling experiences to critical locations of Black radical developments. These delegations endeavored to connect and build community with local activists, artists, and farmers and to engage the Black radical tradition as a precondition for effective and meaningful solidarity in advancing movements for sovereignty, self-determination, reparations, and economic justice. These locations include Cuba, Puerto Rico, and South Africa.Gabriel is the UC Chancellor's Postdoctoral Fellow in the Department of African American and African Studies at UC Davis and he studies Pan Africanism, the Black radical tradition, Marxist theory, abolition theory, and Caribbean and African decolonization. He earned his Ph.D. in African Diaspora Studies and Critical Theory at UC Berkeley.

events.title: CLIMB + Neyman + EECS Seminar with Susan Murphy: Online Reinforcement Learning for Digital Health Interventions in the Dyadic Setting
events.description: Please join us for a joint CLIMB + Neyman + EECS Seminar with Susan Murphy Online Reinforcement Learning for Digital Health Interventions in the Dyadic Setting Abstract We present our ongoing work on the development of an online reinforcement learning (RL) algorithm that personalizes delivery of interventions sequentially, over time, to members of a dyad. The RL algorithm is one component in the design of the digital health intervention. Different RL components target different elements of the dyad; these elements are a target individual, a carepartner and their relationship. The RL algorithm is a multi-agent RL algorithm in which the 3 agents make decisions on the 3 elements of the dyad. We incorporate domain knowledge in the form of approximal causal directed acyclic graphs to speed up online learning in this sparse data setting. This work is motivated by our development of the ADAPTS-HCT multi-agent RL algorithm, designed to improve medication adherence by young adults who have undergone a blood and bone marrow transplant. The RL algorithm will be deployed in a clinical trial in late summer 2026. BioSusan A. Murphy is Mallinckrodt Professor of Statistics and of Computer Science and Associate Faculty at the Kempner Institute, Harvard University. Her research focuses on improving sequential decision making via the development of online, real-time reinforcement learning algorithms. Her lab is involved in multiple deployments of these algorithms in digital health. She is a member of the US National Academy of Sciences and of the US National Academy of Medicine. In 2013 she was awarded a MacArthur Fellowship for her work on experimental designs to inform sequential decision making. She is a Fellow of the College on Problems in Drug Dependence, Past-President of Institute of Mathematical Statistics, Past-President of the Bernoulli Society and a former editor of the Annals of Statistics. CLIMBSeminars are organized by the Center for the Theoretical Foundations of Learning, Inference, Information, Intelligence, Mathematics, and Microeconomics at Berkeley (CLIMB),. CLIMB addresses new conceptual and mathematical challenges arising at the interface between technology, science, and society. The Neyman Seminar (https://statistics.berkeley.edu/research/seminars) is organized by the Statistics Department and covers the range of topics from the applications of statistics to theory. The EECS Colloquium (https://eecs.berkeley.edu/research/colloquium/) is dedicated to hosting presentations at the intersection of Electrical Engineering and Computer Science. The EECS Colloquium provides an opportunity for an exchange of ideas between the department community and the outside world. events.title: Creating a political community of fate in care and caregiving
events.description: With Margaret Levi, Emerita Professor of Political Science, Stanford University Caregiving is essential to the health and well-being of society. It shapes how we raise our children and how we tend to the ill, elderly, and disabled in our families and communities. We rely on paid caregivers in health care, education, and government services to support those who need care beyond what families can provide. Caregiving is also a fundamental human experience: Almost all of us will both care for others and be cared for during our lives. But despite the importance of care work in all its forms — paid and unpaid, in our families, in health care, in education and public services — and despite the demographic changes speeding us toward a care crisis, this work has been largely invisible in the social and human sciences. The solution, argues political scientist Margaret Levi, is to understand care as a widely shared interest and lived experience that can become the basis of an expanded and inclusive community of fate in which people come to recognize a societal responsibility for those in need, even if they are strangers or unlikely to be able to reciprocate. In this talk, Levi will explore the conditions for creating such an expanded and inclusive community of fate in care and the political economic implications of such a strategy.Register Now (https://forms.gle/GJcUtGC8AxirUZiu7) About the speaker Margaret Levi is emerita professor of political science at Stanford University and a senior at the Center on Democracy, Development and the Rule of Law and the Freeman Spogli Institute for International Studies. She is the former Sara Miller McCune Director of the Center for Advanced Study in the Behavioral Sciences (CASBS), where she remains a faculty fellow, and is a senior fellow at the Woods Institute. Levi's research explores how organizations and governments provoke member willingness to act beyond material interest. She is the author or coauthor of numerous articles and six books, including most recently, A Moral Political Economy (Cambridge, 2021). Levi is the winner of the 2019 Johan Skytte Prize and 2020 Falling Walls Prize for Breakthrough of the Year in Social Sciences and Humanities. She became a fellow of the National Academy of Sciences in 2015, the British Academy in 2022, the American Academy of Arts and Sciences in 2001, the American Academy of Political and Social Science in 2017, and the American Philosophical Society in 2018. She was a John Simon Guggenheim Fellow in 2002. She served as president of the American Political Science Association from 2004 to 2005. Levi was the general editor of Cambridge Studies in Comparative Politics. She is co-general editor of the Annual Review of Political Science and on the editorial board of PNAS. She serves on the boards of the Berggruen Institute, the Center for Advanced Studies in the Social Sciences (CEACS), the Research Council of the Canadian Institute for Advanced Research (CIFAR), and CORE Economics.

events.title: MBN Seminar: Identification of Novel Targets to Reverse Hepatic Fibrogenesis
events.description: Dr. Jennifer Y. Chen, Associate Professor, Department of Medicine, Division of Gastroenterology and Hepatology, UC San Francisco Dr. Jennifer Y. Chen is a physician-scientist and hepatologist at the University of California, San Francisco (UCSF). She completed her medical training at Harvard, where she also pursued postdoctoral research in hepatic stellate cell biology and the molecular mechanisms of liver fibrogenesis. Her research program integrates basic, translational, and clinical investigation to advance precision medicine for patients with chronic liver disease. Focusing on the cellular and molecular pathways that drive hepatic fibrosis, her laboratory is developing novel antifibrotic therapies through collaborations with medicinal chemists to design and optimize small-molecule inhibitors that target key fibrogenic pathways. In parallel, her team is discovering and validating biomarkers that improve the diagnosis, risk stratification, and therapeutic monitoring of patients with liver fibrosis. Her work aims to accelerate the translation of mechanistic discoveries into innovative, personalized treatments that improve outcomes for patients with chronic liver disease.

events.title: Remembering the Future: Nuclear Testing, Rising Seas, and The Marshall Islands; Artist and Curator Led Tour with Mark Klett and William L. Fox
events.description: Register Here At Giannini Hall, 36 photographs selected from the recently published Remembering the Future: Nuclear Testing, Rising Seas, and The Marshall Islands (Radius Books, © 2026) by Mark Klett and William L. Fox extend the two men's decades-long collaboration tracing the nuclear history of the American West and the broader Pacific sphere. Installed along the building's main hallway, the images move between the physical remains of nuclear testing—bunkers, craters, camera towers reclaimed by jungle—and the everyday textures of Marshallese life: canoe building, weaving, seawalls raised by hand. Paired with archival images from the testing era and drawn from Fox's field notes and essays, the photo essay holds both histories at once: the violence of nuclear history, and the resilience of a culture that continues to inhabit these islands. Tour will be opened with words from Dean David Ackerly, climate change biologist and professor professor in the departments of Integrative Biology and Environmental Science, Policy, and Management and Dean of the Rausser College of Natural Resources at UC Berkeley. Mark Klett is a photographer interested in the intersection of places, history and time. His background includes working as a geologist before turning to photography. Klett has received fellowships from the Guggenheim Foundation, the Pollock-Krasner Foundation, the National Endowment for the Arts, and the Japan/US Friendship Commission. His work has been exhibited and published widely in the United States and internationally, and is held in over eighty museum collections worldwide. He is the author/co-author of twenty books.Klett is Regents' Professor Emeritus at Arizona State University where he taught for forty years. This event is part of Komij Mour Ijiin/Our Life is Here, a year-long series of exhibitions, installations, courses, and public programs across UC Berkeley during the 2026–27 academic year. Guided by the Environmental Arts and Humanities Initiative, the series centers Marshallese artists and acts of cultural return through satellite exhibitions and installations at Doe Library, BAMPFA, Giannini Hall, Memorial Glade, and Worth Ryder Gallery; a film screening at the School of Journalism featuring responses from faculty and artists; and allied events and courses across campus. Together, these programs invite the UC Berkeley community to engage with Marshallese histories and perspectives while exploring nuclear legacies, climate change, cultural resilience, and our shared futures. The initiative will culminate in Fall 2027 with the full Komij Mour Ijiin/Our Life is Here exhibition at the David Brower Center, incorporating critical and creative contributions from the UC Berkeley community. For questions or accessibility related inquiries please contact Iliana Morton - ilianamorton@berkeley.edu (mailto:ilianamorton@berkeley.edu)"Remembering the Future" photographs by Mark Klett and text by William Fox, Radius Books. events.title: Living Literature: Roland Barthes, Citation, and the Reading of Everyday Life | A Talk with Professor John Lurz (Tufts)
events.description: Please join the UC Berkeley Department of English at 5 pm in Wheeler Hall, Room 300, for "Living Literature: Roland Barthes, Citation, and the Reading of Everyday Life," a talk with Professor John Lurz (Tufts). John Lurz's lecture, drawn from his recent book The Barthes Fantastic: Literature, Criticism, and the Practice of Language (Chicago, 2025), revisits the writings of Roland Barthes to examine citation as an intellectual practice that mobilizes fragments of particular texts to galvanize our conventional or mythologized sense of the world. Enlarging our sense of what we learn as students of literature, Lurz introduces a new conceptual category or way of thinking that he calls "the fantastic," in which the texts we read come to inform the texture of our lives.

events.title: Film Screening: It Will Be Better Before and Temo Re
events.description: It Will Be Better Before began as a collaboration between two directors. After five years, one of the directors, Keto Kipiani, re-edited and modified the film, sharing her perspective and feelings throughout the creation process. "The title, with its mixed tenses that collapse time, conveys the confused desperation of a future torn from one's control … a personal story about hanging onto glimmers of meaning but also, implicitly and inevitably, a national one" (Carmen Gray, Senses of Cinema). With Temo Re, photographer and filmmaker Anka Gujabidze creates a multifaceted portrait of Georgia's capital city, Tbilisi. The protagonist, an actor who earns his living as a motorcycle courier, is played by Temo Rekhviashvili, the author of Courier's Tales, the novel upon which the film is based. Composed of thousands of black-and-white still images, this unique film won the Best Short Film Award when it premiered at the International Film Festival Rotterdam.

events.title: Maayan Levy: Toward the development of metabotherapy
events.description: Diet can be a powerful, low-cost lever for treating disease. We previously showed that a ketogenic diet suppresses intestinal tumorigenesis in mouse models of colorectal cancer, mediated by the metabolite beta-hydroxybutyrate (BHB) acting through HCAR2 to induce the differentiation factor HOPX (Dmitrieva-Posocco et al., Nature, 2022). A follow-up trial in Lynch syndrome patients confirmed that BHB supplementation reduces colonic epithelial proliferation, and a clinical trial for colorectal cancer prevention is now underway (NCT05338307). We asked whether the same metabolite could address a different problem: CAR T cell therapy fails in roughly half of patients and rarely works in solid tumors. Screening diets in mouse lymphoma models, we found that a ketogenic diet- again acting through BHB- potentiates CAR T cell function, fueling the TCA cycle and reprogramming T cells away from exhaustion toward a more cytotoxic state. BHB supplementation alone dramatically improved tumor clearance and survival in lymphoma and solid tumor models, and enhanced T cell metabolic fitness in healthy human volunteers, motivating an ongoing Phase I trial combining BHB with CAR T cell therapy in lymphoma patients. Together, this work suggests that a single, inexpensive dietary metabolite can be repurposed across cancer prevention and immunotherapy to meaningfully improve patient outcomes.Division(s): MTx (Molecular Therapeutics)

events.title: Lecture | Taking God Seriously in Modern Islamic Politics: Muhammad al-Ghazali (1917–1996), Science, and Divine Presence in Twentieth-Century Egypt
events.description: Abstract: In his new book, Mediating God: Muhammad al-Ghazali and the Politics of Divine Presence in Twentieth-Century Egypt, Arthur Zárate argues that although God stands at the center of contemporary Muslim moral and political visions, the deity's presence is often neglected in scholarship. This talk explores why that neglect persists and what comes into focus when theological claims are taken seriously in the study of modern Islamic politics. Focusing on the Egyptian theologian Muhammad al-Ghazali (1917–1996), it examines his engagements with modern scientific discourses to show how science became one avenue through which divine presence was encountered and affirmed. Debates over science, it argues, were simultaneously debates about God, and competing understandings of the natural world underwrote competing visions of political and social reform. Ultimately, the talk proposes "activist theology" as a more adequate framework than "Islamism" for understanding al-Ghazali's politics.Bio: Arthur Zárate is a historian of the modern Middle East whose research explores the intersections of politics, science, and theology in modern Islam. He is the author of Mediating God: Muhammad al-Ghazali and the Politics of Divine Presence in Twentieth-Century Egypt (Oxford University Press, 2025). His work has appeared in Comparative Studies in Society and History and the Journal of the American Academy of Religion, and is forthcoming in the International Journal of Middle East Studies. He is Assistant Professor of Global Humanities at San José State University, where he teaches in the Honors Humanities Program. He is currently writing a second book on Sufism, spiritual experimentation, and Muslim and Coptic saintly mediation in modern Egypt.

events.title: Life ascending: mechanisms of environmental adaptation in extreme high-elevation Andean mice
events.description: A fundamental goal in evolutionary biology is to understand how the realized niche of a given species has been shaped by local adaptation to extreme environmental conditions, such as those that prevail at range margins. Investigation of local adaptation of montane species at their upper elevational range limits may be especially informative in this effort. Andean leaf-eared mice, Phyllotis vaccarum, live on the summits of 6700 m volcanoes in the Puna de Atacama, far surpassing the known elevational range limits of all other terrestrial vertebrates. Such elevations were previously thought to be uninhabitable by mammals due to severe hypoxia and frigid temperatures. In addition to holding the record as the highest-dwelling mammal, P. vaccarum also has the broadest elevational range, as it is distributed from sea level along the desert coast of northern Chile up to the crest of the Andean Cordillera. Here I report results of physiological and genomic analyses that provided new insights into mechanisms of physiological adaptation to extreme elevations in P. vaccarum. Our genomic analysis also revealed unanticipated dimensions of environmental adaptation related to feeding ecology.

events.title: Two Provinces, Two Paths: Canada and the Independence Debate in Alberta and Quebec
events.description: The question of whether to remain in or leave Canada will play a major rzle in upcoming provincial elections in Alberta and Quebec. Proponents of independence in each province offer different arguments rooted in unique regional histories. However, they also share a sense of alienation from "Canadian" culture and national identity. This panel will discuss the recent rise of sovereigntist and independentist politics in each province. What factors are causing this resurgence of sovereigntist feeling? How are proponents of Canadian federalism responding to their grievances? And how are international developments, including heightened Canada-US tensions, shaping the trajectory of these movements?About the PanelistsMartha Hall Findlay is the Director and Palmer Chair in Public Policy, School of Public Policy, University of Calgary; a member of the Expert Group on Canada-U.S. Relations. A former two-term Member of Parliament, she served on the Official Opposition shadow cabinet as well as on committees concerned with trade, finance, and public works. Before politics, she worked as an international corporate lawyer and senior executive for Suncor Energy and the Canada West Foundation. She is currently overseeing the official Alberta government report on the economic impact to the province of leaving Canada.Philippe Gervais is a seasoned leader in communications and public affairs with more than 30 years of experience across the public and private sectors. He currently serves as the Vice-President, Communications and Institutional Relations, for McGill University. Before joining McGill, Mr. Gervais was a Managing Principal for Navigator Ltd, a Canadian crisis management, government relations and public opinion company. He has worked for both the Federal and Quebec provincial governments, and he has advised political campaigns at all levels of government across Canada.Kristina Michaud was elected to Canada's House of Commons at age 26, becoming one of the youngest federal representatives ever elected. From 2019 to 2025, she served as a Bloc Québécois MP and as the party's critic for Public Safety and Climate Change. Originally from eastern Quebec, she now works as a political analyst and commentator for various television and radio programs and writes in La Presse.Martin Pelletier, CFA is a senior portfolio manager, investment fund manager, author, and financial columnist. He is a recognized market strategist, regularly contributing to Canada's Financial Post and appearing in Canadian and US media to provide insights on topics including equity and bond markets, monetary and fiscal policy, and oil and gas and commodities. He is author of Investment Through the Storm, a guide to navigating today's unpredictable global geopolitical landscape.

events.title: Arash Afraz - How Does the Activity of Visually Responsive Neurons Generate Visual Perception?
events.description: We typically study the mechanistic underpinnings of vision by observing how "visually responsive" neurons in the brain respond to and encode visual stimuli. While highly informative, this approach is indirect and correlational and does not reveal the causal contribution of these neurons to visual perception. In this talk, I will introduce a new methodology, Perceptography, that quantitatively and graphically determines the causal role of cortical neurons in perception. I will then propose a new roadmap and theoretical framework for understanding visual perception.

events.title: Ned Wingreen: Collective dynamics in B cell affinity maturation
events.description: In the humoral immune response, B cells that produce high-affinity antibodies are generated through a Darwinian evolutionary process called affinity maturation. Affinity maturation, which takes place in germinal centers (GC), is driven by cycles of selection (mediated by T cells), division, and hypermutation of B cells. Recently, it was found that the T cells themselves also exhibit dynamic behavior throughout the course of the GC reaction, undergoing affinity-dependent proliferation. A model suggests that this reciprocal stimulation enforces a robust "homeostatic" regulation of the relative number of B cells and T cells in the GC, leading to a constant ratio of GC lymphocytes. But the model also points to a problem: the high mutation rate of GC B cells can lead to "backsliding" of affinity. The proposed solution – a fitness-dependent mutation rate – has been experimentally verified, and has implications beyond B cell affinity maturation.Division(s): INFORMAL SEMINAR

events.title: Stone Center for Environmental Stewardship Lecture: Kevin Washburn (Chickasaw), "Tribal Co-Management, Landback, and Indigenous Cosmology"
events.description: Kevin K. Washburn is a Professor of Law at the University of California, Berkeley School of Law. He is part of the advisory group for the UC Berkeley Stone Center for Environmental Stewardship. Professor Washburn's research explores the way federal law and policy works, and sometimes fails, for tribal nations in the United States. In this talk, he will explore the complicated relationships between tribes, conservation advocates, and land conservation policies. He will discuss how, on the one hand, tribes sometimes resent conservation groups because their actions can infringe on tribal sovereignty. On the other hand, conservation groups are sometimes concerned that tribes won't exercise their sovereignty in ways consistent with the goals of the conservation movement. Washburn will describe the dramatic improvement in these relationships in recent years, and the reasons such trust is well-placed and should continue to grow. The special seminar will be held in 132 Mulford Hall and via Zoom. There will be a special reception following from 4:30pm - 5:30pm in the lawn outside Mulford Hall.

Talk Summary: Drawing on insights from the co-authored book The Korean Startup Ecosystem: Past, Present, and Future, this lecture offers an insider's perspective on Korea's evolving innovation landscape. It traces the nation's transition from a conglomerate-driven growth model to an innovation-led economy, highlighting the critical interplay between venture capital, government policy, conglomerates, and entrepreneurial culture. The talk demonstrates how Korea's global cultural powerhouses—including K-pop, K-dramas, and K-beauty—are strategic outcomes of this systematically built ecosystem. Through a comparative lens, the lecture examines the institutional features that distinguish the Korean and U.S. markets across key dimensions like financing, risk tolerance, and policy intervention. It concludes by outlining strategic implications for global founders, investors, and policymakers, followed by an interactive Q&A session. The English edition of The Korean Startup Ecosystem: Past, Present, and Future is available for download for free at the following link for those who are interested: https://bit.ly/4tNQSAJ (https://bit.ly/4tNQSAJ) Speaker Bio: Professor Paik is a tenured professor at the KAIST College of Business and an affiliated professor at the KAIST College of AI. His research explores the intersection of entrepreneurship, innovation, strategy, institutions, and public policy. He serves as an editorial review board member and referee for numerous top-tier academic journals in his field, and his research has appeared in premier publications such as the Strategic Management Journal, Organization Science, Strategic Entrepreneurship Journal, and the Journal of Economics & Management Strategy. Before joining KAIST in 2018, Professor Paik served as an assistant professor at the University of Southern California's Marshall School of Business and Washington University in St. Louis's Olin Business School. He holds a Ph.D. in Economics from the University of California, Berkeley. Prior to his academic career, he was a patent attorney at the leading South Korean law firm Kim & Chang, advising both multinational corporations and entrepreneurial ventures. A seasoned advisor in the innovation ecosystem, Professor Paik cofounded the venture capital firm TBW Investment, which was later acquired via M&A. He is a Board Member of Hanyang Eng Co., a major KOSDAQ-listed semiconductor and high-tech facility engineering firm, and currently serves as a policy advisor to South Korea's National Economic Advisory Council.

events.title: Julia Nelsen | Translation as Rediscovery: Introducing Fausta Cialente
events.description: Fausta Cialente (1898-1994) was one of Italy's most significant twentieth-century authors. Though she won critical acclaim—albeit late in her career—Cialente remained overlooked for decades until the recent rerelease of her literary works in Italian. A Very Cold Winter (Transit Books, 2026) is the first of Cialente's novels to be rediscovered in translation by Julia Nelsen. In conversation with Professor Mairi McLaughlin, Nelsen will discuss her translation of A Very Cold Winter, situate Cialente within the broader landscape of modern Italian and international literature, and explore the role translators play in recovering unsung voices.Julia Nelsen translates between English and Italian. In addition to her work on Fausta Cialente, her essays and translations have appeared in journals including Circumference, Two Lines,Firmament, and the Chicago Review. Alongside translation, she currently serves as policy analyst for the UCLA Academic Senate, and previously taught writing and literature courses and managed international partnerships between Europe and the West Coast. She holds a PhD in Comparative Literature from UC Berkeley and a Masters in European languages from the University of Milan.Mairi McLaughlin is Professor and Chair in the Department of French and an Affiliated Member of the Departments of Linguistics and Italian Studies at UC Berkeley. She specializes in French/Romance Linguistics and in Translation Studies and has published extensively on language contact, the language of the media, and journalistic and literary translation. events.title: This Death is Not One
events.description: In conversation with Salar Mameni, Associate Professor of Ethnic Studies at UC Berkeley The publication of The Right to Maim by Jasbir K. Puar in 2017 was critical to advancing studies on disability and to further articulating how the body figures in the nexus of capacity and debility across racializing and extractive neoliberal lines. It offered a complex and rigorous anti-capitalist account of disability that is useful to both scholarly work and political and social organizing. However, despite its paramount contribution to scholarship on Palestine, delivered by its scathing analysis of the Israeli biopolitical policy—its right to maim—in how the injured Palestinian body is produced and reproduced, its reception was difficult, and hard to stomach. It cohered a political logic in writing before it was visibly evident on the ground. In the moment and aftermath of the Great March of Return (2018-19), Puar's offerings became much harder to ignore, as the event crystallized a mass maiming campaign of Palestinian protesters inside the edges of the militarized borders of Gaza.This Death is Not One (Bilnaes 2026) is the first translation into Arabic of the chapter "Will Not Let Die": Debilitation and Inhuman Biopolitics in Palestine, alongside the postscript of The Right to Maim. Not simply a reissue of previously published work or a translation, This Death is Not One includes a new preface from Jasbir K. Puar revisiting the right to maim from within this moment of genocide in Gaza that interrogates the new vectors of living and dying under settler-colonialism, and how maiming, in fact, speaks of extermination; an introduction by Nasser Abourahme reflecting on the book's stakes in the present and its reception in the past, alongside searing analysis of genocide in excess of the law, and what this reveals and forecloses in how we understand the juridical body and militancy in the wake of Zionism; and original drawings by Xaytun Ennasr that inscribe a relation between land and body mapped through cosmological patterns tracing the relation between martyrs, who are referred to as moons, and the moon, a symbol for martyrdom in Palestine.

events.title: Architecting Human Power in the Age of AI (2026 Fall NOW Encore Series)
events.description: 2026 NOW Encore Series (https://hr.berkeley.edu/development/career-development/workshops) In a workplace increasingly shaped by artificial intelligence, many professional development sessions focus on what tools to learn next. This session takes a different approach. It focuses on what AI cannot replace: the distinctly human ability to decide what matters, what you stand for, and how you choose to show up. This is not an AI skills workshop. It is an invitation to become more intentional about your human advantage. As AI expands what is possible, our opportunity is not to compete with technology, but to become clearer about what makes us uniquely valuable and then use AI to amplify it. By knowing what deserves your attention, what guides your decisions, and how you want to show up, you can engage AI with greater clarity and intention rather than simply using it to do more, faster. Led by Executive Coach and former Fortune 500 Marketing Leader Sarah Peterson, this interactive 90-minute session combines provocative ideas, personal reflection, and practical application. Drawing on her own journey from high-achieving executive through burnout and realignment, Sarah introduces her Leadership DNA Pyramid, a framework inspired by the strategy used to build iconic brands and adapted to help individuals navigate change, complexity, and an increasingly AI-enabled workplace. Participants will work with three dimensions of the broader Leadership DNA framework that become increasingly important as AI accelerates how we work: Priority, Value, and Presence. They will make three intentional choices: one priority to focus their energy, one value to guide their decisions, and one quality of presence to embody in how they work and lead. They will then move from insight to implementation by identifying the behaviors and actions that will bring those choices to life over the next 90 days. Together, these choices create a personal compass for working and leading with greater clarity and intention in an AI-enabled world.Learning Outcomes: –Recognize their distinctly human contribution as a source of advantage in an AI-enabled workplace. –Define one priority that deserves their focus and energy over the next 90 days. –Identify one value to intentionally guide their choices and decisions. –Choose one quality ofpresence they want to embody in how they lead, collaborate, and contribute. –Turn Priority, Value, and Presence into Practice by defining concrete behaviors and actions they can begin applying immediately.Registrants will be sent a Zoom link and bCal invite as this virtual workshop date draws near.

events.title: A Conversation with Senator Lisa Murkowski
events.location: Hertz Hall, 101 Cross-Sproul Path, Berkeley, CA 94704
events.description: Join the Goldman School of Public Policy for an in-person conversation with U.S. Senator Lisa Murkowski, one of the Senate's most independent voices and a leading voice on political leadership and bipartisan governance in an era of deep political polarization. Over more than two decades in the U.S. Senate, Murkowski has helped shape some of the nation's most consequential policy debates while earning a reputation for independence, institutional stewardship, and a willingness to challenge presidents and party leaders alike. Drawing on her memoir, Far From Home: An Alaskan Senator Faces the Extreme Climate of Washington, D.C., she will reflect on the defining moments of her career, the evolution of American politics, and what it means to govern with conviction in a divided democracy. The discussion will explore Murkowski's journey from Alaska to the U.S. Senate, her historic 2010 write-in reelection campaign, and the transformation of American politics from the Tea Party era to today. As institutions face growing public scrutiny and political divisions continue to deepen, she will offer a candid perspective on the challenges confronting American democracy, the future of bipartisan governance, and the role of political leadership and public service in sustaining democratic institutions.This event is part of the Goldman School of Public Policy's Democracy Book Club series, which features authors whose work enriches our understanding of democracy by examining the institutions, policies, and civic traditions that shape democratic life. —Lisa Murkowski is a third-generation Alaskan proudly serving as the state's senior senator. Since joining the U.S. Senate in 2002, she has earned a reputation for her collaborative approach and her ability to work across the aisle to reach commonsense solutions. She and her husband live in Anchorage, Alaska, where they raised their two sons.David C. Wilson is the dean of the Goldman School of Public Policy and a Professor of Public Policy at the University of California, Berkeley. A leading scholar of political psychology and public opinion, his research explores race, democracy, and political behavior. Before joining Berkeley, he held senior academic leadership roles at the University of Delaware and worked with the Gallup Polling Organization. Wilson is also a U.S. Army veteran who served 19 years in the Army Reserves, including tours during Operations Desert Storm and Iraqi Freedom.

events.title: Dr. Os Keyes, "The Life and Death of the Life and Death Committee"
events.description: The story of the Seattle Artificial Kidney Center's "Life and Death Committee", or "God Squad" - a lay panel tasked with deciding who received treatment, and correspondingly, lived and died - is a classic one within both the history of medicine and the history of bioethics. But much of what we know about it, how we conceptualize it, and correspondingly, the lessons we draw from it, is, Dr. Keyes argues, false. Drawing on newly-discovered archival resources, this talk revisits the shifting function and viability of the Life and Death Committee over time, demonstrating that its purpose was broader than often-conceived, and that its' eventual fate calls into question many of the conclusions historians have drawn about it. RSVP: https://forms.gle/HsSUUoqqdW8uwicq5 (https://forms.gle/HsSUUoqqdW8uwicq5)Os Keyes is a postdoctoral fellow at the University of Massachusetts Lowell. Their scholarship in the history of medicine focuses on the structure of decision-making in spaces from kidney dialysis to gender-affirming care, and has been published in venues including the Bulletin of the History of Medicine.

events.title: Karen Van Dyck | The Greek Alphabet in America
events.description: The history of Greek assimilation in America can be traced in the slow erasure of Greek as a symbol of difference and indecipherability, the most recognizably unrecognizable alphabet – "It's all Greek to me!" By the 1930s and 1940s, looking and sounding different led to the substitution not only of different faces and races, but of typefaces. If, during the mid-century, nations were intent on keeping things as separate as possible and popular fiction and film made sure Greeks and Greek in America were erased and the Latin alphabet won out, in the 1970s and 1980s, a more cosmopolitan moment, Greek's indecipherability became the grounds for literary experimentation and, particularly for women writers, a "politics of transliteration." The idea that Ancient Greek and English were superior to Modern Greek was replaced by a multilingual understanding that more than one language and alphabet could creatively coexist.Karen Van Dyck, Kimon A. Doukas Professor of Modern Greek Literature in the Classics Department at Columbia University, works on questions of translation, migration, gender and classical reception. She is the founding director of Hellenic Studies and an active member of the Institute of Comparative Literature and Society and the Istanbul and Athens Global Centers. Her translations includeThe Greek Poets: Homer to the Present (Norton, 2010), Austerity Measures: The New Greek Poetry(2016, Penguin) and Margarita Liberaki's Three Summers (NYRB, 2019)If you require an accommodation for effective communication (ASL interpreting/CART captioning, alternative media formats, etc.) or information about campus mobility access features in order to fully participate in this event, please contact ies@berkeley.edu with as much advance notice as possible and at least 7-10 days before the event.

events.title: The Smart Curb: How Cities Can Control Their Most Valuable Asset
events.description: Gene Oh, CEO of Tranzito, will present The Smart Curb: How Cities Can Control Their Most Valuable Asset at the ITS Berkeley Transportation Seminar on Sept. 25, 2026. Join us for cookie hour at 2:30 in the ITS Library, hosted by TRANSOC.Abstract: The curb is the most contested real estate in all city urban cores, and it's allocated to whoever arrives first. Ride-hail, on-demand delivery, and shared micromobility have layered ever growing demand onto a finite supply legislated by multiple agencies with overlapping jurisdiction and objectives. The resulting costs are not paid by the operators generating them, but by bus riders stuck behind double-parked pickups and corridor communities absorbing the emissions - a transfer from the haves to the have nots. Pricing and enforcement alone cannot close the gap, and autonomy will only widen it: AVs need curb space that is predictable and reservable. Until this is solved, AVs cannot scale. The solution is to grow supply. Gene Oh will present a "stacking" approach - a single linear foot serving several use cases across the day, once exclusive curb contracts give way to dynamic, networked regulation - and argue that it takes a property manager of the curb, arbitrating access on behalf of public agencies.Bio: Gene Oh is the founder and CEO of Tranzito, with over 20 years in new mobility. He leads the company's strategy to help cities actively manage the curb, the most contested space on the street, positioning Tranzito as the property manager of the public right-of-way. Gene's view is that as ride-hailing, shared micromobility, delivery, and autonomy drive up demand for curbspace, agencies need to manage private operators rather than compete with them, keeping public transit as the backbone of the system. Under his leadership, Tranzito grew from secure bike parking into citywide smart infrastructure, including the $500M+ LA STAP program (3,000+ smart bus shelters and 200 urban panels) and the 97-hub LADOT Integrated Mobility Hubs program, where he serves as Executive Director. Gene treats this infrastructure as a connected network of smart-city nodes, tied together by Tranzito's open CurbOS platform, and designed the public-private partnership models that let agencies partner with private operators at the LADOT and Caltrain SF mobility hubs. His next focus is smart loading zones and dynamic curb management, which combine sensing, digital signage, policy, enforcement, and field operations into a single managed program launching through the IMH network. Gene specializes in strategic design, stakeholder management, and business development, and keeps Tranzito self-funded to stay focused on public benefit.

events.title: Inorganic Chemistry Seminar
events.description: Phillip Milner, Associate Professor, Cornell UniversityTaming the Halogens using Metal-Organic Frameworks Fluorinated molecules represent a double-edged sword: they are present in 30% of pharmaceuticals and agrochemicals, but are also persistent organic pollutants of growing concern due to their long environmental lifetimes and high global warming potentials. Herein, we will discuss how porous materials such as metal-organic frameworks (MOFs) present a unique opportunity to capture and utilize fluorinated (and other halogenated) building blocks to design new catalysts and reagents for applications in the synthesis of complex molecules. We will first focus on catalytic strategies that leverage MOFs bearing metal-halogen bonds as recyclable catalysts for challenging reactions such as halogen exchange, C-H functionalization, and contra-thermodynamic alkene isomerization. Then, we will discuss how MOFs can be used to directly capture fluorinated gases to allow for their safe handling as solid reagents, enabling a diverse range of thermal, photochemical, and electrochemical reactions. Last, we will show how ozone-depleting and greenhouse gases can be captured from realistic mixtures and employed directly as building blocks for fluorochemical synthesis.The Inorganic Seminar Series is sponsored by Earl L. Muetterties lecture fund

events.title: Music Studies Colloquium: Hilde Roos (University of Stellenbosch)
events.description: Staging Settler Society: Opera Production in NamibiaHilde Roos (University of Stellenbosch) This presentation examines opera production in Namibia from 1960 onwards. Its primary focus is on opera production before Namibia's independence in 1990, although some attention will also be given to developments after independence. Drawing on the framework of settler colonialism and archival materials, the presentation reconstructs a largely undocumented cultural history. Building on the work of Patrick Wolfe and Lorenzo Veracini, it conceptualises settler colonialism as an ongoing structure and analyses opera not simply as an imported European art form, but as part of the cultural infrastructure that sustained settler society in Namibia during the period of South African occupation. Produced under the auspices of the Arts Association (AA) of Windhoek and later the South West African Performing Arts Council (SWAPAC), more than 25 opera productions were staged in Windhoek during South African occupation. These productions featured artists from Namibia and Europe, as well as visiting companies from South Africa. The presentation will furthermore investigate how opera functioned in relation to racial segregation, land occupation, and institutional life, asking how performance practices contributed to the formation of settler identity and the normalisation of apartheid within Namibian society. During South African occupation, the settler community in Windhoek consisted primarily of Afrikaans- and German-speaking populations. Attention will be given both to the prominence of European repertoire and to the archival silences surrounding indigenous Namibian participation. By situating operatic activity within broader systems of governance and cultural power, while remaining attentive to the lingering memory of the genocide of the Herero and Nama peoples (1904–1908), this paper engages with the role of so-called high culture in colonial contexts and contributes to emerging intersections between opera studies and settler colonial theory. A reception will follow.

events.title: Establishing Chronology in Tibetan art: a Study of Taklung Paintings
events.description: This lecture addresses chronology in early Tibetan art. Dr. Casey highlights over a decade of research on a group of approximately 100 paintings from Taklung and Riwoche monasteries in Tibet. The main purpose of the study has been to establish a reliable foundation for assigning dates to Taklung paintings. The Taklung painting corpus particularly lends itself to the task of building a chronology. Almost three-quarters of the paintings bear inscriptions with chronological implications. Using visual lineages (the succession of teachers represented in the top, side, and, occasionally, the bottom registers of paintings), inscriptions, narrative scenes (in which principal structures in the Taklung Monastery compound may be linked to specific dates), and style analysis, the speaker identifies fundamental parameters that help to create firm chronological designations for these c. twelfth to mid-sixteenth century paintings. Tibetan textual historians and historians of Tibetan religion will appreciate the evidentiary underpinnings of the chronology put forth. And anyone interested in understanding the history of Tibetan Buddhist culture will appreciate the wealth of information contained in these remarkable, often very well preserved works of art.Jane Casey is an art historian specializing in Himalayan art. Educated in the History of Science (A.B.) and in Fine Arts (A.M. and Ph.D.) at Harvard University, since 1991 she has worked as an independent art historian, curating exhibitions at The Metropolitan Museum of Art in New York and at Casa Asia, Barcelona. She is a Guest Professor at the Zhejiang University Center for Buddhist Art in Hangzhou, and a Research Fellow in Tibetan Art at the Palace Museum in Beijing. She resides in Marlborough, New Zealand.

events.title: Rethinking the Republican Interregnum in South Vietnam (1964-1967)
events.description: Speaker: Y Thien Nguyen (Assistant Professor of Asian Pacific Studies, California State University, Dominguez Hills) This talk reframes the widely disparaged interregnum period in South Vietnam (1963-1967) as a critical juncture in which civil society and non-state actors actively shaped the political realm, contributing to the rise and fall of governments and eventually to the emergence of the Second Republic of Vietnam (1967-1975). In addition to exploring the routinization of oppositional politics, it charts the development of a dominant discourse of "true democracy and freedom" which conditioned the actions and political language of state and non-state actors as well as popular apprehensions of political legitimacy.This talk is funded byThe Republic of Vietnam Endowment for Vietnamese Studies,made possible by the generous donation fromMr. and Mrs. Nguyễn Đức Cường.Speaker bio: Y Thien Nguyen specializes in the study of modern Vietnam and Vietnamese refugee experiences. His work examines the ideological, political, and institutional connectivity between the Republic of Vietnam and Vietnamese America. He received his PhD in Sociology from Northwestern University and previously served as a Teaching Fellow in South East Asian History at the University of Leeds, UK and a Research Associate for the US-Vietnam Research Center at the University of Oregon. He is currently completing his book manuscript entitled Diasporic Legacies: The Making and Remaking of Vietnamese Anticommunism. He has published multiple academic works on the Republic of Vietnam, the Vietnamese diaspora, and various sociopolitical issues related to the Vietnamese American community. Beyond his immediate academic duties, Dr. Nguyen also serves on the Board of Director for the US-Vietnam Research Center, the Boat People SOS Center for Community Advancement, and offers consulting and grant writing services to Vietnamese American non-profit organizations.

events.title: Film Screening: Taming the Garden
events.description: With astonishing cinematic style, Taming the Gardentracks the surreal uprooting of ancient trees from their Georgian locales. With each removal, tensions flare between workers and villagers. Some see financial incentives—new roads, handsome fees—while others angrily mourn the loss of what was assumed to be an immovable monolith of their town's collective history and memory. With a steady and shrewdly observant eye, Salomé Jashi documents a single man's power over Earth's natural gardens: how majestic living artifacts of a country's identity can so effortlessly become uprooted by individuals with no connection to the nature they claim as their own.

events.title: Georgian Cinema Now Symposium—Activism in Authoritarian Times: The Republic of Georgia as a Case Study
events.description: Free and open to the public, this symposium offers an invaluable introduction to the current political and cultural context in the Republic of Georgia. Guest speakers will offer a range of perspectives, from analyzing the political situation under the current Georgian Dream government to sharing experiences from the field as activists on the frontlines fighting for civil liberties, especially freedom of speech and LGBTQ+ rights. We will hear from journalists, media commentators, cultural historians, teachers, and independent filmmakers on the challenges and threats they face as a result of the Georgian government's introduction of the Foreign Agent Law—censorship, arrests, trials, and imprisonment—and parallels with broader global threats to democracy. The symposium will feature two panels, "Modern Georgia's Political History" and "Reports from the Field by Georgian Independent Filmmakers." In between, we will screen two recent documentaries on the impact of the current authoritarian government.

events.title: [UC Berkeley campus premiere] A Job in the Shade: The Emily Vasquez Story
events.location: Chevron Auditorium, International House (2299 Piedmont Avenue, Berkeley, CA)
events.description: About the Film This inspiring documentary chronicles the extraordinary life of Judge Emily Vasquez, the first Latina appointed in 2001 to the Sacramento County Superior Court in its history. Through intimate interviews with family members, friends, colleagues, and mentees, A Job in the Shade explores Judge Vasquez's remarkable journey from the agricultural fields of California to the courtroom. The film highlights a lifetime of service, leadership, and mentorship while demonstrating how education can transform lives and expand opportunities for future generations. Through her strength of character, hard work, and keen intellect, Judge Vasquez defied the odds. Judge Vasquez has made it look easy with her many accomplishments but her many achievements did not come easy (not when you one of the first and come from humble beginnings). Her parents were poor, immigrant farmworkers from Mexico. As a child, she lived in labor camps and worked in the fields when school was not in session to help supplement the family income. She spent her early years living in tents and one-bedroom shacks with everyone, including her parents sleeping in the same room as her siblings. The bathroom was an outhouse. From her childhood in California's Central Valley, working alongside her poor farmworker parents, to her groundbreaking legal career, Judge Vasquez's story is one of resilience, determination, and the transformative power of education.Presented by:UC Berkeley Division of Equity & Inclusion Latinx Thriving Initiatives The Spencer Group In partnership with:University Development and Alumni Relations (UDAR) UC Berkeley College of Letters & Science Cal Alumni Association

events.description: Georgia's movement to teach English to schoolchildren is the backdrop for this beautifully observed documentary about an English teacher, Bradley Nelson from South Africa, and his experiences in a remote Georgian village, Sajijao. There he encounters both the warmth of the local community, and some resistance to the "linguistic revolution" as a national initiative. A finely drawn portrait of a critical moment in Georgia's development as an independent nation in the post-Soviet era. Before construction begins on a major housing complex in Bakhmaro, a resort town in western Georgia that travelers visit for the special healing properties of the air, filmmaker Anka Gujabidze observes life as it is. Employing superimpositions and dissolves, this documentary portrait ruminates on the changes that will come with construction and what will be lost.

events.title: Film Screening: An Incomplete Day in the History of Georgia 10.06.93.
events.description: Derived solely from video recordings of Georgian parliamentary proceedings on June 10, 1993, when Eduard Shevardnadze was the head of state, An Incomplete Day in the History of Georgia presents the debate surrounding the introduction of Georgia's national currency coupon to replace the Russian ruble. Members of parliament voice their concerns from the floor, questioning the resolutions presented by the vice prime minister and president of the National Bank. How should the country's leaders proceed in light of domestic challenges such as starvation, fuel shortages, budget shortfalls, and rapid inflation? Viewed with hindsight, this document from the early days of Georgian independence reminds us how fragile the democratic process can be.

events.title: Probabilistic Operator Algebra Seminar: Free Bakry-Emery Calculus
events.location: to attend via Zoom email David Jekel (djekel@uottawa.ca) remote on-line talk
events.description: Speaker: Martin Peev, University of OxfordWe prove a free probabilistic Bakry-Emery criterion for the Poincare Inequality and Logarithmic Sobolev Inequality. Our approach relies on a noncommutative extension of the Carre du Champ operator and its iteration to the setting of Free Probability. I will show how one can formulate a positive curvature condition in terms of direct formulae involving th potential of a Gibbs state. I will then present how one can employ these abstract curvature conditions to prove a (non-universal) free poincare Inequality and a Logarithmic Sobolev Inequality in this setting. I will particularly stress where classical methods have to be adapted in order to accommodate the tensorial nature of the free derivative. This talk is based on joint work with Ajay Chandra and Masha Gordina.

events.title: Ashok Prasad: Cell Shapes and Cytoskeletal Networks: Morphological Analysis of Cellular Identity
events.description: Cell morphology offers a powerful and relatively underutilized lens for understanding cell state and behavior. While transcriptomic and proteomic profiling have revolutionized our capacity to characterize cells, quantitative morphological features can provide complementary insights into cell state and function. In this talk, I will present some of our work demonstrating that cells can be robustly classified using microscopy images and morphological metrics, explore some of the links between cell and nuclear morphology and discuss our current efforts to develop morphological representations of the actin cytoskeleton and other dynamic polymer networks using simulations. This work contributes to a broader vision of morphology-based phenotyping and modeling as a bridge between structure and function in living systems.Division(s): INFORMAL SEMINAR

events.title: The Impact of Early Contexts on Life-Course Development
events.description: The earliest years of life are shaped not only by relationships between children and caregivers, but also by families' experiences with health care, housing, economic security, community support, and public systems. This session brings together pediatrician Dr. Dayna Long, family leader and advocate Hope Williams-Burt, and lactation consultant and community-based leader Brandi Gates Burgess for a conversation about how these conditions shape pregnancy, infancy, early development, and family well-being—particularly for Black families. Drawing on clinical expertise, lived experience, and community practice, the panel will explore how culturally grounded, relationship-centered supports can build trust and improve outcomes; what it means to treat families as partners in care, research, and systems design; and how universities, public institutions, and community organizations can work together to translate knowledge into meaningful change.Speakers:Brandi Gates Burgess (https://www.breastfriendslactation.org/meet-us), Founder and Executive Director, Breast Friends Lactation Dayna Long (https://www.ucsfbenioffchildrens.org/providers/dayna-long), MD, Professor of Pediatrics, UCSF School of Medicine; Co-Director, Center for Child and Community Health, UCSF Benioff Children's Hospital Oakland Hope Williams-Burt (https://voicesforbirthjustice.org/portfolio/hope/), Mother, Community Organizer, Consultant) Moderator: Katie Albright, Equity and Excellence in Early Childhood, UC Berkeley For more information, please see: https://ihd.berkeley.edu/fall-2026-colloquium-series (https://www.google.com/url?q=https://ihd.berkeley.edu/fall-2026-colloquium-series&sa=D&source=calendar&ust=1787080597707872&usg=AOvVaw04YjoBvi1rdt5nQNY9hmyI)If you require an accommodation for effective communication (ASL interpreting/CART captioning, alternative media formats, etc.) or information about campus mobility access features in order to fully participate in this event, please contact 510-828-2681. events.description: A talk by Pariroo Rattan (https://sociology.northwestern.edu/people/faculty/visiting/pariroo-rattan.html), Postdoctoral Fellow in Science in Human Culture in the Department of Sociology at Northwestern University, that examines why marginalized street vendors in India continue to embrace Aadhaar and digital payments despite their shortcomings, arguing that these technologies foster a powerful sense of political belonging and direct connection to the nation-state.Lawrence Cohen (https://sseas.berkeley.edu/people/lawrence-cohen), Professor of Anthropology and of South & Southeast Asian Studies; Chair, Department of South & Southeast Asian Studies; Co-Director, Medical Anthropology Program, UC Berkeley will serve as discussant. Event moderated by Sai Balakrishnan (https://ced.berkeley.edu/people/sai-balakrishnan), Associate Professor of City & Regional Planning, UC Berkeley. Event moderated by Sai Balakrishnan (https://ced.berkeley.edu/people/sai-balakrishnan), Associate Professor of City & Regional Planning, UC Berkeley. ————–DATE: Mon, September 28, 2026 TIME: 12:30-2 pm PST VENUE: 10 Stephens Hall LIVESTREAM: On FB at ISASatUCBerkeley (https://www.facebook.com/ISASatUCBerkeley) —————-About the talk: Why do marginalized citizens in India continue to embrace biometric identification and digital payment technologies even when these systems routinely fail to deliver their promised economic inclusion? Digital India is a flagship policy of the Government of India to foster "economic growth combined with social inclusion." Central to Digital India is the Aadhaar card, a biometric identification now distributed to over 1.3 billion Indians, and a real time mobile payment technology, Unified Payments Interface (UPI), that has significantly replaced cash transactions. Technological promises to improve governance and economic opportunities are often not fully realized and create new sources of friction, especially for citizens in the informal economy such as street vendors. Nevertheless, many street vendors regard digital identification and payments as signs of economic and national progress. Why does there continue to be faith in techno-utopia even when its promises fall short, and what can this tell us about the nature of contemporary populist politics? Through interviews, archival work, discourse analysis and ethnographic research with street vendors in Delhi from 2020–2024, I argue that digital technologies acquire political force for marginalized citizens not simply through coercion or what they enable materially, but through the political relationships they establish between marginalized citizens and the nation-state. While the bureaucratic state was historically built as an instrument for advancing national development and extending citizenship rights, contemporary populist politics increasingly represents bureaucratic mediation itself as an impediment to democratic responsiveness and national progress. I use technology to illuminate some of the core tensions in the moral relations, state obligations, and forms of political belonging that constitute the foundations of citizenship in contemporary India.About the Speaker:Pariroo Rattan (https://sociology.northwestern.edu/people/faculty/visiting/pariroo-rattan.html) is a Weinberg College Postdoctoral Fellow in Science in Human Culture and the Department of Sociology at Northwestern University. She will also be teaching at the Department of Anthropology at Northwestern. Pariroo is a recent PhD graduate from Harvard University, where she was a long-standing Fellow at the HKS Science, Technology and Society (STS) program and received a secondary field in Music. Her doctoral dissertation is titled "A Marketplace for Populism: The Moral Politics of Digitization in India's Informal Economy" and studies the relationship of the digital economy with mediating state institutions and nation-building in India, through an ethnography of street vendors in New Delhi using digital biometric ID Aadhaar and payment system Unified Payments Interface. She also works comparatively on citizen resistance to legal data regulation regimes across the US, EU and China. Apart from digitization, Pariroo is writing about topics relating to the law such as the politics of evidence in the Harvard affirmative action lawsuit, and on the acoustic and sound politics of the urban economy. Her work has been supported by the Wenner Gren Foundation, Weatherhead Center for International Affairs at Harvard, and the Berkman Klein Center for Internet and Society among others, and has recently been published by the Economic and Political Weekly. _________________ Event made possible with the support of the Sarah Kailath Chair of India Studies (http://southasia.berkeley.edu/sarah-kailath-chair-memorial-lecture) Like us on FACEBOOK (https://www.facebook.com/pages/Center-for-South-Asia-Studies/76502306608) For DIRECTIONS to the Institute please enter "Institute for South Asia Studies" in your google maps or click this GOOGLE MAPS LINK (https://www.google.com/maps/dir//Institute+for+South+Asia+Studies,+10+Stephens+Hall,+Berkeley,+CA+94720/@37.8710692,-122.2585002,19z/data=!4m16!1m7!3m6!1s0x80857c25babcc33d:0xe2ff7d5c1483db5a!2sInstitute+for+South+Asia+Studies!3b1!8m2!3d37.8710952!4d-122.2576645!4m7!1m0!1m5!1m1!1s0x80857c25babcc33d:0xe2ff7d5c1483db5a!2m2!1d-122.2576645!2d37.8710952).PARKING INFORMATION (http://southasia.berkeley.edu/parking-around-campus)Please note that parking is not always easily available in Berkeley. events.title: Consumer Preference Modeling at Scale: A Generative Model for Cart Building (Srikanth Jagabathula, NYU)
events.description: Title: Consumer Preference Modeling at Scale: A Generative Model for Cart BuildingAbstract: How do customers build their online shopping carts across multiple product categories, and how do operational factors such as prices, delivery fees, and promotions influence their choices? Existing multi-purchase choice models in operations, marketing, and economics often overlook the dynamic and sequential nature of cart-building and struggle with scalability in real-world scenarios involving millions of customers and thousands of products. Machine learning models, while scalable, are often opaque and fail to capture problem-specific nuances. We leverage the latest developments in generative AI to bridge this gap by combining the scalability of machine learning with the structure of economic choice theory. We model a customer's cart building process as a sequential decision problem, in which the customer sequentially selects products based on their needs, preferences, and the operational context, which includes recommendations and promotions. Each customer is a reinforcement learning agent who sequentially selects products to maximize their overall reward. Using the observed basket purchase data as samples of expert demonstrations, we leverage techniques from inverse reinforcement learning and generative AI to infer the underlying reward function of the customer and train a generative model of customer purchase behavior. This model allows us to simulate individual customer cart purchases under various counterfactual settings. We implement our methods using a large dataset from a leading quick-commerce platform in India, comprising 8.5 million orders spanning 2000 product categories from 350,000 customers. Our model successfully scales to such large data sizes and predicts customer carts with a high degree of accuracy. Our model's structural insights reveal that customers strongly respond to free delivery over flat discounts of the same value, highlighting the behavioral characteristic of avoiding additional service fees. Our counterfactual analyses reveal how increasing the threshold for free delivery impacts cart value and product demand, with discretionary items like chips and longer shelf-life items like onions experiencing an increase in demand as thresholds rise.Bio: Srikanth Jagabathula is the Robert Stansky Research Faculty Fellow; Professor of Technology, Operations, and Statistics; and Academic Director of the Khubani BS in Business, Technology, and Entrepreneurship program at the NYU Stern School of Business. He was also a Visiting Associate Professor of Technology and Operations Management at Harvard Business School, and teaches operations management and AI/ML at the undergraduate, graduate, PhD, and executive levels. He holds a Ph.D. and S.M. in Electrical Engineering and Computer Science from MIT, and his research has appeared in NeurIPS, the Journal of Machine Learning Research, IEEE Transactions on Information Theory, Management Science, Operations Research, and Marketing Science. Recent work includes generative models of consumer shopping behavior, unstructured-text models for commodity-price forecasting, reinforcement learning for dynamic pricing, and a benchmark of 23 frontier AI models on the CFA Level III exam. He pioneered the use of large-scale choice models for operations problems, and has co-founded companies applying this work to pricing, recommendations, and supply-chain decisions. His honors include the NSF CAREER Award, the MSOM Young Scholar Prize, the Wickham-Skinner Early-Career Research Accomplishments Award, more than ten best-paper awards, NYU Stern's Distinguished Teaching Award, and recognition by Poets & Quants as a Top 40 Under 40 business professor. He serves as Department Editor at Management Science and as Associate Editor at Operations Research and Manufacturing & Service Operations Management.

events.title: AI & Disability: A Roundtable Discussion feat. Jeff Nagy, Renée Cummings, and Os Keyes
events.description: A History & Theory of New Media event with Jeff Nagy, Assistant Professor, Communication and Media Studies, York University; Renée Cummings, Professor of Practice, School of Data Science, University of Virginia, and Nonresident Senior Fellow and Co-Director, AI Equity Lab, Brookings Institution; and Os Keyes, Postdoctoral Fellow, University of Massachusetts, Lowell - Monday, September 28, 2026 5:00 — 6:30 PM Eugene Jarvis Auditorium,Grimes Engineering Center (http://engineering.berkeley.edu/about/facilities/grimes-engineering-center/) RSVP here (http://docs.google.com/forms/d/e/1FAIpQLSdsmOw4XW_mhfHzcHEg012STGGi9YE_lwF5AYv-7wTx4xVmJg/viewform?usp=publish-editor)! Save the event to your bCal here (https://calendar.google.com/calendar/event?action=TEMPLATE&tmeid=NzBtNDI4MWUzNzcwOXZucDA1N3R2M2MyZ2UgZDV1NWVrN2o4aXBvZDBvOGlxNDE1ZTFhdnNAZw&tmsrc=d5u5ek7j8ipod0o8iq415e1avs%40group.calendar.google.com)! - What does AI have to do with disability, and what is it doing to disability? This question undergirds a roundtable discussion featuring Jeff Nagy, Renée Cummings, and Os Keyes. In brief individual presentations, followed by a moderated discussion, these three experts in the field will tackle the question of AI and disability from a range of distinct and overlapping perspectives. Professor Nagy will examine the remaking of psychiatric disability in an AI era through the case of algorithmic depression diagnostics. Tracing a deep history of attempts to bring computing to bear on depression, he argues that the shift from clinic to program and platform, and the substitution of machine learning features for diagnostic criteria, are rewiring the political economy of diagnosis and overwriting disability identities. Through close reading of contemporary systems and the datasets they depend on, he reveals an emergent technopolitics of disability in action, one that operates at cross-purposes with disability community and activism. Professor Renée Cummings wil discuss what happens when automated systems become gatekeepers of opportunity for individuals with disabilities. Focusing on the data infrastructures governing healthcare, education, employment and public services, she exposes how incomplete datasets, inaccessible design, and reductive classifications can convert ableism into computational logic. Through the lens of data justice, she will confront the ethics of algorithmic exclusion: whose needs are recognized, whose experiences are misread, and who is excluded altogether. Centering accessibility, disability justice, and community expertise, Professor Cummings argues that disabled people must possess meaningful power to design, govern, challenge and—when necessary—refuse the systems shaping their lives. Finally, Dr. Keyes will ask what the history of computational psychiatry teaches us about the political economy of diagnostics.The role of AI in psychiatry is often framed as novel, and focused on improving efficiency and patient access to care. But neither is the case. AI has a long history in the upper echelons of psychiatry, as a field and a practice, and that history has consistently been entangled with broader political conflicts over who plays a role in shaping diagnosis and treatment., and under what conditions. Beginning with the start of computational diagnostics in the 1960s, he will trace out the history of how (and why) computational approaches to psychiatry have come in and out of vogue, arguing that the ultimate purpose of these diagnostic tools is to reshape the political economy of diagnosis and disability. About Jeff Nagy Jeff Nagy is an Assistant Professor in the Department of Communication and Media Studies at York University. He is a historian of computing and AI, currently focused on the intersection of AI development, the behavioral sciences, and disability. He holds a PhD in Communication from Stanford University. With the DISCO Network, he is a co-author of Technoskepticism: Between Possibility and Refusal (Stanford University Press, 2025). His research and writing have appeared in Parapraxis, n+1, New Media and Society, Technology and Culture, and elsewhere. About Renée Cummings Professor Renée Cummings is an internationally recognized AI governance leader, criminologist, public interest technologist, and public sector intelligence futurist whose work is helping shape how governments, institutions, and organizations prepare for the intelligence age. She is widely recognized as one of the leading global voices advancing responsible AI, trustworthy public sector AI, innovation governance, algorithmic accountability, and the governance frameworks required to strengthen public trust, democratic resilience, and institutional integrity. An award-winning AI innovator and internationally sought-after keynote speaker, Professor Cummings serves as Professor of Practice at the University of Virginia School of Data Science, where she teaches future leaders how to excel with AI and deliver AI excellence. She is also a Nonresident Senior Fellow and Co-Director of the AI Equity Lab at the Brookings Institution and serves as Co-Chair of the Global Academic Network at the Centre for AI and Digital Policy (CAIDP), one of the world's leading organizations dedicated to AI governance, policy, and digital rights. About Os Keyes Dr. Os A. Keyes is a Postdoctoral Fellow at the University of Massachusetts, Lowell. A widely published and award-winning scholar of everything from the history of medicine to critical approaches to Artificial Intelligence, their first book, Trans Science, is under contract with University of Washington Press. About History & Theory of New Media Lecture Series The History & Theory of New Media Lecture Series brings to campus leading humanities scholars working on issues of media transition and technological emergence. The series promotes new, interdisciplinary approaches to questions about the uses, meanings, causes, and effects of rapid or dramatic shifts in techno-infrastructure, information management, and forms of mediated expression. Presented by BCNM, these events are free and open to the public.

events.title: Five Years after the Youth Protests: The Thai Monarchy Strikes Back
events.description: Speaker: Pavin Chachavalpongpun (Professor, Center for Southeast Asian Studies, Kyoto University) This talk discusses the Thai monarchy's strategic response to the 2020 youth-led protests, which called for reforms to the royal family's place in national life. The speaker argues that King Vajiralongkorn did not merely seek to restore the status quo but executed a profound transformation which he terms 'overt power codification and defensive hyper- personalisation.' This shift converted informal influence into visible, legally codified, and personally commanded authority, entrenching absolute power within the constitutional framework to neutralize reformist momentum. Speaker bio: Pavin Chachavalpongpun is a professor at the Center for Southeast Asian Studies, Kyoto University. He is the chief editor of the online journal Kyoto Review of Southeast Asia, in which all articles are translated from English into Japanese, Thai, Bahasa Indonesia, Filipino, Vietnamese, Burmese and Khmer. Earning his PhD from the School of Oriental and African Studies, University of London, Pavin is the author and editor of several books, including the upcoming Kings in the American Mirror: Two Centuries of U.S.-Thai Monarchy Relations (University of Hawai'i Press).
