events.title: Synchro and SimTraffic for Signal Coordination
events.description: Description This four-session online course (4 hours per session) provides beginning-to-intermediate training in Synchro and SimTraffic software and the recently published Highway Capacity Manual (HCM) 7th Edition: A Guide for Multimodal Mobility Analysis (TRB 2022 and HCS7). Using a combination of interactive lecture, question and answer, and virtual computer lab, you will become proficient in the network coding and use of Synchro and SimTraffic for signal optimization and coordination projects. Working on a real-world multi-modal project, students will use Synchro to incorporate a Bing aerial background, add/modify roadways, input intersection geometrics, enter multi-modal traffic volumes (cars, trucks, pedestrians, and bicycles), and signal timings to replicate / validate existing operations for signalized and unsignalized intersections and roundabouts. Students will also use Synchro to evaluate and develop optimal signal timing plans that reduce delays, stops, congestion, fuel consumption, and greenhouse gas emissions. The seamless integration of Synchro with SimTraffic, a microsimulation software, will be used to evaluate intersection operations and compare the differences between "isolated - macro-level" Synchro and "network-wide - micro-level" SimTraffic analysis that is recommended for multi-modal, closely spaced intersections and congested corridors. Lastly, this course will teach you how to review and understand the potential differences in delay, level of service, and queuing analysis when using the empirical (Synchro) analysis or the micro-simulation (SimTraffic) analysis. Topics IncludeDetailed review of Synchro input requirements Developing a Synchro network for a real-world multi-modal project Analysis of signalized, unsignalized and roundabout intersections using Synchro Multi-modal vehicle, pedestrian and bicycle LOS using HCM 7th Edition Optimizing signal timings for a single intersection that is added to an existing corridor Optimizing signal timings for a group of intersections Seemless Integration of SYNCHRO with SimTraffic SimTraffic Model Calibration and Application What You Will Learn Using a real-world project in a virtual computer lab class setting, students will be able to interact with the instructor as they learn how to develop a network and use the Synchro and SimTraffic software. This includes incorporating a Bing aerial background, add/modify straight and curved roadways, inputting intersection geometrics and pocket lengths, entering multi-modal volumes (cars, trucks, peds, and bicyclists), and signal timings to replicate / validate existing operations analysis for signalized and unsignalized intersections and roundabouts. You will learn the steps used to optimize and coordinate a group of intersections to reduce delays, stops, congestion, fuel consumption, and greenhouse gas emissions. Lastly, you will learn how to review and understand the analysis results and the potential differences when using the empirical (Synchro) analysis or the micro-simulation (SimTraffic) analysis for signal coordination projects. The materials in this course are based on the following references:Transportation Research Board. Highway Capacity Manual, 7th Edition, 2022 CUBIC Transportation Systems. Synchro Studio 12 Traffic Signal Software -User Guide, 2024 Who Should Attend No prior experience using Synchro and SimTraffic is necessary. This course is designed for traffic engineers, planners, and technicians in both public agencies and private firms who engage in improving signal system optimization and coordination projects using the integrated Optimization Module in the Synchro software.

events.title: Lecture | Towards a Transnational Disability Justice: Wounded Bodyminds and the Politics of Survival
events.description: In her new book, Disabling Relations (https://www.google.com/url?q=https%3A%2F%2Ftupress.temple.edu%2Fbooks%2Fdisabling-relations&sa=D&source=calendar&ust=1788721620000000&usg=AOvVaw2AEfvc0GMN5Yf3xDPscb0e), Dr. Kazemi draws on thirteen years of ethnographic research, hundreds of interviews, and her own lived experience to invite readers to bear witness to the lives of disabled dissidents, veterans, and civilians in the aftermath of Iran's 1979 Revolution. Her analysis spans multiple sites of disablement and survival, including dissidents incarcerated and tortured by the Islamic Republic, veterans and civilians wounded in and by the Iran-Iraq War, survivors of state-sanctioned punitive limb amputation, and survivors of gender-based violence. Through the concepts of "wounding" and "disability consciousness," Kazemi theorizes disability as a historical process of becoming and remaining disabled through unequal social relations of power, while also examining how survivors make meaning of, negotiate, and resist the conditions of their disablement.

events.title: Robert G. Strand | Nordic Capitalism: Lessons for Realizing Sustainable Capitalism
events.description: Why do the Nordics consistently rank among the world's happiest, most prosperous, and most trusted societies? What lessons might the Nordics offer the United States at a moment when many people feel growing frustration and anxiety about the direction of American capitalism?Nordic Capitalism: Lessons for Realizing Sustainable Capitalism (2026, Cambridge University Press; open access:https://bit.ly/3MSvrOp (https://bit.ly/3MSvrOp)) by Robert G. Strand explores a simple but urgent idea: capitalism must be rooted in democracy if it is to support freedom, shared prosperity, and sustainability. Drawing on research, lived experience, and comparative analysis between the Nordics and the United States, Strand argues that the Nordic countries offer practical inspiration for reimagining capitalism in the twenty-first century. "Where democracy is in charge of capitalism, the people win. When capitalism is in charge of democracy, the oligarchs win. In this important book, Robert G. Strand shows how democracies can stay in charge. Nordic Capitalism explains that the Nordic nations can be a model for the US, and how democratic capitalism serves the many, not the few." — Robert B. Reich, Former U.S. Secretary of Labor and Professor Emeritus of Public Policy, UC Berkeley Dr. Robert G. Strand is the founding Executive Director of the Nordic Center at UC Berkeley and Executive Director of the Center for Responsible Business at Berkeley Haas, where he serves on the faculty. He is also Associate Professor at Copenhagen Business School. His research examines how Nordic societies have organized capitalism and how companies pursue responsible and sustainable business, with attention to applications for reimagining American capitalism. Before joining UC Berkeley in 2014, he served as Assistant Professor at Copenhagen Business School following a decade in corporate America with IBM and Boston Scientific. He received a Ph.D. in Corporate Social Responsibility from Copenhagen Business School, an MBA in International Business from the University of Minnesota, and a B.S. in Industrial Engineering from the University of Wisconsin. He was a U.S. Fulbright Scholar to Norway at the Norwegian University of Science and Technology (NTNU).If you require an accommodation for effective communication (ASL interpreting/CART captioning, alternative media formats, etc.) or information about campus mobility access features in order to fully participate in this event, please contact ies@berkeley.edu with as much advance notice as possible and at least 7-10 days before the event.

events.title: Student Faculty Macro Lunch: "How Artificial Intelligence Shapes Science: Evidence from AlphaFold"
events.description: Abstract: We study how a frontier AI model affects scientific discovery by examining the release of the AlphaFold2 algorithm and its impact on structural biology and related fields of science. Structural biology is the field of science concerned with understanding the structure of proteins. Researchers in this field historically devoted substantial time and resources to experimentally solving three-dimensional protein structures. AlphaFold can predict these structures without running experiments. In July 2021, researchers gained access to hundreds of thousands of these AI-predicted structures virtually overnight. Yet, to date, we find that the rate of experimental structure determination has remained almost unchanged. Instead, researchers appear to use predicted structures to facilitate and complement experimental structure determination. Looking at downstream science that builds on protein structures, we find that basic research on proteins that had no structural information prior to AlphaFold increases by 23 to 32% relative to proteins that already had a structure, with the effects increasing dramatically over time. This represents a significant shift in the direction of research toward less-studied proteins. By contrast, the response of applied R&D, as measured by patents referencing those proteins, has been far more muted.

events.title: Seminar 221, Industrial Organization: Lucio Wasserman "Shrinkflation: What Happens When Package Sizes Change?"
events.description: JMC PracticeAbstract: Package sizes are one of the main features of consumer goods and one of the determinants of unit prices. However, they have received little research attention. This paper develops a method to identify size changes at scale, opening the door to systematic studies of this issue. We apply it to retail scanner data and show that size reductions are considerably more common than increases. Next, we estimate the size elasticities of demand over time using an event study approach. We find different dynamics in response to size increases and decreases. The demand response to size increases is immediate and stable over time. On the contrary, after size decreases, demand has a sluggish response: the size elasticity is smaller in the short term than in the medium term. An incentivized shopping experiment shows that individuals deviate from optimal behavior by responding less to size than to price, and provides evidence of attention as a mechanism. With the experiment, we test policy interventions, showing that the display of unit prices and of sizes more prominently can reduce welfare losses. On the other hand, size change labels can generate the opposite bias, with individuals responding to sizes more than what is optimal. We explain the empirical results with a dynamic demand that allows for inattention, paired with a supply model in which firms strategically advertise size increases but not reductions. Finally, using model-derived sufficient statistics, we evaluate the effect of inattention and of related policies on consumer surplus.Draft of the paper (https://drive.google.com/file/d/1_dmfFkjdc4QwcMT6gSoWWerCMXLU5spC/view)

events.title: David Szanton | India's Mithila Painting: Home, Rituals and Traditions
events.description: A talk by David Szanton (https://ethnicartsfoundation.com/about/), President of the Ethnic Art Foundation (EAF) and Former Executive Director of International and Area Studies, UC Berkeley, drawing on his newly edited volume, India's Mithila Painting (https://uwapress.uw.edu/book/9780295753225/indias-mithila-painting/), co-edited with Paula Richman. The presentation will examine the long-term transformation of Mithila painting from a domestic ritual practice into a distinctive indigenous art form characterized by an expanding repertoire of themes, styles, and subjects. Through an illustrated discussion, Szanton will consider the work of contemporary practitioners, focusing on the ways in which established visual forms and stylistic conventions are adapted to address immediate social, cultural, and political concerns. He will also discuss a significant turning point in the late 1960s, when paper became an important medium for Mithila artists, facilitating new modes of production, circulation, and artistic experimentation. The talk will further explore the diversity of artists and stylistic approaches that have emerged over subsequent decades, while highlighting the important role of the Ethnic Art Foundation in supporting artists and advancing the recognition and wider appreciation of Mithila painting.Event moderated by Lawrence Cohen (https://sseas.berkeley.edu/people/lawrence-cohen), Professor of Anthropology and of South & Southeast Asian Studies; Chair, Department of South & Southeast Asian Studies; Co-Director, Medical Anthropology Program, UC Berkeley. ————–DATE: Tue, Sept 29, 2026 TIME: 5-6:30 pm PST VENUE: 10 Stephens Hall Event live streamed on FB at ISASatUCBerkeley (https://www.facebook.com/ISASatUCBerkeley) ——��—–About the Book: Since at least the fifteenth century, Hindu women in the Mithila region of northern India have been painting images of deities, flora and fauna symbolizing fertility and prosperity, and floor designs that sacralize sites for ritual within their homes. Their artwork remained ephemeral since its plant-based colors faded over time. In response to an extended drought that led to widespread crop failure in the 1960s, the Indian government's All India Handicraft Board provided high-quality paper to the women of Mithila to test the income-generating possibilities of transferring wall and floor artwork to a new medium. The unique Mithila aesthetic, novel compositions, and precise linework won enthusiastic buyers in New Delhi and abroad. The small number of women painters expanded across the ranks of the social hierarchy and even included a few men. They developed individual styles and depicted novel subjects such as village history, their own life stories, the tsunami in Sri Lanka, social justice, protecting trees, and changing social norms. Major international museums now house Mithila collections, and individuals around the world own paintings. This volume, the first to present an up-to-date analysis of the history and practitioners of Mithila painting, includes contributions from Mithila artists, anthropologists, art historians, historians of Indian religions and specialists of visual culture, gender studies, and translation studies.About the Speaker:David Szanton (https://ethnicartsfoundation.com/about/) is an American anthropologist renowned for his extensive work in South Asian studies and education policy. Beyond his roles at the Social Science Research Council (SSRC) and the University of California, Berkeley, Szanton has collaborated with several esteemed institutions. He has authoredMithila Painting: The Evolution of an Art Form(2007) andMany Visions, Many Versions: Art from Indigenous Communities in India(2017). In 1971, he served as an assistant to Howard G. Schaller in the Ford Foundation's Southeast Asia office, contributing to the foundation's initiatives in the region. In 1980, Szanton co-founded the Ethnic Arts Foundation (EAF), a nonprofit organization dedicated to promoting and supporting Mithila art—a traditional women's art form from the Mithila region of India and Nepal. As president of the EAF, he has been instrumental in fostering cross-cultural understanding and appreciation through the arts. David's enduring commitment to anthropology, education, and the preservation of indigenous art forms underscores his significant contributions to these fields. events.title: Tobias Rees: What was intelligence?
events.description: The dual quests – to understand intelligence as it arises in biology and to build it in machines of our own making – have been with us for nearly a century. While neuroscience and psychology seek to characterize intelligence in terms of underlying neural mechanisms and emergent behavior, we still lack a set of principles that can account for how the interactions of many neurons within a brain give rise to intelligent behavior. Meanwhile, modern AI is following a largely empirical path to create a new technology without scientific foundation. While the resulting algorithms exhibit intriguing behavior, the working principles are unknown, usage risks are incalculable, and the path to further development is unclear. The premise of this seminar is that the current century will see the emergence of a new scientific discipline – the Science of Intelligence – that seeks to elucidate universal principles that govern intelligent systems, be they biological or machine, and that this will provide both much needed insight in neuroscience and a solid foundation for technological development. The seminar will meet weekly, featuring speakers from across campus and elsewhere, who will share their views on the open questions, topics of study and debate, and relevant disciplines that a science of intelligence will encompass. events.title: Geography Colloquia Series - California Agriculture and the Seeding of Silicon Valley
events.description: In the years immediately following World War II, California's Santa Clara Valley was an agricultural breadbasket to the world. A mere 30 years later, the Santa Clara Valley would be known as 'Silicon Valley', and would be the most technologically productive region on the planet. This transition from an agricultural economy to an urbanized, technological economy came to be seen as aberrational, or even an object of nostalgia. But in fact, the midcentury period of rapid suburban development out of an agricultural landscape laid the foundation for the housing and labour markets that came to characterize the contemporary Silicon Valley. This talk will discuss how the years following the Second World War set the stage for what Silicon Valley would become today. It argues that the roots of Silicon Valley's current housing and labor system were based in the agricultural regime of the immediate post-World War II period and the subsequent Cold War economy. Jeannette Estruth is an Assistant Professor of History at Santa Clara University and a Faculty Associate at the Harvard Berkman- Klein Center for Internet and Society. Estruth's writing has appeared in the Washington Post, The Drift, Urban History, IEEE Annals of the History of Computing, the Business History Review, and Enterprise and Society, among others. She is currently completing her book manuscript, "Think Different: Silicon Valley Activism and the Making of Modern American Politics," which explores the history of social movements, the technology industry, and ideological formation in the United States.

events.title: MBN Seminar: The surprising functions of adipocyte extracellular vesicles
events.description: Dr. Clair Crewe, Assistant Professor, Cell Biology & Physiology, Washington University School of MedicineTitle: The surprising functions of adipocyte extracellular vesiclesSummary: Adipose tissue (AT) protects other tissues from lipotoxicity during overnutrition by storing lipids and releasing adipokines that regulate systemic metabolism. In obesity, AT becomes dysfunctional, leading to ectopic lipid deposition, inflammation, insulin resistance, and oxidative stress that contribute to diseases such as type 2 diabetes and cardiovascular disease. From the discovery of leptin almost 30 years ago we have come to appreciate the robust role that adipokines have in inter-organ crosstalk to regulate metabolism in physiology and pathophysiology. Recently, us, and others, have demonstrated a new language that adipocytes use to communicate with other organs, extracellular vesicles (EVs). This language is powerful as these membrane-enclosed vesicles can carry any macromolecule including miRNAs, RNA, or enzymes, resulting in robust functional modulation of receiving cells at all levels of regulation, transcription, translation, and signaling. In obesity, AT releases more EVs that can propagate inflammatory and insulin resistance signals. This talk will explore the unexpected and broad functions of adipocyte EVs and factors that regulate adipocyte EV signaling. We found that adipocyte-derived EVs participate in inter-organ signaling by transferring damaged mitochondria to the heart, which may modulate cardiovascular outcomes in obesity. At the adipose tissue level, we found adipocytes EVs can signal to surrounding cells to recruit mRNA to restore expression deficits. These findings highlight adipocyte EVs as surprisingly versatile signaling system that may fundamentally reshape how we think about adipose tissue communication across the body.

events.description: Anna Dziapshipa was born in Tbilisi to an Abkhazian father and a Georgian mother. This situation had a profound effect on her childhood and identity, caught in the middle of two warring countries. In Self-Portrait Along the Borderline, the filmmaker returns to the Abkhazian family home built by her grandfather, located in a country that is off-limits to Georgian citizens and still not recognized by Georgia.

events.title: Are We Living in a 1938 Moment? How Autocracies Threaten the West
events.description: Are We Living in a 1938 Moment? How Autocracies Threaten the West Thursday, October 1, 12:30 – 2 pm *Lunchtime talk* Institute of International Studies 223 Philosophy HallREGISTER (https://forms.gle/aJvKjMEtZbCn3H1JA)The warning signs of the 1930s feel alarmingly familiar today: nationalist rhetoric, revisionism, military rearmament, political polarization. The liberal order is eroding, autocracies are rearming, and the West appears weaker than at any point in decades. In this book talk, historian and security expert Dr. Moritz Pöllath argues that these patterns function as an early warning system for the present: a new authoritarian axis — Russia, China, North Korea, Iran — is forming, exploiting a strategic power vacuum to impose a world order beyond freedom and democracy. The years ahead may prove decisive: between 2027 and 2030, the world may decide whether it descends into a new global systemic conflict, with a possible attack on Taiwan as its most dangerous flashpoint. Moritz Pöllath is an Assistant Professor of Public History at Ludwig Maximilian University Munich, where he teaches courses on the History of Democracy, US History, the Cold War, and history teaching methods for secondary schools. He studied Diplomatic and Military History at Hawaiʻi Pacific University and American History at the University of Cologne. His first book, Out-of-Area? NATO and Decolonization in Africa and Asia 1949–1961 (2017), explores the roots of NATO's global security policy during the early Cold War; his second book (habilitation), Narrating Freedom: Challenges to American and German Master Narratives in the 21st Century, was completed in 2023. He has held visiting professorships at the University of Leipzig and was previously a visiting scholar at the University of California, Berkeley. He is a fellow of the Cold War Studies Program at Harvard University and the University of Udine.

Kelley of Our History Has Always Been Contraband: In Defense of Black Studies.Sarah Haley's research areas include African American and queer history, feminist historical methods, carceral history, and prison abolition. She organizes with Scholars for Social Justice and is director of the Institute for the Study of Sexuality and Gender at Columbia University.

events.title: Chases, clusters, and surfin' birds: Effects of group flight on locomotor biomechanics and energetics
events.description: Context matters in locomotion biomechanics, through direct effects such as differences in terrain or the environment altering the physics of locomotion, and indirectly when different contexts alter the underlying trade-offs between different approaches to movement. Group or collective movement represents one such context and here I use field recordings and laboratory experiments to explore how group interactions affect fundamental aspects of locomotor biomechanics and energetics in bird flight. Specific examples include tandem flights in Cliff Swallows, the cluster flocks of shorebird species across a range of body sizes, and an experimental wind tunnel examination of the energetics of European Starlings flying solo and in small groups. These specific examples demonstrate the importance of group movement context in bird flight while also suggesting similar context-driven changes in other organisms, in other environments, and during other behaviors.

events.title: CCB Seminar: Markus Covert - The E. coli Whole-Cell Modeling Project: Accelerating Discovery via Comprehensive Biological Simulation
events.description: Abstract: Francis Crick first called for a coordinated worldwide scientific effort to determine a "complete solution" of the bacterium Escherichia coli. We have been working for some years now to complete a model of E. coli that takes into account all of the known functions of every well-annotated gene, in order to better understand and predict the behavior of this scientifically-relevant and industrially-significant model organism. Now that a majority of the annotated gene functions have been added to the model, our simulations have generated biological insights that change our perspectives about cellular biology and physiology. As examples, I will present our new findings regarding how metals are utilized in E. coli, as well as the effect of gene organization into operons, and the impact of engineering new gene content into the chromosome.Bio: Markus Covert is the Ram Shriram Chair and Professor of Bioengineering at Stanford University. Over the course of his career, his lab has generated several new exciting technologies to measure, analyze, and mathematically model the behaviors of individual cells. The lab is probably best known for constructing the first "whole-cell" computational model, which explicitly represents all known gene functions and molecules in a bacterial cell - an advance which was highlighted by the journal Cell as a highlight publication of the 40-year history of that journal. Markus is the author of the textbook Fundamentals of Systems Biology: from Synthetic Circuits to Whole-Cell Models. He has received several awards for his efforts to develop new technologies, in particular the NIH Director's Pioneer Award, and the Paul G. Allen Family Foundation Distinguished Investigator and Discovery Center awards. He has also consulted in industry, including on the scientific advisory board of Emerald Cloud Labs, and as an inaugural Ambassador at X Labs, (previously Google [X]). Finally, Markus has taught one of the most popular courses at Stanford for several years, an integrated "lecture, lab and lunch" course entitled Bon Appétit, Marie Curie! The Science of Haute Cuisine.

events.title: Authors Meet Critics: "Demos: How the People Ruled Athens"
events.description: REGISTER (https://forms.gle/KddCT6ubaNBAkJXY8) Join us on October 1 for an Authors Meet Critics panel on the book Demos: How the People Ruled Athens, by Daniela Cammack, Assistant Professor of Political Science at UC Berkeley, with a courtesy appointment in the Department of Ancient Greek and Roman Studies (formerly Classics). Professor Cammack will be joined in conversation by James Porter, Distinguished Professor and Irving Stone Chair in Literature in the Department of Rhetoric at UC Berkeley, and Kinch Hoekstra, Chancellor's Professor of Political Science and Law at UC Berkeley. This event is co-sponsored by the UC Berkeley Institute of Governmental Studies and the Departments of Political Science and Ancient Greek & Roman Studies. The Social Science Matrix Authors Meet Critics (https://matrix.berkeley.edu/category/event-type/authors-meet-critics/) book series features lively discussions about recently published books authored by social scientists at UC Berkeley. For each event, the author discusses the key arguments of their book with fellow scholars. These events are free and open to the public.About the Book In ancient Greece, demokratia meant "rule by the people"—but what people, and how did they rule? Scholars have long argued that demokratia signified the rule of all adult male citizens over themselves. In Demos, Daniela Cammack counters this view by arguing that demokratia meant rule by the crowd that assembled when a public meeting was held. This crowd was the demos, which the Greeks distinguished from orators, generals, councilors, public benefactors, and other civic leaders. Drawing on literary and epigraphical evidence as well as the key theoretical insights of Aristotle and Hobbes, Cammack explains how constantly changing masses of ordinary ancient Greek men ruled while their leaders were ruled over. This political system relied on kratos, the power to prevail militarily, epitomized by the victories of the Athenian demos in civil conflicts around 508 and 404 BC. In peacetime, the superior strength of the demos revealed itself in large, frequently summoned crowds of ordinary citizens acting as policymakers, legislators, and (crucially) judges, who wielded great power over politicians. Aristotle characterized the years 403 to 322 as the era of "ultimate democracy," and it was during this period that the Athenians pulled off a feat unmatched by modern democrats: making use of talented and ambitious leaders without being ruled by them. By contrast, the Greeks called rule by elected office-holders "oligarchy." As people today lose faith in democratic institutions, Cammack's account prompts us to ask if we've been doing democracy all wrong—or even at all.PanelistsDaniela Cammack (https://polisci.berkeley.edu/people/person/daniela-cammack) is Assistant Professor of Political Science at UC Berkeley, with a courtesy appointment in the Department of Ancient Greek and Roman Studies (formerly Classics). She holds a B.A. in Modern History and English Literature (2002) from Oxford, an M.Phil. in Political Theory and Intellectual History (2005) from Cambridge, and a Ph.D. in Political Theory (2013) from Harvard, where her dissertation, Rethinking Athenian Democracy, won Harvard's Noxon Toppan Prize for the best dissertation in Political Science. Before moving to Berkeley in 2019, she was a Junior Fellow in Harvard's Society of Fellows and an Assistant Professor at Yale. Over the past decade, she has published in numerous edited volumes and journals including Political Theory, History of Political Thought, The Journal of Political Philosophy, Polis, The Journal of Politics, Classical Quarterly, Classical Philology, and The Journal of Sortition. Cammack studies the differences and similarities between ancient and modern democratic ideas and practices, focusing on the themes of crowd power, deliberation, representation, and sovereignty. Authors of special interest are Aristotle, Hobbes, and Rousseau. Her first book, Demos: How the People Ruled Athens, will be published in May 2026 by Princeton University Press. A sequel, entitled What was Democracy? A Short History, is in progress and also under contract with Princeton.Kinch Hoestra (https://polisci.berkeley.edu/people/person/kinch-hoekstra) is Chancellor's Professor of Political Science and Law at UC Berkeley. He works on the history of political, moral, and legal thought, especially ancient, renaissance, and early modern political philosophy. Recent contributions to ancient political thought include "Athenian Democracy and Popular Tyranny," "Thucydides and the Politics of Necessity" (with Mark Fisher), and "The Liberties of the Ancients" (with Quentin Skinner). Another focus of Hoestra's research has been the philosophy of Thomas Hobbes (including studies of his theory of equality, obligation, democracy, tyranny, mixed government, natural law, and the rationality of justice); he co-edited The Oxford Handbook of Hobbes. Work that bridges these two areas includes "Hobbes and Aristotle on the Foundation of Political Science" (with Nicholas Gooding), "Hobbes's Thucydides", "Thucydides in the Renaissance and Reformation", and "The Melian Dilemma". From 1996 to 2007, he was a member of the Faculty of Philosophy at the University of Oxford, where he regularly taught graduate students in the Faculty of Classics and the Department of Politics and International Relations.James Porter (https://vcresearch.berkeley.edu/faculty/james-porter) is Irving Stone Professor in Literature and Distinguished Professor in Rhetoric. His teaching and research has followed a few different trajectories. One is a study of Nietzsche's thought, early and late (Nietzsche and the Philology of the Future and The Invention of Dionysus: An Essay on 'The Birth of Tragedy' (both Stanford University Press, 2000). Another is a study of models of aesthetic sensation, perception, and experience in ancient Greece and Rome, which he explored in The Origins of Aesthetic Thought in Ancient Greece: Matter, Sensation, and Experience (Cambridge University Press, 2010; pbk. 2016). A continuation of this inquiry is The Sublime in Antiquity (Cambridge University Press, 2016; pbk. 2020), which received the C. J. Goodwin Award of Merit from The Society for Classical Studies (2017). A further strand is Jewish literary and critical thought in authors from Spinoza to Freud, Adorno, and Arendt. His most recent book is Homer: The Very Idea (University of Chicago Press, 2021; pbk. 2023), which captures some of his interest in classical reception studies. Current projects include Existence, Crisis, and Faith: Selected Essays and Letters by Rachel Bespaloff, a Cambridge Critical Guide to The Birth of Tragedy (co-edited with Michael Forster), and The Cynics: A Very Short Introduction. Dylan Riley (https://sociology.berkeley.edu/faculty/dylan-john-riley) studies capitalism, socialism, democracy, authoritarianism, and knowledge regimes in a broad comparative and historical perspective. His first book, The Civic Foundations of Fascism in Europe: Italy, Spain, and Romania 1870-1945 (Johns Hopkins University Press, 2010), argues that fascist regimes arose paradoxically on the basis of strong civil societies in the pre-fascist period. Reviewers have called this book "the most original and provocative new analysis of the preconditions of Fascism that has appeared in years", and "brilliant and courageous". A second book, How Societies and States Count: A Comparative Genealogy of Censuses (with Rebecca Jean Emigh and Patricia Ahmed in preparation for Palgrave), argues, against state centered accounts of official information that censuses work best where there is intense interaction between state and society. He has started a new project investigating the connection between the meaning and substance of democracy in interwar and post-war Europe. Riley has also published articles in the American Journal of Sociology, American Sociological Review, Catalyst, Comparative Studies in Society and History, Comparative Sociology, Social Science History, The Socio-Economic Review, and the New Left Review. He is a member of the editorial committee of the New Left Review.

events.title: Erin Schuman: The 2026 Carla & Corey Lectureship Series
events.description: The Department of Neuroscience and the Helen Wills Neuroscience Institute (HWNI) are delighted to announce the 2026 Carla & Corey Lectureship Series. This event, created through the generosity of co-founding directors of the Helen Wills Neuroscience Institute, Dr. Carla Shatz and Dr. Corey Goodman, will bring outstanding neuroscientists to our campus to share their research and engage with our vibrant, interdisciplinary scientific community, spanning the full breadth of mind and brain science. This year's guest speaker will be Dr. Erin M. Schuman (https://brain.mpg.de/schuman), Professor and Director of the Max Planck Institute for Brain Research in Frankfurt, Germany, and soon-to-be Director of University College London Queen Square Institute of Neurology. The Schuman lab's long-standing research interest is the study of cellular mechanisms and neural circuits that underlie information processing and storage. The lab focuses on the molecular and cell biological processes that control protein synthesis and degradation in neurons and their synapses. The complex morphology of neurons, with most synapses located hundreds of microns from the cell body, presents a logistical challenge for the establishment, maintenance and modification of local synaptic proteomes. For her groundbreaking work on local protein translation in neurons and the establishment of its importance for brain development and plasticity, Dr. Schuman has been awarded the 2026 Kavli Prize in Neuroscience (https://www.kavliprize.org/bio/erin-schuman). The event will take place October 1, from 4-6pm at the David Brower Center, with a reception to follow. Join us for an inspiring afternoon of conversation and meaningful connections as we delve into the latest advances in neuroscience.

More than a neutral vessel for narrative, vaṭivam offers a way to understand form as an aesthetic practice, a material structure, and a response to changing social worlds. Bringing together scholars working across literature, performance, visual culture, cinema, and digital media, the conference will examine how Tamil narrative forms have been made and remade across time. events.title: Defending Democracy Online Through Social Media: Deep Fakes and Our Cognitive Security, with Alexa Koenig
events.description: Digital technologies are rapidly transforming how people live their lives, including their access to information. Social media and smartphones are affecting both the creation and consumption of news — trapping consumers in information "silos" that obscure alternate points of view — while deep fakes are threatening the quality of information found online. All of this raises significant risks for the functioning of our democracy. Dr. Alexa Koenig will discuss this new information environment, some of the challenges it poses for democracy — including our sense of cognitive security — and opportunities for uncovering the truth in this digital age.About the Speaker Dr. Alexa Koenig is faculty director of Berkeley's MacArthur-Award Winning Human Rights Center; co-founder of U.C. Berkeley's Investigations Lab; and a research professor at Berkeley Law, where she focuses on the role of new and emerging technologies in human rights research and investigation.

events.title: Welfare Effects of Information Provision on Environmental Externalities | Zac Pond
events.description: Job Market PresentationAbstract Information provision is frequently used to motivate prosocial behavior, yet its impacts on welfare are rarely measured. I study these impacts by combining a signaling model with a series of randomized experiments on personal carbon emissions. The model generates predictions for how information provision can directly affect consumer welfare by altering the relationship between emissions and inferred altruistic type. I implement three interventions, two that provide participants with private information about their emissions and one that publicly reveals them, and measure their welfare effects with an incentive-compatible willingness to pay elicitation. The private information interventions are positive-sum in consumer welfare, whereas public recognition is negative-sum. Nevertheless, 16 to 25 percent of participants pay to avoid receiving private information. Under public recognition, relatively high emitters incur significant utility losses while relatively low emitters receive no gains. I use these estimates to compare the social efficiency of different forms of information provision on externalities.

events.description: Oct 2: Nicholas Isherwood (MORRISON)TITLE: TESSITURA: VOCAL REGISTERSCONCERT: 8pm CNMATBIO: The Franco-American bass Nicholas Isherwood did musical, literary and theatrical studies at Oberlin College (B.A. in French Literature, B.M. in voice with Richard Miller), The Actors Centre in London and the Ecole des Hautes Etudes (D.E.A. in Musicology). An eclectic artist, Isherwood has sung medieval music with Joel Cohen, baroque music with William Christie, the Magic Flute at the Salle Pleyel, Wagner's Meistersinger with Zubin Mehta, several world premieres by Karlheinz Stockhausen and an evening at the Knitting Factory with Steve Lacy. His interest for contemporary music has led him to work with composers such as Sylvano Bussotti, Elliot Carter, George Crumb, Mauricio Kagel, György Kurtág, Olivier Messiaen, Giacinto Scelsi, Karlheinz Stockhausen and Iannis Xenakis as well as the leading composers of younger generations. He has performed both the Bach and Gubaidulina St. John Passions with Helmuth Rilling and improvised with Joëlle Léandre, Steve Lacy, David Moss and Sainkho Namtchilak. Isherwood has sung on five continents, including the greatest theaters in Europe and the United States (Ravinia, Tanglewood, the Disney Hall, La Scala, the Teatro dell'Opera in Rome, Covent Garden, the Châtelet, the Théatre des Champs Elysées, the Philharmonie, the Royal Festival Hall, the Concertgebouw, the Biennale in Munich, all three Berlin opera houses, the Moscow Conservatory, the Konzerthaus in Vienna, the Salzburg Festival, the Aix Festival, etc.) and with world class orchestras and ensembles (London Philharmonic, RAI Orchestra, the Philharmonic Orchestra in Paris, the London Sinfonietta, the SWR Orchestra, the Ensemble Intercontemporain, the Ensemble Modern, the Arditti and Diotima Quartets, etc.) Isherwood has recorded 70 CDs for labels such as Erato, Naxos, NEOS, Stockhausen Verlag and Harmonia Mundi. He has participated in films with Stockhausen, Aperghis and Frize for Arte, the WDR and the INA. In addition to his work as a singer, he has directed contemporary music theatre (SMIO in Orléans, Sons d'Hiver, Parvis St. Jean in Dijon, Teatro Regio in Torino, Stuttgart Opera, Tadashi Suzuki's theatre in Togamura, Deutsche Oper Berlin, etc.) and taught master classes in 5 languages on the French Art Song (USC, UdK), Olivier Messiaen (cnsmd in Paris), baroque singing (Cal State LA) and contemporary singing (Salzburg Mozarteum, ARIAM, UdK in Berlin, Munich Conservatory, Milan Conservatory, etc.), given lectures (Harvard, USC, Penn, Stanford, Berkeley, Freie Universität Berlin, IRCAM, etc.) and composed several pieces for voice (2 commissions from the DRAC and one from Art Zoyd). Nicholas Isherwood has taught at numerous universities in the United States, as well as the Ecole Normale de Musique and the Conservatoire National Supérieur in France, the UdK in Berlin and the Hochschule für Musik in Munich. He has published a book, "The Techniques of Singing" (Bärenreiter, 2013), as well as three peer reviewed articles (LIM, the Journal of Singing, Vox Humana). He is professor of singing at the Conservatoire du Pays de Montbéliard and professor of contemporary singing at the Conservatorio di Santa Cecilia.

events.title: Transportation Opportunities and Priorities for a New California Governor
events.description: ITS Berkeley will present Transportation Opportunities and Priorities for CaliforniaRoundtable at 3 p.m. in the Bauer Wurster Hall Auditorium on Oct. 2, 2026. ITS Berkeley will present the Transportation Opportunities and Priorities for a New California Governor Roundtable at 3 p.m. in the Bauer Wurster Hall Auditorium (room 112) on Oct. 2, 2026. Panelists will examine the major challenges facing California, explore how state leaders may address them, and review work in progress by the current administration. The conversation aims to identify lessons learned to better understand the immediate policy issues and responses. Key topics for the discussion include transportation funding, the future of transit ridership, state and national electric vehicle policies, deployment of autonomous vehicles, using vehicle miles traveled as a metric to evaluate climate impacts from transportation projects, along with progress in land use planning to help mitigate broader system impacts. Moderator: Egon Terplan, Senior Policy Advisor Panelists: Ken Alex, Director of the Project Climate at UC Berkeley Scott Moura, UC Berkeley Civil and Environmental Engineering Professor and Partners for Advanced Transportation Technology Director Susan Shaheen, UC Berkeley Civil and Environmental Engineering Professor and Transportation Sustainability Research Center Director Laura Tolkoff, SPUR Transportation Policy Director Bios:Ken Alex is the Director of Project Climate at the University of California, Berkeley, focusing on the most promising climate solutions and moving them more quickly to policy and scale. From 2011 to 2018, Ken was a Senior Policy Adviser to Governor Jerry Brown, Director of the Governor's Office of Planning and Research, and Chair of the Strategic Growth Council, focusing on climate, energy, environment, and land use issues. Before joining the Governor's Office, Ken was the Senior Assistant Attorney General heading the environment section of the California Attorney General's Office, and the co-head of the Office's global warming unit. From 2000 to 2006, Ken led the California Attorney General's energy task force, investigating price and supply issues related to California's energy crisis. Ken is a graduate of Harvard Law School and holds a B.A. in political theory from the University of California at Santa Cruz.Scott Moura is a Professor in Civil & Environmental Engineering (http://ce.berkeley.edu/), Director of the Energy, Controls, & Applications Lab (eCAL), and Faculty Director of PATH (https://path.berkeley.edu/). He received the B.S. degree from the University of California, Berkeley, CA, USA, and the M.S. and Ph.D. degrees from the University of Michigan, Ann Arbor (http://www.umich.edu/), in 2006, 2008, and 2011, respectively, all in mechanical engineering. From 2011 to 2013, he was a Post-Doctoral Fellow at the Cymer Center for Control Systems and Dynamics (http://ccsd.ucsd.edu/), University of California, San Diego (https://ecal.berkeley.edu/www.ucsd.edu) and a Visiting Researcher at the Centre Automatique et Systèmes (http://cas.ensmp.fr/), MINES ParisTech (http://www.mines-paristech.fr/), Paris, France in 2013. His research interests include control, optimization, and AI for batteries, electrified vehicles, and distributed energy resources.Susan Shaheen is a professor in Civil and Environmental Engineering at the University of California, Berkeley. She also co-directs the Transportation Sustainability Research Center of the Institute of Transportation Studies (ITS)-Berkeley and is the director of the UC ITS' Resilient and Innovative Mobility Initiative. Throughout her more than 25-year career, Shaheen has focused on sustainable transportation technologies, environmental/energy policy, behavioral understanding and environmental impacts. She is recognized as a leading international expert in innovative mobility strategies and was among the first to research and write about the changing dynamics in several areas, including shared mobility and autonomy. Her research focuses on electrification and alternative fuels, innovative mobility strategies, behavioral dynamics and public policy as it relates to sustainable transportation and social equity. Shaheen earned a Ph.D. from UC Davis and a M.S. from the University of Rochester. She is a member of the Transportation Research Board's (TRB) Executive Committee – serving as chair in 2021 and vice-chair in 2020 – and the California Transportation Foundation Board since 2022, where she serves as co-chair of the Scholarship Committee. Shaheen received the 2017 Roy W. Crum award from TRB for her distinguished achievements in transportation research. In 2016, she was named one of the top 10 academic thought leaders in transportation by the Eno Transportation Foundation. She has co-authored and edited three books focused on innovative and sustainable mobility, as well as authored or co-authored over 85 journal articles, 35 book chapters, and 200 technical papers and reports. Living in Orinda, California, Shaheen loves spending time with her husband, two boys, two cats, family, students and friends. She is grateful to live in such a beautiful place that reminds her every day of her deep passion for preserving the environment and planet for everyone to enjoy, especially future generations.Egon Terplan is CA FWD's Regionalism Fellow. In that role he researches and writes about opportunities to strengthen and improve California's system of regional economic development and planning. He has served as an advisor and consultant to CA FWD since 2022. He is concurrently a Senior Fellow at UC Berkeley's Institute of Transportation Studies where he studies and writes about the future of transit, downtowns, and cities. He continues to maintain a portfolio of external clients focused strategy and policy advisory services. Prior to 2022, Egon was the Senior Advisor for Economic Development and Transportation within the Governor's Office of Planning and Research and the California Strategic Growth Council. In that role he helped launch and manage "Regions Rise Together" a Governor's initiative which resulted in the creation of the Community Economic Resilience Fund (now California Jobs First) and the Regional Early Action Planning Grants 2.0. He also led interagency efforts around the future of regional planning and transportation investment. Prior to joining the Governor's office, Egon was the Regional Planning Director at San Francisco Planning and Urban Research (SPUR), the Bay Area's urban policy think tank. While at SPUR, Egon authored or co-authored dozens of reports and policy studies on the intersections of economic development, regional planning, workforce preparation, land use, transportation, and governance. Egon also spent more than five years with ICF International managing regional economic development strategy projects and advising cities and regions throughout the world on economic development and competitiveness. Egon received a Master of City Planning from UC Berkeley's College of Environmental Design and graduated Phi Beta Kappa from Swarthmore College in Pennsylvania. He has been a visiting professor and lecturer at UC Berkeley, Stanford University, the University of San Francisco, and San Jose State University. From 2021 to 2023 he held the Robert S. Cornish Endowed Chair of Regional Planning and Lecturer in City & Regional Planning at UC Berkeley.Laura Tolkoff is SPUR's transportation policy director. She believes that a sustainable transportation system is the scaffolding for a society that cares for the environment, that embraces public life, and that is healthier, more just, and more prosperous. In addition to overseeing SPUR's transportation portfolio, her areas of focus include public transit, land use integration, project delivery, governance change, and interregional coordination. Laura has worked for SPUR since 2015 in various roles, overseeing several strategic local and regional initiatives and was SPUR's first San Jos�� policy director from 2015 to 2017. Prior to joining SPUR, Laura held a senior role managing the energy and environment program at Regional Plan Association (RPA) in the New York Metropolitan area during and after Hurricane Sandy. She spearheaded federal, state, and regional reforms and worked in coalition to launch a federal design competition that brought over $1 billion to local climate resilience projects. Laura earned a Master's degree in urban and environmental policy and planning from Tufts University and a Bachelor's degree in media studies from the University of California at Berkeley. She is an American Leadership Forum senior fellow and was named to Mass Transit magazine's "Top 40 under 40" in 2019.

events.title: "Anti-Muslim Racism and Genocide" Featuring Prof. Sherene Razack (UCLA)
events.location: 3335 Dwinelle Hall (Level C) University of California Berkeley, CA 94720-2550
events.description: Event Description: This presentation examines anti-Muslim race-making and the question of Palestine; it explore how the figure of the Muslim is transformed into a racial rather than an exclusively religious figure in the colonial imaginary. Speaker bio: Sherene H. Razack is a Distinguished Professor and the Penny Kanner Endowed Chair in the Department of Gender Studies, UCLA. She is an interdisciplinary critical race and feminist scholar whose work engages several fields including Sociology, Legal Studies, Gender Studies, Ethnic Studies, American Studies and Political Science. With a central focus on racial violence, she explores how imperialism, colonialism, capitalism and patriarchy interlock to produce and sustain a racially structured world where racialized populations are marked as disposable and subjected to an unrelenting violence. She is the founder of the Racial Violence Hub, a virtual network of scholars (Racialviolencehub.com). Her books and publications examine settler colonialism, colonialism, neo-colonialism and global white supremacy with a particular focus on the gendered effects of anti-Indigenous, anti-Black, anti-Asian and anti-Muslim racism as they operate in law. Her two most recent books are: Nothing Has to Make Sense: Upholding White Supremacy Through Anti-Muslim Racism (2022) and Dying from Improvement: Inquests and Inquiries into Indigenous Deaths in Custody (2015).

events.title: Film Screening: Band of Outsiders
events.description: Would-be tough guys Franz (Sami Frey) and Arthur (Claude Brasseur) have little better to do than drive around Paris and act out scenes from B movies. But when they team up with Franz's English-class crush, wide-eyed Odile (Anna Karina), to plot a burglary, they stumble into the gap between playacting and reality. Jean-Luc Godard said, "It is not the people who are important, but the atmosphere between them." The atmosphere arises not only from the actors' interplay—their dance in a café and their sprint through the Louvre are among the most memorable and joyous moments in Godard's cinema—but also from Raoul Coutard's exquisitely bleak cinematography and Michel Legrand's jaunty, melancholy score.

events.title: Roadway Geometric Design in California
events.description: Description This dynamic three-day, in-person course provides a deep dive into the principles and best practices of roadway geometric design in California. Built for professionals looking to strengthen or refresh their roadway design knowledge and expertise, the course begins with the latest transportation planning perspectives and emerging multimodal design philosophies that prioritize safety, mobility, and accessibility for all road users. Students will work directly with the industry's most essential design resources, including the Caltrans Highway Design Manual (HDM), the AASHTO Greenbook, PROWAG, the 2026 California MUTCD, and other key state, federal, and local guidelines. Through real world examples, students will learn how to apply geometric design principles to evaluate constraints, solve design challenges, and develop context sensitive solutions for various design projects. This fast-paced, interactive course blends expert instruction, case studies, group problem solving, and hands-on exercises modeled on real projects. Students are expected to have prior knowledge of or experience with geometric design of roadways, and familiarity with the HDM, AASHTO, and CA MUTCD. Key Topics IncludeGeometric Design Basics & Planning Context Modern Design Philosophy for All Users Design Standards & Guidance (HDM, AASHTO, NACTO, PROWAG, CAMUTCD) Traffic Operations: LOS, Capacity, and VMT Roadway Segment Design (Cross Sections, Profiles, Drainage, Superelevation) Horizontal & Vertical Curve Design Sight Distance Fundamentals (Stopping, Passing, Intersection, Ped/Bike) Intersection Design (Radii, Turn Pockets, Curb Ramps, Signals, Roundabouts) Bikeway Design (Class I-IV Facilities) Pedestrian Facilities Design & Accessibility (ADA/PROWAG) Temporary Traffic Control & Work Zone Design Freeway Design Elements (Interchanges, Merge/Diverge, Mainline) What You Will Learn Students will gain a strong understanding of the principles and best practices of geometric design across multiple roadway functional classes, along with the external factors that influence design decisions. Who Should Attend This course is intended for transportation engineers and technicians who have some basic prior knowledge of or experience with geometric design of roadways, as well as for those more experienced who seek a refresher course. Requirements A laptop computer is not required but is encouraged for group exercises and individual break-out sessions. Participants should bring a pencil, pen, notebook, and engineer's scale for in-class exercises, and are encouraged to print out the course materials (electronic PDF to be provided) prior to the class.

events.title: CSLS Speaker Series: Losing the Law: How Legal Polarization Threatens American Democracy (Princeton University Press, 2026)
events.organizer: Center for the Study of Law and Society
events.description: featuring Deborah Pearlstein, Director, Program in Law and Public Policy and Visiting Professor in Law and Public Affairs, Princeton UniversityAbstract: The norms that have separated law from politics in America are eroding, making government by constitutional democracy increasingly hard to sustain. Losing the Law tells the story of how we came to this precarious moment. This powerful, persuasively argued book describes how a decades-long revolution in professional culture and legal thought is fueling the nation's authoritarian slide. It also offers essential guidance on what we can do to change course, not just by crafting institutional reforms but by resetting professional incentives and popular beliefs about the power and limits of the rule of law in constitutional governance. Looking behind the well-recognized politics of red and blue, Deborah Pearlstein charts the independent rise of "legal polarization"—a growing divide between lawyers and judges who believe there should be a difference between law and politics and those who no longer do. Drawing on original interviews and archival research, a close reading of American law and legal thought, and a sobering accounting of recent events, she unearths the conservative legal movement's foundation-shifting secondary effects as it established a new career pipeline from law school to judgeship, promoted partisan loyalty above professional responsibility, and popularized legal theories in irreconcilable conflict with long-settled understandings of how law worked. From the early role of unitary executive theory in kneecapping major post-Watergate reforms to originalism's inevitable rejection of precedent, Pearlstein traces how legal polarization has supercharged democratic backsliding under Trump 2.0. An urgent call to action by one of today's foremost legal minds, Losing the Law lays out the complex task ahead for those committed both to understanding the depth of the current crisis and to reestablishing sustainable constitutional governance in the years ahead. Cosponsored with the Edley Center on Law and Democracy (https://www.law.berkeley.edu/research/edley-center-on-law-and-democracy/)and the Thelton E. Henderson Center for Social Justice (https://www.law.berkeley.edu/research/thelton-e-henderson-center-for-social-justice/)

events.title: Distributionally Robust Newsvendor on a Metric (Vineet Goyal, Columbia University)
events.description: Title: Distributionally Robust Newsvendor on a Metric Abstract:We consider a fundamental generalization of the classical newsvendor problem where the seller needs to decide on the inventory of a product jointly for multiple locations on a metric as well as a fulfillment policy to satisfy the uncertain demand that arises sequentially over time after the inventory decisions have been made. To address the distributional-ambiguity, we consider a distributionally robust setting where the decision-maker only knows the mean and variance of the demand, and the goal is to make inventory and fulfillment decisions to minimize the worst-case expected inventory and fulfillment cost (where the expectation is taken over the worst case choice of distribution with given mean and variance). We present a significant generalization of the classical result of Scarf (1958) and give a policy with strong theoretical guarantees as well as good practical performance while maintaining the simplicity and interpretability of the solution in Scarf (1958). In particular, our policy first identifies a hierarchical clustering of the locations, and assigns a "virtual-underage cost" for each cluster. Our inventory solution ensures that for each cluster, the total inventory in the cluster is at least as large as the inventory level suggested by Scarf's solution for the virtual-underage cost if the cluster was a single point. We present a worst-case performance guarantee for our policy and also demonstrate that the policy performs well in practice. To the best of our knowledge, this is the first algorithm with provable performance guarantees. (This is joint work with Ayoub Foussoul)Bio: Vineet Goyal is a Professor in the Department of Industrial Engineering and Operations Research, and the Chair of the Center of Financial and Business Analytics at the Data Science Institute at Columbia University. He received his Bachelor's degree in Computer Science from Indian Institute of Technology, Delhi in 2003 and his Ph.D. in Algorithms, Combinatorics and Optimization (ACO) from Carnegie Mellon University in 2008. Before coming to Columbia, he spent two years as a Postdoctoral Associate at the Operations Research Center at MIT. He is interested in the design of efficient and robust data-driven algorithms for large scale dynamic optimization problems with applications in revenue management and healthcare operations. His research has been continually supported by grants from NSF and industry including NSF CAREER Award in 2014 and faculty research awards from Google, IBM, Adobe and Amazon.

events.title: Itay Budin: "The private life of lipids: small chemical changes that shape cell membranes"
events.description: Abstract: Our lab investigates how – and why – cells control the composition of their lipid membranes. In this talk, I will focus on our efforts to uncover how lipid composition is controlled in intracellular membranes and describe emerging biophysical models to explain its chemical diversity in cells. I will first highlight recent studies that demonstrate how surprisingly small modifications to lipid molecules drive membrane function. In the other, we uncovered how the shape of phospholipids – described by their spontaneous curvature – is a biophysical parameter that drives habitability and is actively maintained by distinct pathway in lipid metabolism. I will then focus on new chemical biology approaches we have developed to map phospholipids in cell membranes and determine factors that control their trafficking. A key advance has been the use of fluorogenic dyes in biorthogonal labeling reactions to enable compartment- and leaflet-specific detection of phospholipid pools. These tools allow cell biologists to interrogate lipid trafficking at ever-greater spatial details.

events.title: Decision Making with AI: Think Better, Choose Smarter (2026 Fall NOW Encore Series)
events.description: 2026 NOW Encore Series (https://hr.berkeley.edu/development/career-development/workshops) We are rapidly heading into an AI-driven future. At first, we feared it might cost us jobs, but now we see the bigger risk: it could cost us our judgment. When we outsource our thinking to fast answers, we lose the ability to ask better questions. To be ready for this future — to truly empower it — we must strengthen our uniquely human potential: clarity, critical thinking, and decision-making. That's what this workshop is about. In this interactive, hands-on session, participants will learn how to frame better decisions — before they ever open a chatbot. Using a practical tool called the Decision Framing Canvas, they'll work through a real business case and discover how to define decisions as real, actionable choices (not just goals or problems). At every step, participants will collaborate with AI — not to skip the thinking, but to deepen it. They'll use AI to challenge assumptions, expand options, and uncover what might be missing. This workshop helps participants take back control of their thinking in an AI-saturated world. It's not about better prompts — it's about better minds. Participants will walk away with a repeatable method to make smarter, clearer decisions in their daily work — and a deeper understanding of how to use AI not just as a tool, but as a thinking partner. No technical background required. Just bring your brain, your curiosity, and your favorite LLM (ChatGPT, Claude, Gemini, etc).Learning Outcomes: –Use the Decision Framing Canvas to define complex decisions as actionable choices between real options clearly. –Collaborate with AI to challenge assumptions, uncover blind spots, and expand decision options before jumping to solutions. –Learn key principles for working effectively with AI as a thinking partner — and apply them immediately to real decision-making scenarios.Registrants will be sent a Zoom link and bCal invite as this virtual workshop date draws near.

events.title: Failure by design: The California energy crisis and the limits of market planning
events.description: With Georg Rillinger, Assistant Professor of Technological Innovation, Entrepreneurship, and Strategic Management, MIT Sloan School of Management The Western U.S. energy crisis was one of the great financial disasters of the past century. The crisis began in April 2000, when price spikes started to rattle California's electricity markets. Decades later, some blame economic fundamentals and ignorant politicians, while others accuse the energy sellers who raided the markets. In Failure by Design, sociologist Georg Rilinger offers a different explanation, one that focuses on the practical challenges of market design. The unique physical attributes of electricity made it exceedingly difficult to introduce markets into the coordination of the electricity system, so market designers were brought in to construct the infrastructures that coordinate how market participants interact. An exercise in social engineering, these infrastructures were intended to guide market actors toward behavior that would produce optimal market results and facilitate grid management. Yet, though these experts spent their days worrying about incentive misalignment and market manipulation, they unintentionally created a system riddled with opportunities for destructive behavior. Join us at BESI for this talk as Rillinger illuminates the California energy crisis and develops a broader theoretical framework for thinking about markets as the products of organizational planning and the limits of social engineering.Register Now (https://forms.gle/NGwAc9WuQseojhox9) About the speaker Georg Rilinger is an assistant professor of economic and organization sociology at MIT Sloan School of Management, where he holds the Fred Kayne Career Development Professorship. His research examines organizational, cultural, and political reasons why technocratic expertise — from Nobel Prize-winning market designers to financial regulators — so often fails to prevent market failures, drawing on archival research, interviews, and ethnographic methods. He is the author of Failure by Design: The California Energy Crisis and the Limits of Market Planning (University of Chicago Press, 2024), which won the Viviana Zelizer Prize for Best Book in Economic Sociology. His work has appeared in the American Journal of Sociology, Socio-Economic Review, Theory and Society, and others.

events.title: How to Survive Authoritarianism: A Russian's Phrasebook for Everyday Life in America
events.description: How to Survive Authoritarianism: A Russian's Phrasebook for Everyday Life in America Thursday, October 6, 12:30 - 2 pm Lunchtime Talk Institute of International Studies, 223 Philosophy HallREGISTER (https://forms.gle/yD8LTQaNvyDeTDCa6)How to Survive Authoritarianism (https://wwnorton.com/books/9781324098799) offers Americans the tools needed to face the threat of authoritarianism today—from a country that's been surviving it for a century. Across the globe, far-right extremists are gaining power as checks and balances between branches of government dissolve at alarming rates. Author and activist Maria Kuznetsova and researcher Dan Storyev - who grew up in 2000s Russia when Vladimir Putin was tightening his grasp on the country and suffocating civic life - share the language that allowed them to talk about authoritarianism and to subvert it. Friends of Kuznetsova and Storyev's began asking what life was like in Russia, most having never experienced a dictatorship but increasingly worried they were about to learn. In attempting to answer their friends' questions of "How do you overcome fear of the state?" and maybe the most harrowing, "When is it too late?," Kuznetsova and Storyev draw upon their own experiences and the broader cultural memory of Russia to explore the basics of how authoritarian structures are built, and how ordinary people can resist. How to Survive Authoritarianism offers one hundred Russian idioms and turns of phrase for this purpose, from "apparatchik" to "samizdat." Some, like "power vertical," coined by Putin, give name to a hyper-centralized form of government with a top-down hierarchy of power. Others are more playful, like mnogohodovochka ("master plan"), used to deride bizarre, misguided state measures. Taken together, they make up the vocabulary we need to understand what is really taking place in our current moment and offer a roadmap to what might still lie ahead. In Russia, the dual reality of the truth, and what is called the truth by the government, has been the law of the land for generations. Over the years, a vernacular of double-speak emerged, one that helped everyday people make sense of how illiberalism makes itself known in daily life.

events.title: Lily Beckett | Poems on the London Underground (and Beyond)
events.description: Since 1986, Poems in the Underground has enabled commuters on London to randomly encounter poetry – classic and contemporary, British and international – while traveling on the tube, via poster cards slotted in the carriage advertising spaces. In conversation with Professor Eric Falci, Lily Beckett's talk will explore the history, development, and impact of Poems on the Underground as a public poetry project. Founded by Judith Chaiken (a native New Yorker), the idea for the project arose in the middle of Thatcher's premiership, a political moment characterised by an ideological turn away from the public and towards the private. Since its founding, the project has continued, uninterrupted, for 40 years, and has inspired multiple spin-off schemes abroad, with poetry being installed on transit systems in cities like Dublin, Paris, and New York. Adopting a socio-poetic angle, this talk offers Poems on the Underground as a prompt for further considering the value of poetry in public spaces. What does poetry do for the 'travelling public' of modern cities – whether in the 1980s in Britain under Thatcher, or today, anywhere in the world, in the age of AI?Lily Beckett is undertaking a PhD in Comparative Literatures and Cultures at the University of Bristol. She is currently a visiting scholar at UC Berkeley's Institute of European Studies. Her thesis investigates the connections between intermedial poetics and radical politics in the latter decades of the 20th century, across a range of global contexts. Before Bristol, she completed her master's degree in Comparative Literature at King's College London, and her undergraduate studies in Classics and English at Oxford University. She recently appeared on Soho Radio to discuss the lasting relevance of the 18th century poet William Blake, and her research papers can be found (or are forthcoming) in the academic journals Interfaces and Women's Studies.Eric Falci is a professor in the Department of English. He is the author of three books: Continuity and Change in Irish Poetry, 1966-2010 (2012); The Cambridge Introduction to British Poetry, 1945-2010 (2015); and The Value of Poetry (2020), as well as a number of essays on Irish and British poetry. With Paige Reynolds, he co-edited Irish Literature in Transition, 1980-2020 (2022). He is the series editor of Cambridge Elements in Poetry and Poetics, and the editor of the Cambridge History of Irish Poetry, scheduled to be published in 2026. He is also the author of a book of poetry, Late Along the Edgelands (2019). His research focus concerns the problem of form in twentieth and twenty-first century poetry. He teaches classes on modern Irish and British literature, and poetry.

events.title: Amara Ali | Beyond Delhi and Lucknow: The Lives of Urdu in Twentieth-Century Kashmir
events.description: A talk by Amara Ali, (https://sseas.berkeley.edu/people/amara-ali) Lecturer in Urdu, Department of South and Southeast Asian Studies, UC Berkeley, that examines twentieth-century Kashmir as a distinctive center of Urdu literary culture through the evolution of Shia marṣiya.Event moderated by Munis D. Faruqui (https://sseas.berkeley.edu/people/munis-d-faruqui/), Director, Institute for South Asia Studies; Director, Global, International & Area Studies (GIAS); Sarah Kailath Chair of India Studies; Professor, South & Southeast Asian Studies, UC Berkeley. ————–DATE: Tue, October 6, 2026 TIME: 5-6:30 pm PST VENUE: 10 Stephens Hall —————- ABSTRACT The history of Urdu has largely been told through its major centers, Delhi and Lucknow, with other regions positioned as peripheral recipients of a tradition formed elsewhere. This talk turns to Kashmir to complicate that geography, taking the twentieth century as its focus. This was a period in which Kashmir developed its own robust institutions of Urdu literary production and appreciation, from madrasas and administrative offices to mushāʿira gatherings and radio broadcasts. Multilingualism has long been part and parcel of Kashmiri intellectual and cultural life, with different languages holding prominence in different periods: Sanskrit, then Persian, and eventually Urdu. To trace how this played out in the twentieth century, the talk turns to Kashmiri Shia marṣiya, a devotional genre, and its jadīd (modern) forms, which register this movement between languages and make visible Kashmir's own productive engagement with Urdu. SPEAKER BIOAmara Ali (https://sseas.berkeley.edu/people/amara-ali) is a Lecturer in the Department of South and Southeast Asian Studies. Her research centers on the interplay of Urdu, Hindi, and Kashmiri literary traditions and Islam in South Asia. Her doctoral dissertation provides a literary examination of the Kashmiri marsiya (an elegiac poem), analyzing how this local form articulates a unique Kashmiri aesthetic, while remaining in critical dialogue with the broader Urdu, Persian, and Arabic literary traditions. Earlier, she completed her master's studies at the University of Cambridge, focusing on the celebrated Urdu poets Mirza Ghalib and Faiz Ahmed Faiz.Event Poster TBA —————— Event is FREE and OPEN to the public. events.title: Zionism in Translation: Encounters in the German-Hebrew Archive
events.description: n her new book, Zionism in Translation: Encounters in the German-Hebrew Archive, Na'ama Rokem investigates written exchanges by a range of literary twentieth century authors, including Hannah Arendt, Gershom Scholem, Yehuda Amichai, Ludwig Strauss, Erich Auerbach, Walter Benjamin, Leah Goldberg, Peter Szondi, Paul Celan, and Tuvia Ruebner. This remarkable bilingual archive encompasses not only letters but also drafts, reviews, and other ephemeral documents. Written in German and Hebrew, these documents were sent to and from Jerusalem, primarily in the decades following 1948. The writers at the center of Rokem's study contend with the genocidal violence that brought the rich historical relation between German and Hebrew to a seeming end. They also grapple, in different ways, with the new reality in Israel/Palestine in the wake of the founding of the State of Israel and the Palestinian Nakba. The bilingual conversation that crosses over between German and Hebrew in these letters thus centers around the question of Jewish fate in the twentieth century and is immersed in negotiations about Jewish nationalism, the Zionist movement, and the possibilities of Jewish poetry. In the space between German and Hebrew, Rokem argues, the protagonists of her study articulate forms of ambivalence and doubt that remain absent from their published writings. In this book presentation, Rokem will discuss forms of belonging and resistance that emerged in relation to the Zionist movement throughout the twentieth century, contributing to a more nuanced understanding of Jewish nationalism and its discontents.To register for this event, please click this link. (https://forms.gle/5p6thMQDtfz5LarP8)Na'ama Rokem teaches Hebrew and Comparative Literature at the University of Chicago, where she has served as director of the Joyce Z. and Jacob Greenberg Center for Jewish Studies and as chair of the Department of Comparative Literature. Zionism in Translation: Encounters in the German-Hebrew Archive (University of Chicago Press, 2026) is her second book. Her first book, Prosaic Conditions: Heinrich Heine and the Spaces of Zionist Literature, was published by Northwestern University Press in 2013. It uses the case of the reception and translation of the works of German-Jewish poet Heinrich Heine to argue that prose - as a figure of thought, a mode and a medium - played an instrumental role in the literary foundations of the Zionist revolution. Currently, she is working as one of the co-editors of the forthcoming Volume IV.2 of the Critical Edition of the Complete Works of Hannah Arendt (https://hannah-arendt-edition.net/index.html?lang=en) (Essays and Short Writings on Jewish Politics) and starting a new research project on Zionism and pedagogy. Rokem has been involved in a number of collaborative projects, including The Quest for Modern Language: Between the Mediterranean and the Black Sea (https://neubauercollegium.uchicago.edu/research/the-quest-for-modern-language-between-the-mediterranean-and-black-sea-1820-1948#:~:text=This%20is%20a%20collaborative%2C%20multidisciplinary,19th%20and%20early%2020th%20centuries.), and Translation Networks and the Stakes of Comparison: Convergences and Crossings Between Arabic and Hebrew (https://neubauercollegium.uchicago.edu/research/translation-networks), both sponsored by the Neubauer Collegium on Culture and Society at the University of Chicago, and the Oak Woods Cemetery (https://www.oakwoodsproject.org/) project, a public history initiative that uses a historic cemetery in Woodlawn as a site for teaching, programming, and researching the history of the South Side of Chicago, with a particular interest in the complexly intertwined histories of African Americans and Jews in the city. This project has received funding from the NEH, the Mellon Foundation, and the Women's Board at the University of Chicago. ��� If you require an accommodation for effective communication (ASL interpreting, alternative media formats, etc.) or information about campus mobility access features in order to fully participate in these events, please contact Jennifer Lipscomb at jlipscomb@berkeley.edu (mailto:jlipscomb@berkeley.edu?subject=Accommodation%20Needed%20for%20CJS%20Event) with as much advance notice as possible.
