events.title: Dean's Speaker Series: Lynn Barr on Reimagining Public Health
events.location: Berkeley Way West, 2121 Berkeley Way, Colloquia Room 1104
events.description: UC Berkeley School of Public Health Dean's Speaker Series: Lynn Barr on Reimagining Public Health October 6, 2026 5:30-7:00 p.m. Followed by reception 7:00–8:00 p.m. *or online via Zoom 2121 Berkeley Way, Colloquia Room 1104 (BWW 1st Floor) Featuring Caravan Health and Rural Health Innovation Program Founder Lynn Barr, (https://publichealth.berkeley.edu/articles/spotlight/alumni/a-transformational-legacy-for-public-health) MPH '11With an introduction from Dean Michael C. Lu. Health care innovator Lynn Barr has been at the forefront of a movement to reimagine healthcare for rural communities across the United States. After founding Caravan Health to help small, rural health care providers team up to manage patient care and the Medicare system, Barr was appointed to the Medicare Payment Advisory Commission, which advises Congress Medicare policy in 2022. Appalled by the low vaccination rates and corresponding high death rates from COVID-19, she founded UC Berkeley's Rural Health Innovation Program in 2023, which educates and mentors public health professionals from rural communities to empower them to drive changes in both policy and practice, providing 100 full-ride MPH scholarships to date in 30 states. Barr has led programs that have improved care for more than one million Medicare patients, and she's not done yet. At this special Dean's Speaker event, Barr will talk with Kimberly MacPherson (https://publichealth.berkeley.edu/people/kimberly-macpherson), faculty director for the Rural Health Innovation Program and MPH/MBA Program at UC Berkeley School of Public Health, about the lessons she's learned throughout her esteemed career on how and why to influence policy for the better health of all. events.title: Berkeley Book Chat with Diego Pirillo
events.description: The Atlantic Republic of Letters (Pennsylvania, 2026) offers an alternative intellectual history of early America. Focusing on Benjamin Franklin's Philadelphia, the book frames Euro-American colonialism as an intellectual enterprise, established not only through military and economic means but also through books, ideas, and cultural institutions. Through extensive archival research, Diego Pirillo (Italian) brings together two interconnected histories. First, he recovers the place of British America in the cosmopolitan world of the Republic of Letters, studying the communication system that facilitated the transatlantic circulation of knowledge. Second, he shows that knowledge was weaponized in the effort to survey and control North America. While fashioning themselves as independent and cosmopolitan scholars, Franklin and his associates were in fact deeply tied to political power and tailored their ideas to the needs of their patrons. They served as agents of empire and helped to devise and put into practice the colonial project. Not only were books, libraries, and cultural institutions funded by the wealth created by the slave trade and the expropriation of Indigenous land, but, as Pirillo argues, the very taxonomies and classification systems that Euro-American scholars devised directly shaped the colonial enterprise. The Atlantic Republic of Letters illuminates the relationship among books, intellectuals, and colonial governance, and explores the ways in which knowledge circulated and shaped conquest. Pirillo is joined by Brian DeLay (History). After a brief discussion, they respond to questions from the audience.

events.title: Tang Music in Contemporary China: Sensing Artistry Through Time
events.description: Tang Music in Contemporary China: Sensing Artistry Through Time October 8 Keynote Lecture (125 Morrison Hall) October 9 (125 Morrison Hall) October 10 (Hertz Hall)— Full program will be available later this spring — The resplendent court-entertainment music of the Tang dynasty (618–907 CE), born from cultural exchange along the early Silk Road, has always loomed large in histories of Chinese music. But in today's China, reconstructive performances of this music have begun to assert its place — as living, breathing performance art — in concert halls and social media feeds, too. This conference brings together scholars and performers from across the world, including leading and emerging experts from China, to present, evaluate, and propel forward global scholarly and artistic discourse on Tang music in the contemporary world. Papers will explore the material culture of the Silk Road, early notations and musical instruments, techniques of historical reconstruction and performance, and the place of historical music and dance in contemporary Chinese society. Three leading ensembles from China and the United States will give live performances of Tang music and dance, followed by a roundtable discussion bringing scholarship and performance into critical dialogue.

events.title: Cycads, Wild Black Peppers, and Amazonian roots: the role of plant specialized chemistry at three different scales
events.description: Specialized metabolites play critical roles in plant evolution and ecology, yet most of what we know about this rich and diverse organic arsenal comes from foliar tissues and local scales. As chemical ecology is being transformed by higher-resolution instrumentation and novel machine-learning approaches for data processing and analysis, scientists have ventured into larger-scale studies (geographically, environmentally, and phylogenetically). Furthermore, a more "holistic" understanding of plant chemistry has highlighted key differences in the likely mechanisms driving the evolution of chemical diversity across plant tissues. In this talk, I will present three research projects that highlight the role of plant specialized metabolites across different scales (from local to regional). This project also highlights fundamental trade-offs and constraints on phytochemical arsenals across plant tissues (leaves, roots, and seeds).

events.title: 2026 Gerald D. Feldman Lecture | Reckoning with the Past in Germany and the United States: The Case for Thinking Comparatively about Reparative Justice
events.description: German atonement for the Holocaust has been widely hailed by the international community as a paragon of national reckoning, and over the last decade, African American intellectuals such as Ta-Nehisi Coates have explicitly invoked Germany as a useful model in their calls for Americans to confront the legacy of slavery and other forms of state-sanctioned racism. In this lecture, Rita Chin, will trace the complicated, fraught 80-year process by which Germans have dealt with the Nazi past, focusing on developments and debates in the Federal Republic. She will consider the specific ways in which the German case is instructive for Americans seeking to pursue redress but also explore how Germany's vaunted memory culture has become fossilized such that it has sometimes become a stumbling block for a German society struggling to respond to contemporary challenges. Thinking comparatively about how to reckon with legacies of state-sanctioned racial harm, oppression, and violence not only presents Americans with a concrete template for imagining what reparative justice might look like, Chin suggests, it may also help Germans acknowledge the shape-shifting aspects of racism and perhaps even rethink some of the outdated aspects of their memory culture. Rita Chin, Louise A. Tilly Collegiate Professor of European History and Associate Dean of Social Sciences of the Rackham Graduate School at the University of Michigan, is a historian of modern Europe with particular expertise in immigration and human mobility, race and ethnicity, and colonialism and post-colonialism. Trained in European cultural and intellectual history, she has sought to apply these modes of inquiry to her ongoing interest in how difference and diversity have shaped the very terms of modern Germany and Europe more generally. Her research and writing have been supported by the SSRC, the Woodrow Wilson International Center for Scholars, the ACLS Burkhardt Fellowship for Recently Tenured Scholars, the Institute for Advanced Study in Princeton, and the John Simon Guggenheim Memorial Foundation. events.title: Matthew Shutzer | Until the Last Ton: Fossil Fuels in India from Empire to the Climate Crisis
events.description: A talk by Matthew Shutzer (https://history.berkeley.edu/people/faculty/current/matthew-shutzer), Assistant Professor of History, on his new book, Until the Last Ton: Fossil Fuels in India from Empire to the Climate Crisis (https://press.princeton.edu/books/hardcover/9780691265919/until-the-last-ton?srsltid=AfmBOorxSc-xwrFM8YrmGZbYMJ4vEm3ZcucGahHadYBaRZA9ySGhXWds), a panoramic historical account of India's ascent in the global fossil economy. Event moderated by Sharad Chari (https://geography.berkeley.edu/professor-sharad-chari), Associate Professor of Geography, UC Berkeley. ————–DATE: Thu, Oct 8, 2026 TIME: 5-6:30 pm PST VENUE: 10 Stephens Hall Event live streamed on FB at ISASatUCBerkeley (https://www.facebook.com/ISASatUCBerkeley) ————–About the Book: India is today one of the world's largest producers and consumers of fossil fuels, driving new investments in the global fossil economy and achieving record-breaking levels of coal extraction at home. As the planet burns from climate change, this entrenchment of fossil fuel dependence has left many searching for how we arrived at this point. Until the Last Ton provides a sweeping new appraisal of this planetary dilemma, uncovering how India became part of an emerging fossil capitalism that continues to shape the present. Matthew Shutzer recasts the origins of the fossil economy by showing how European industrialization unleashed a global search for fossil energy in the colonial world. Placing India at the center of this history, Shutzer traces how the highland forests of eastern India became early frontiers for global coal investment, transforming this landscape into the largest site of imperial overseas coal production across a century of colonial rule. At the heart of these shifts was a legal framework of subterranean property, which redefined local relations of land ownership and social power, while tying the growth of India's fossil economy to the progressive ecological destruction of the forest frontier. Following these dynamics into the postcolonial period, Until the Last Ton reveals the enduring impacts of colonial property on independent India's energy history, shedding new light on postwar struggles for energy development and resource sovereignty, as well as the violent conflicts over mining dispossession that have haunted India's economic ascent in an age of climate crisis.About the Author:Matthew Shutzer (https://history.berkeley.edu/people/faculty/current/matthew-shutzer) is Assistant Professor of History at University of California, Berkeley. He is an environmental historian of South Asia. His research and teaching focus on the place of the environment in global history, with particular attention to fossil fuels, agriculture, forests, climate change, and environmental politics. His work also connects global environmental history to histories of law, capitalism, post-colonial development, the earth sciences, and photography. His book, Until the Last Ton: Fossil Fuels in India from Empire to the Climate Crisis, is the first history of fossil fuels in colonial and post-colonial South Asia. It traces India's rise as a world-leading fossil economy in the twentieth century and examines the processes of empire, capitalism, and agroecological change that shaped this transformation. The book moves beyond the prevailing focus in the environmental history of energy on production and consumption, offering instead a longer-term perspective on land, subsurface property rights, geological knowledge, and mining conflicts. In doing so, it reveals the central role of agrarian development in shaping India's trajectory of fossil fuel dependence. Shutzer is currently working on a second book project examining climate change and the making of the Third World after 1945. Before joining the History Department at UC Berkeley, Shutzer taught as an Assistant Professor in the Department of History at Duke University. He previously served as a Junior Scholar at the Harvard Academy for International and Area Studies at Harvard University and as an S.V. Ciriacy-Wantrup Fellow in Natural Resource Economics and Political Economy in the Department of Geography at UC Berkeley. He has also worked as a researcher on several projects related to the implementation of India's Forest Rights Act in western Odisha. Along with Rebecca Herman, Rebecca McLennan, and Bernadette Perez, Shutzer is one of the faculty conveners of the Berkeley Workshop on Environmental History, based in UC Berkeley's Department of History. events.title: The Significance of Postcolonial Fascism in Cold War Korea
events.location: Institute of East Asian Studies, Conference Room, 2111 Bancroft Way, 5th Floor, Berkeley, CA 94720
events.description: Speaker: Sungik Yang (Arizona State University) Hybrid Event | RSVP/Registration Required RSVP for In Person Attendance at Bottom of Page Register for Virtual Attendance - COMING SOON Note: This event will begin on "Berkeley Time" at 5:10 PM. Talk Summary: The years after Korea's independence from Japanese colonial rule in 1945 were a time of extreme crisis that opened a space for fascist ideologies and discourses to gain ascendancy. In response to national division and political polarization and violence, there arose a heavily nationalist ruling discourse that openly promoted the supremacy of the homogeneous ethnic nation above all competing forms of identity while rejecting core tenets of Western liberalism, containing strong parallels with fascist ideologies in Europe and Japan. Furthermore, this hegemonic discourse pervaded Korean political culture for decades, helping to prop up authoritarian regimes in the country until the 1980s. This discourse, which I call "transcendent nationalism," was a product of the intersection of Korea's postcolonial and Cold War conditions. It sought to overcome Cold War divisions through an embrace of the Korean nation while maintaining colonial-era suspicions of Western capitalist modernity. Ultimately, the fascistic aspects of South Korea's post-1945 political culture reveals the liminal position that Koreans found themselves in during the Cold War, being pulled into the U.S.'s anticommunist orbit but expressing discomfort with American political and cultural hegemony. In addition, postcolonial Korea emerges as an intriguing case study to better understand the nature of fascism as a political discourse promoting an alternative form of modernity that rejected those of capitalist liberalism and communism. By analyzing how fascism took root in a postcolonial nation-state after World War II, we can also gain an understanding of fascism's enduring appeal in global politics even today. Speaker Bio: Sungik Yang is an assistant professor of history at Arizona State University. He is a political and intellectual historian of modern Korea, focusing on political ideology, nationalism, democracy, and historical memory. His forthcoming book is titled Nation Transcendent: Postcolonial Fascism in Cold War Korea.

events.title: Glenn T. Seaborg Memorial Lectures in Inorganic Chemistry
events.description: Erwin Reisner, Professor of Energy and Sustainability, University of CambridgeSolar Chemical TechnologiesInspired by the blueprint of photosynthesis, creating synthetic systems for the direct conversion of sunlight into sustainable fuels has long been a defining ambition of chemistry. While decades of research have been spent on developing solar water splitting catalysts to produce green hydrogen, recently a new generation of photosynthesis-inspired architectures capable of directly converting sunlight, carbon dioxide and carbon waste streams has emerged. This advance has been made possible by developing and integrating metal complex and biological catalysts with semiconductor materials and electrodes, together with the engineering of bespoke devices. This lecture will first introduce functional mimics of photosynthesis, which couple semiconductor light absorbers with immobilised (bio)catalysts to achieve solar-driven carbon dioxide fixation alongside water oxidation to oxygen. Next, an alternative strategy will be presented that replaces the challenging water oxidation reaction by the oxidation of waste biomass and plastics. This concept, termed solar reforming, simultaneously improves reaction thermodynamics, enhances overall rate of catalysis, and creates economic value through oxidative valorisation while simultaneously generating clean fuel. The ongoing demonstration of outdoor solar plastic reforming at the kilogram and square-metre scale illustrates the growing potential of this approach as a practical route towards circular solar-powered manufacturing. The lecture will close by giving an overview of emerging frontiers in integrated solar chemistry, including atmospheric CO₂ utilisation, advanced light-management strategies, and solar-powered cascade catalysis for selective chemical organic synthesis. Together, this presentation aims to provide a compelling vision for a new generation of solar technologies that combine carbon capture, plastic and biomass waste valorisation, and renewable chemical manufacturing in integrated, scalable systems. More information: https://www-reisner.ch.cam.ac.uk/

events.title: Critical Conversations: Transforming the Field of Black Studies with Selina Makana
events.description: Materialist Nationalism: Challenging the Heroic Masculinist Rendering of the Nation Nation building exists in an uneasy and fraught relationship with women. On the one hand, nations revere women for their social reproductive labor. In twentieth-century Africa, nationalist movements deployed the figure of "Mama Africa" to galvanize the masses for the fight for independence. On the other hand, women and girl women's bodies were used as battlefields in wars and political repression in the colonial and postcolonial period, albeit in different ways. This lecture focuses on Selina Makana's new book, Beyond the Battlefield: Women and the Nation in Twentieth-Century Angola (https://www.ohioswallow.com/9780821426739/beyond-the-battlefield/), to examine the meanings and complexities of Angolan women's lived experience of war and militarism and reveal the extraordinary means by which they contend with and contest the politics of the nation. Selina Makana is an Assistant Professor of African history at the University of Memphis. Her research and teaching interests focus on African history, gender and militarism, and African diaspora studies. Her first monograph, Beyond the Battlefield: Women and the Nation in Twentieth-Century Angola (Ohio University Press, 2026), probes the relationship between women, war, and nationalist politics in Angola. She is currently working on her second book project Paranoia and Pathology in the Colony: Hygiene, Health, and Colonial Governance in Early Twentieth-Century Angola, that examines the entwined histories of public health and colonial governance in Angola. She has published articles in Meridians: Feminism, Race, Transnationalism; Gender and History; and The Oxford Research Encyclopedia of African Women's History.

events.title: Organic Chemistry Seminar
events.description: Jared Shaw, Professor, UC DavisStereoselective Synthesis with Rhodium Carbenes and NitrenesLow-valent reactive intermediates of carbon and nitrogen—namely, transition-metal complexes of carbenes and nitrenes—display diverse and powerful reactivity in the synthesis of complex organic molecules. Our group has focused on rhodium carbene complexes derived from substrates that lack electron-withdrawing groups. The diminished electrophilicity of these intermediates imparts exceptional functional group tolerance, enabling the construction of architecturally complex organic frameworks. The development of new methods and their application to the synthesis of a variety of heterocycles, including several natural products, will be presented. In parallel, analogous transformations involving rhodium nitrenes have been employed to generate complex heterocycles. The discovery of the first five-membered aromatic heterocycles featuring point chirality within the ring will be described, along with discussion of their distinctive structural characteristics.The Organic Seminar Series is sponsored by the William G. Dauben lecture fund

events.description: A talk by Indranil Chakravarty (https://indrachakra.com/), film historian, screenwriter, and author, based on his new book, The Tree Within: Octavio Paz's Years in India (https://0235947a.streak-link.com/C3VGHy6fX8I10Qk1JABJW9Rn/https%3A%2F%2Fwww.amazon.com%2FTree-Within-Mexican-Laureate-Octavio%2Fdp%2F0143471651%2F%3F_encoding%3DUTF8%26pd_rd_w%3DF95xZ%26content-id%3Damzn1.sym.4efc43db-939e-4a80-abaf-50c6a6b8c631%253Aamzn1.symc.5a16118f-86f0-44cd-8e3e-6c5f82df43d0%26pf_rd_p%3D4efc43db-939e-4a80-abaf-50c6a6b8c631%26pf_rd_r%3DVR6CA1607Z5S9X17FJWB%26pd_rd_wg%3Dvlupw%26pd_rd_r%3D12aba704-4be6-41aa-b6f0-8da866b68464%26ref_%3Dpd_hp_d_atf_ci_mcx_mr_ca_hp_atf_d), that explores how Octavio Paz's years as Mexico's ambassador to India transformed his personal life, poetry, philosophy, and understanding of cultural exchange.Atreyee Gupta (https://arthistory.berkeley.edu/people/atreyee-gupta), Associate Professor of Global Modern Art and South and Southeast Asian Art, will serve as discussant. Event moderated by Munis D. Faruqui (https://sseas.berkeley.edu/people/munis-d-faruqui/), Director, Institute for South Asia Studies; Director, Global, International & Area Studies (GIAS); Sarah Kailath Chair of India Studies; Professor, South & Southeast Asian Studies, UC Berkeley.The Tree Within (https://www.amazon.com/Tree-Within-Mexican-Laureate-Octavio/dp/0143471651/?_encoding=UTF8&pd_rd_w=F95xZ&content-id=amzn1.sym.4efc43db-939e-4a80-abaf-50c6a6b8c631%3Aamzn1.symc.5a16118f-86f0-44cd-8e3e-6c5f82df43d0&pf_rd_p=4efc43db-939e-4a80-abaf-50c6a6b8c631&pf_rd_r=VR6CA1607Z5S9X17FJWB&pd_rd_wg=vlupw&pd_rd_r=12aba704-4be6-41aa-b6f0-8da866b68464&ref_=pd_hp_d_atf_ci_mcx_mr_ca_hp_atf_d) is the enchanting story of Octavio Paz's passionate love-affair with India where he served as Mexico's ambassador in the 1960s. Immersing himself in the country's rich cultural life and contemplative traditions, Paz travelled widely, forged deep friendships with some of India's finest minds, and produced several of his most inspired poetry and essays. It was here that he met the love of his life and experienced what he called his 'second birth'. In this richly textured and erudite work, Chakravarty reconstructs the inner journey of the poet by delving into multilingual archives, declassified diplomatic files, personal letters, and intimate interviews. Blending biography, cultural history, and literary criticism, The Tree Within is a luminous testament to the enduring alchemy between India and the world through one of the greatest writers of the 20th century.Indranil Chakravarty (https://indrachakra.com/) has taught film history and screenwriting over two decades at film institutes in India and abroad, and has made several documentaries. He studied at Presidency College (Calcutta), Escuela Internacional de Cine y TV (EICTV) in Havana, and earned PhD from Victoria University of Wellington, New Zealand. He has published extensively in international research journals about biopics, literary biography and cosmopolitanism. His earlier book publications include The New Latin American Cinema, India's Audiovisual Market, and one in Spanish titled Redescubriendo a Tagore. events.title: Berkeley Book Chat with Diana Martinez
events.description: During US colonial rule in the Philippines, reinforced concrete was used to the near exclusion of all other building materials. In Concrete Colonialism (Duke, 2025), Diana Martinez (Architecture) examines the motivations for and lasting effects of this forgotten colonial policy. Arguing that the pervasive use of reinforced concrete revolutionized techniques of imperial conquest, Martinez shows how concrete reshaped colonialism as a project that sought durable change through the reformation of environments, colonial society, and racialized biologies. Martinez locates the origins of this material revolution in the development of Chicago, highlighting how building this urban center atop exceptionally challenging geology made it possible to transform diverse global ecologies. She details how the material's stability, plasticity, strength, and other qualities served the shifting imperatives of the US colonial regime, playing a central role in defending territory, controlling disease, and constructing monuments to nation and empire. By describing a world irreversibly remade, Martinez urges readers to consider how colonialism persists — in concrete forms — despite claims of its conclusion. Martinez is joined by Matthew Shutzer (History). After a brief discussion, they respond to questions from the audience.

events.title: Aaron Gitler: Granulin loss and TMEM106B risk converge on lysosomal C-terminal fragment pathology in frontotemporal dementia
events.description: Frontotemporal dementia (FTD) is the second most common cause of dementia after Alzheimer disease. Mutations in GRN, which encodes progranulin, are a major cause of FTD. Common genetic variants in the TMEM106B gene modify risk of FTD and the effect is especially strong in GRN mutation carriers. Intriguingly, in GRN mutation carriers, being homozygous for the protective TMEM106B haplotype seems to confer near lifetime protection against FTD. Despite the strong genetic link between GRN and TMEM106B, how these two genes interact mechanistically has remained unresolved. Recent studies have revealed that a C-terminal fragment of TMEM106B forms amyloid fibrils and accumulates in the brains of older individuals and patients with neurodegenerative disorders, including FTD. How the production of this fragment connects to granulin deficiency is also unknown. Using lysosome immunoprecipitation, we show that granulin deficiency drives the accumulation of the TMEM106B C-terminal fragment within lysosomes in Grn-knockout mice and GRN-null human iPSC-derived neurons. Recombinant progranulin supplementation reduced TMEM106B C-terminal fragment accumulation. Isogenic neurons carrying the TMEM106B risk allele displayed allele-dose-dependent fragment accumulation that was reversible by progranulin. Structural and genetic analyses demonstrated that TMEM106B dimerization stabilizes the protein and limits C-terminal fragment formation. These findings define a lysosomal pathway linking granulin deficiency to TMEM106B C-terminal fragment accumulation and explain how protective TMEM106B alleles can confer resistance to FTD, even for GRN mutation carriers.Division(s): MTx (Molecular Therapeutics)

events.title: The neural basis of cuttlefish camouflage and social behavior
events.description: All animals form internal neural representations of the external world that guide their behavior. Cuttlefish, coleoid cephalopods related to octopus and squid, perform visually driven adaptive camouflage by dynamically altering the color, pattern, and texture of their skin to create an approximation of their surroundings – a process directly controlled by the brain. Thus, cuttlefish perform a remarkable sensorimotor transformation: they recreate what they see on their skin, generating a motor output that approximates the sensory input itself. In addition to camouflage, cuttlefish use their dynamic skin to communicate with conspecifics using a series of innate skin patterns that reveal the animal's internal state. We are using the cuttlefish skin behaviors to understand how the physical properties of the visual world are represented by patterns of neural activity in the brain, and how this representation is transformed into an approximation of the physical world on the skin. We have performed a series of experiments to develop the dwarf cuttlefish, Ascarosepion bandense, as a model to investigate the neural basis of camouflage and social communication. We have sequenced the genome, developed gene editing techniques, completed a 3D brain atlas, developed camouflage and social behavior paradigms, examined dwarf cuttlefish behavior in the wild, and adapted miniscopes for underwater imaging. Furthermore, we recently succeeded in generating transgenic cuttlefish that express genetically-encoded calcium indicators in the brain, permitting the live imaging of neural activity. We are now using these technologies to simultaneously record neural activity and measure behavior to uncover how visual information is deconstructed in the brain, and then reconstructed into an image of the physical world on the skin.

events.title: Munis D. Faruqui | Aurangzeb 'Alamgir and the Mughal Empire: A History Retold
events.description: Please join us for a special book launch celebrating Aurangzeb 'Alamgir and the Mughal Empire: A History Retold (https://www.cambridge.org/core/books/aurangzeb-alamgir-and-the-mughal-empire/A6421F92BBEEBA78238E75F4D636E7C0), the new work by Munis D. Faruqui (https://sseas.berkeley.edu/people/munis-d-faruqui/), Director of the Institute for South Asia Studies and Professor of South and Southeast Asian Studies at UC Berkeley. In this compelling reassessment, Professor Faruqui offers a fresh and nuanced account of Aurangzeb's reign, illuminating the ambitions, conflicts, and political pressures that shaped the Mughal Empire at a pivotal moment in its history. The conversation will be moderated by Abhishek Kaicker (https://history.berkeley.edu/abhishek-kaicker), Associate Professor of History at UC Berkeley. ————–DATE: Thu, Oct 15, 2026 TIME: 5-6:30 pm PST VENUE: 10 Stephens Hall ————– ABOUT THE BOOKAurangzeb 'Alamgir (r. 1658–1707) was the last of the so-called 'great' Mughal emperors. He remains a controversial historical figure: castigated for religious intolerance and placed at the centre of a narrative of Mughal decline by some; considered a great Muslim hero by others. In this richly researched exploration of Aurangzeb 'Alamgir's life and times, Munis D. Faruqui contests such simplistic understandings to unearth a more nuanced picture of the emperor and his reign. Drawing on a large and varied archive, Faruqui provides new insights into the emperor's rise to power, his administrative and religious policies, and the role of the imperial eunuchate and harem. By unpicking the complex dynamics of a long reign, from Aurangzeb 'Alamgir's accession to the last weeks of his life and his eighteenth-century memorialisation, this remarkable new history cuts through the many myths that have obscured the extraordinary life story of Emperor Aurangzeb 'Alamgir. SPEAKER BIOMunis D. Faruqui (https://sseas.berkeley.edu/people/munis-d-faruqui/) is a historian and the holder of the Sarah Kailath Chair of India Studies. His focus is on the Muslim experience in South Asia, especially during the Mughal period. His books include Princes of the Mughal Empire, 1504-1719 (Cambridge University Press, 2012), Expanding Frontiers in South Asian and World History, co-edited with Richard Eaton, David Gilmartin and Sunil Kumar (Cambridge University Press, 2013), and Religious Interactions in Mughal India, co-edited with Vasudha Dalmia (Oxford University Press, 2014). His most recent book is titled Aurangzeb 'Alamgir and the Mughal Empire: A History Retold (Cambridge University Press and Juggernaut Press, 2026). He is co-editor-in-chief, along with Ali Anooshahr, of the Journal of Mughal Studies. In 2014, Dr. Faruqui was one of three faculty recipients of UC-Berkeley's Distinguished Teaching Award. The award recognizes teaching that "incites intellectual curiosity in students, engages them thoroughly in the enterprise of learning, and has a lifelong impact." Dr. Faruqui is the current Director of both the Institute for South Asia Studies and the Global, International & Area Studies unit. In addition to the Department of South and Southeast Asian Studies, Dr. Faruqui is affiliated with the Department of History and the Department of Middle Eastern Languages and Cultures. events.title: Glenn T. Seaborg Memorial Lectures in Inorganic Chemistry
events.description: Erwin Reisner, Professor of Energy and Sustainability, University of CambridgeSemi-artificial Photosynthesis using Formate Dehydrogenase Semi-artificial photosynthesis interfaces biological catalysts with synthetic light absorbers to overcome the inherent limitations of both artificial and natural photosynthesis. Furthermore, this emerging approach can also unlock novel reaction pathways and chemistries with significant technological potential and thus provides new opportunities that are currently not available in solar fuels or algae research. This presentation will summarise our progress in integrating the redox enzyme formate dehydrogenase into bespoke hierarchical 3D electrode scaffolds, photoelectrodes and semiconductor powders. Specifically, formate dehydrogenase immobilised on electrodes enables catalytic CO₂ reduction to formate with electrochemical reversibility and can thus operate at very low overpotential with high selectivity. The design principles for the integration of formate dehydrogenase in bespoke synthetic 3D electrode scaffolds and a detailed analysis of the biocatalyst-material interface will be presented. The understanding of the biotic-abiotic interface ultimately allows for the rational wiring of the biocatalyst into photoelectrochemical and photocatalytic systems for the solar synthesis of fuels and chemicals. Overall, the lecture aims to demonstrate that formate dehydrogenase should be considered as unique model electrocatalyst for CO₂-to-formate conversion in solar catalysis as it enables performance currently not achievable by synthetic catalysts. A recent review on this topic is available: Liu et al., Chem. Rev., 2026, 126, 8034–8088 (https://doi.org/10.1021/acs.chemrev.6c00095).

events.title: Student Faculty Macro Lunch: "Risk Appetite and Monetary Transmission"
events.description: Abstract: We construct a new high-frequency measure of changes in risk appetite around Federal Open Market Committee (FOMC) meetings. Fed policy actions and communication have substantial effects on risk appetite, consistent with the literature on the risk-taking channel of monetary policy. Most of the variation in asset prices and risk appetite is unexplained by conventional interest-rate surprises, which points to an important role of risk appetite in monetary transmission. Proxy SVARs with two separately-instrumented monetary policy shocks—a risk-free rate shock and a risk appetite shock—show the empirical importance of this channel. Risk appetite shocks have large, significant, and theory-consistent effects on inflation, output and employment. By contrast, the effects of risk-free rate shocks become insignificant or switch signs as soon as a risk-appetite shock is included in the VAR setup. Our evidence suggests that monetary transmission works primarily through risk asset prices and risk appetite. Standard estimation of monetary transmission based solely on interest-rate surprises misses most of these effects for two main reasons: First, the impact of interest-rate policy on asset prices is time-varying and state-dependent. Second, central bank communication can affect risk appetite and asset prices in ways that go beyond changes in the expected policy path.

events.title: Jürgen Dinkel | All remains in the Family: A History of Inheritance in the US and Europe Since 1800
events.description: Over the next 25 years, Americans will inherit more than $100 trillion. Economists anticipate a "great wealth transfer" from the Baby Boomer generation to their children and grandchildren. At the same time, this enormous wealth will be distributed extremely unevenly throughout society. While a select few will inherit vast fortunes, many will inherit little, nothing at all, or even debt. This raises questions with renewed urgency—questions that have been debated in the transatlantic world since the American and French Revolutions: Who should receive a deceased person's estate? Who counts as family? Who should decide how an estate is distributed? How can the unequal distribution of inherited wealth be justified, and how can the rights to private property and equal opportunities be reconciled? In his lecture, Jürgen Dinkel traces the history of inheritance in the US and Europe since 1800. He demonstrates how governments, families, and individuals repeatedly negotiated the transfer and distribution of estates, thereby also renegotiating kinship relations, the bonds between the individual, the family, and the state, as well as the legitimization of wealth inequalities within their societies. Ultimately, this lecture contributes to the new histories of capitalism, the family, and the state, arguing that Euro-American societies from the 19th to the 21st century are fundamentally structured around inheritance and the family. Jürgen Dinkel is Professor of Modern and Global History at the University of Leipzig. His research focuses on the history of colonialism and decolonization, the Global South in World Politics, and European social history. His most recent publications include: Acknowledgments: The History of Academic Gratitude, in Bulletin of the German Historical Institute, Washington D.C. 76 (Fall 2025); "'The Rich Uncle from America': Transnational Inheritance Transfers between the United States, Germany, and Russia, 1840s–1980s," Law and History Review (2025); and "The Non-Aligned Movement: The Role of Diplomacy in Third-worldism and the Global South," in Oxford Handbook on the History of the Global South (Oxford UP, 2025). He has taught at the University of Michigan, the University of Miami, and, since 2003 as a professor of law at Berkeley. Simon is the author of three books and many articles on the criminal legal system in the United States and its relationship to shifts in American society and democracy. Omar Khan walks through the nearly five thousand year old city of Mohenjo-daro, discusses recent speculations about the Great Bath and the so-called Stupa mound, and raises many unanswered questions about this Bronze Age civilization while sharing recent perspectives and information. events.description: In the spring of 1985, thousands of UC Berkeley students took to Sproul Plaza to demand the University divest from companies doing business in apartheid South Africa—the culmination of over a decade of organizing. Featuring Jeff Chang, Pedro Noguera, Andrea Prichett (panelists), and Rickey Vincent (tour leader) —students who were directly involved in the movement—the symposium will feature a panel discussion, collection viewing, and tours to create space to explore the stories, complexities, and nuances behind the anti-apartheid movement. events.title: Inorganic Chemistry Seminar
events.description: Brandon Barnett, Assistant Professor, University of RochesterNon-Heme Iron Enzyme Mimicry Through Confinement Biological enzymes have evolved over billions of years to mediate kinetically challenging transformations under mild conditions and with excellent selectivities. Inspired by nature, our group works at the interface of bioinorganic chemistry and materials science toward the precise engineering of void spaces that can kinetically stabilize high-valent, bio-inspired complexes. This talk will focus principally on the chemistry of bio-inspired high-valent iron-oxo and iron-nitrosyl species that have been kinetically stabilized through confinement within a rigid macrocycle. The unique thermal stabilities of these species enable novel investigations of their photochemical behaviors both in solution and in the solid state. Most notably, photocrystallographic studies have illuminated novel C–C cleavage reactions mediated by "oxyl"-type excited states of a confined high-spin iron(IV)-oxo. Mechanistic studies of reactions arising from direct photoexcitation of this complex will be discussed. At the end of the talk, I will briefly highlight our work using dynamic porous solids for separation science and energy storage.The Inorganic Seminar Series is sponsored by Earl L. Muetterties lecture fund

events.title: (Julia Mahamid) Kuggie-Vallee Lecture: "In-cell structural biology at a systems level"
events.description: Kuggie-Vallee Lecture: (https://thevalleefoundation.org/programs/kdl) Recent technological breakthroughs in cryo-electron tomography (cryo-ET) open the disruptive possibility to image macromolecular complexes in their native cellular or multicellular context at close to atomic resolution, and can directly reveal how their different conformational states and interaction networks are linked to biological functions. We advance sample preparation techniques for in-cell cryo-ET, including cryo-focused ion beam thinning and 3D correlative (super resolution) fluorescence microscopy. Preparations of such site-specific 'electron-transparent windows' enable the assignment of macromolecular structures directly from the high-resolution three-dimensional stills captured by cryo-ET when aided by an array of methods, including computational patter recognition and novel developments of genetically-encoded molecular tags. Furthermore, integration of multiple data sources is key to the interpretation of the mined structural signatures. For example, using the genome-reduced human pathogen Mycoplasma pneumoniae as a minimal cell model, we established the synergistic application of whole-cell crosslinking mass spectrometry and cellular cryo-ET to determine an in-cell integrative structural model of actively transcribing RNA polymerases coupled to translating ribosomes. Our contributions to computational methods now allow resolving these molecular machines to high resolution, reveal small molecule antibiotics bound to their active site in ribosomes within the intact pathogen, provide snapshots of their structural dynamics, and illuminate functions of previously unknown macromolecular complexes. Such integration of cutting-edge methods unlocks an enormous potential for mechanistic understanding at a system-spanning level by in-cell structural biology.

events.title: Berkeley Book Chat with David Henkin
events.description: In Out of the Ballpark (Oxford, 2026), David Henkin (History) reconsiders the character, meaning, and delights of baseball by exploring the game's unusual features and the sport's many resonances with other aspects of modern life. To this end, he abandons several assumptions and mythologies that underlie most approaches to histories of baseball: that it is unique among sports and fundamentally different from other kinds of entertainment; that it is specific to the United States; that it has changed fundamentally in recent years; and that the keys to understanding it lie primarily in examining what happens on the field of play. Instead, Henkin moves across time and space to examine baseball's history since the nineteenth century and beyond US borders. He takes readers inside the structures of clubs and leagues, interprets the sacred scripture of rulebooks, and illuminates some of baseball's rites and rituals that are often associated with honor and manhood. He charts baseball's significance along the routes of American and Japanese imperial expansion and the shifting maps of race and ethnicity in the US. Baseball is found at negotiating tables that pit capital against labor and in pivotal moments in the history of mass media. He shows us how baseball might offer a complex and capacious space for thinking about such things as spectatorship, success, community, order, and contingency in the modern world. Henkin is joined by Alva Noë (Philosophy). After a brief discussion, they respond to questions from the audience.

events.title: Marius Wernig: Human iPS cell-derived microtissues to study neurodegenerative disease
events.description: Human induced pluripotent stem cells (iPSCs) and embryonic stem cells (ESCs) havebecome valuable tools to investigate disease mechanisms because they can bedifferentiated into various somatic cell types, including those of the central nervoussystem (CNS), which are difficult to obtain from primary sources. Microglia are theimmune cells of the central nervous system and are thought to be key players inboth physiological and disease conditions. Several microglial features are poorlyconserved between mice and human, such as the function of the neurodegeneration-associated immune receptor Trem2. iPSC-derived microglia offer a powerfulopportunity to generate and study human microglia. However, human iPSC-derivedmicroglia often exhibit activated phenotypes in vitro, and assessing their impact onother brain cell types remains challenging due to limitations in current co-culturesystems. We developed fully defined brain microtissues, composed of human iPSC-derived neurons, astrocytes, and microglia, co-cultured in 2D or 3D formats. Ourmicrotissues are stable and self-sufficient over time, requiring no exogenouscytokines or growth factors. All three cell types exhibit morphologies characteristicof their in vivo environment and show functional properties. Co-cultured microgliadevelop more homeostatic phenotypes compared to microglia exposed toexogenous cytokines. Hence, these tri-cultures provide a unique approach toinvestigate cell-cell interactions between brain cell types. We found that astrocytesand not neurons are sufficient for microglial survival and maturation, and thatastrocyte-derived M-CSF is essential for microglial survival. Single-cell and single-nucleus RNA sequencing analyses nominated a network of reciprocalcommunication between cell types. Brain microtissues faithfully recapitulatedpathogenic α-synuclein seeding and aggregation, suggesting their usefulness ashuman cell models to study not only normal but also pathological cell biologicalprocesses.Division(s): MTx (Molecular Therapeutics)

events.description: Speaker: Janet Poole (University of Toronto) Hybrid Event | RSVP/Registration Required RSVP for In Person Attendance at Bottom of Page Register for Virtual Attendance - COMING SOON Note: This event will begin on "Berkeley Time" at 5:10 PM. Talk Summary: COMING SOON Speaker Bio: Janet Poole teaches in the fields of Korean literature and literary translation at the University of Toronto. Her most recent book Patterns of the Heart and Other Stories (Columbia University Press, 2024) presents an introduction to the little known modernist writer Ch'oe Myŏngik (1903-?). Born and based in Pyongyang throughout his career, Ch'oe's work lovingly details life in that city and chronicles the hopes and dreams for a new society in the age of decolonization. A dedicated literary translator, Poole has also translated works by mid-twentieth century writer Yi T'aejun (1904-?), publishing a collection of his anecdotal essays (Eastern Sentiments) and a selection of his short stories (Dust and Other Stories). A new book project, "Decolonizing Style: Going North and the History of Korean Modernism," looks at the writings of Korea's modernist writers and artists who crossed the 38th parallel into what was to become the Democratic People's Republic in the late 1940s. The project follows upon an earlier study of modernist responses to the fascist regime of the late colonial era, When the Future Disappears: The Modernist Imagination in Late Colonial Korea (Columbia University Press, 2014).

events.description: In conjunction with the exhibition Private Frontiers (https://bampfa.org/program/campus-collaborations-private-frontiers-media-legacies-cold-war), BAMPFA presents A Missing Can of Film (2025), a 44-minute essay film by artist and filmmaker Naeem Mohaiemen. Commissioned by the EVA International and the Kochi-Muziris Biennale, the project explores the legacy of slain Bangladeshi filmmaker Zahir Raihan and the unresolved complexities of the 1971 Bangladesh Liberation War The screening will include a conversation between Naeem Mohaiemen (https://www.shobak.org/there) and Tausif Noor (https://arthistory.berkeley.edu/people/tausif-noor), Assistant Curator at BAMPFA. Co-sponsored by the Institute for South Asia Studies (http://southasia.berkeley.edu/), The Subir & Malini Chowdhury Center for Bangladesh Studies (http://chowdhurycenter.berkeley.edu/), and the South Asia Art Initiative (https://southasia.berkeley.edu/initiatives/SAAI) at UC Berkeley. —DATE: Thu, Oct 29, 2026 TIME: 7-8 pm PST VENUE: BAMPFA TICKETS: Tickets for BAMPFA members are now on sale.Tickets for the general public go on sale Friday, August 7 at 11 AM. Buy tickets HERE (https://secure.bampfa.org/33280/33347?_gl=1*ev5un9*_ga*NzQxNDczMzYzLjE3ODU5NjA0MTU.*_ga_SDH80YD3Z1*czE3ODU5NjA0MTUkbzEkZzEkdDE3ODU5NjA5OTAkajYwJGwwJGgw) —About the Film Commissioned by EVA Ireland International and the Kochi-Muziris Biennale, AMissing Can of Film (2025) traces the lost-left politics buried within Zahir Raihan's Stop Genocide (1971)—a film edited in the style of Soviet Realism and Third Cinema during the 1971 Bangladesh Liberation War. Raihan, a novelist and director, was abducted only forty-five days after the end of the war. A Missing Can of Film combines scenes from Stop Genocide with footage shot at the Bangladesh Film Development Corporation after the nation's 2024 July Student "Monsoon" Uprising, interrogating the film canister as a vessel of contested history.About the Artist/FilmmakerNaeem Mohaiemen (https://www.shobak.org/there) imagines rhizomatic families, malleable borders, and socialist utopias– beginning from postcolonial markers and then radiating outward to unlikely transnational alliances. In spite of underscoring a tendency toward misrecognition of allies, the hope of a future global left, against current categories of race, religion and nation, drives the work. He is author of Prisoners of Shothik Itihash (Kunsthalle Basel, 2014); editor of Chittagong Hill Tracts in the Blind Spot of Bangladesh Nationalism (Drishtipat, 2010); and co-editor w/ Lorenzo Fusi of System Error: War is a Force that Gives us Meaning (Sylvana, 2007).About the DiscussantTausif Noor (https://arthistory.berkeley.edu/people/tausif-noor) is Assistant Curator at the Berkeley Art Museum and Pacific Film Archive, where he helped organize the exhibition To Exalt the Ephemeral: The (Im)Permanent Collection. He previously worked as the Spiegel-Wilks Curatorial Fellow at the Institute of Contemporary Art at the University of Pennsylvania and at the Whitney Museum of American Art. Noor's writing, for which he has received awards from the Andy Warhol Foundation Arts Writers Grant and the Robert B. Silvers Foundation, has been published in various periodicals and journals, including the New Yorker, the New York Times, the New York Review of Books, Art History, and Artforum, as well as in various artist catalogues and edited volumes. He holds degrees from Dartmouth College and Goldsmiths, University of London and is a PhD candidate in History of Art at the University of California, Berkeley. ————————- Like us on FACEBOOK (https://www.facebook.com/pages/Center-for-South-Asia-Studies/76502306608) Follow us on TWITTER (https://twitter.com/ISASatBerkeley) For DIRECTIONS to the Institute please enter "Institute for South Asia Studies" in your google maps or click this GOOGLE MAPS LINK (https://www.google.com/maps/dir//Institute+for+South+Asia+Studies,+10+Stephens+Hall,+Berkeley,+CA+94720/@37.8710692,-122.2585002,19z/data=!4m16!1m7!3m6!1s0x80857c25babcc33d:0xe2ff7d5c1483db5a!2sInstitute+for+South+Asia+Studies!3b1!8m2!3d37.8710952!4d-122.2576645!4m7!1m0!1m5!1m1!1s0x80857c25babcc33d:0xe2ff7d5c1483db5a!2m2!1d-122.2576645!2d37.8710952).PARKING INFORMATION (http://southasia.berkeley.edu/parking-around-campus)Please note that parking is not always easily available in Berkeley. events.title: Merck Symposium
events.description: Jim Morken, Professor & Louise and Jim Vanderslice and Family Chair, Boston CollegeCatalytic Stereoselective Synthesis with Boron ReagentsChiral organoboronic esters are versatile intermediates for chemical synthesis. Not only are these compounds stable under a variety of reaction conditions, they are generally non-toxic and can be transformed with minimal generation of hazardous waste. An important feature of aliphatic organoboronic esters is that the boron atom may be replaced with an array of different functional groups through efficient, stereospecific transformations. This seminar will cover new strategies for the construction of alkylboronic esters from simple starting materials in a catalytic enantioselective fashion, and will also discuss ways in which these compounds can functionalized by catalytic stereospecific couplings. In addition, application of organoboronate-based transformations to address compelling problems in chemical synthesis will be discussed. Professor James Morken was born in Concord, California and obtained his B.S. in chemistry in 1989 from UC Santa Barbara working with Prof. Bruce Rickborn. He obtained his Ph.D. from Boston College in 1995 with Prof. Amir Hoveyda and was an NSF Postdoctoral Fellow with Stuart Schreiber at Harvard University. In 1997, he became an Assistant Professor of Chemistry at the University of North Carolina at Chapel Hill. He was promoted to Associate Professor in 2002 and in 2006 joined the faculty of Boston College. In 2014, he was named the Louise and James Vanderslice and Family Chaired Professor of Chemistry at Boston College. Professor Morken's research focuses on the development of transition-metal-catalyzed asymmetric processes and their use in complex molecule synthesis. He is particularly interested in the study and development of catalytic enantioselective reactions involving organoboron reagents. Because of the broad array of reactions that available to organoboronates, these types of process can be employed to address a number of compelling problems in the construction of organic frameworks.

events.title: Harold S. Johnston Lecture
events.description: Steven Brown, Deputy Director, NOAA Chemical Sciences LaboratoryPyrogenic Skies: Photochemistry, heterogeneous chemistry and air quality impacts of wildfire smoke As wildfires have increased in frequency and intensity across North America, their emissions have become a driver of regional air quality degradation. Biomass burning is a large source of ozone precursors, nitrogen oxides (NOx) and volatile organic compounds (VOCs), as well as particulate matter that impacts air quality directly and also drives heterogeneous chemical processes. Photochemistry within smoke plumes creates pyrogenic ozone over a variety of timescales, leading to short- and long-range transport and widespread increases in the ozone background. Mixing and entrainment of smoke that is rich in pyrogenic VOCs into NOx-rich urban areas alters regional photochemistry and can further enhance ozone production. However, aerosol loads associated with smoke layers may also suppress photochemistry. Heterogeneous chemistry in smoke plumes influences atmospheric composition through a different set of chemical cycles that affect both the lower and upper atmosphere. A series of recent airborne and ground-based field studies has investigated these chemical processes in biomass burning influenced air. These include the 2019 Fire Influence on Regional to Global Environments and Air Quality (FIREX-AQ), the 2022 California Fire Dynamics Experiment (CalFiDE), the 2023 Atmospheric Emissions and Reactivity Observed from Megacities to Marine Areas (AEROMMA) campaign, the 2024 Utah Summer Ozone study, and others. These studies provide new insights into the biomass burning influence on tropospheric ozone at all scales, from near field plume chemistry to the global remote troposphere, and from the continental background to local urban influence.

events.title: Berkeley Book Chat with Atreyee Gupta
events.description: Atreyee Gupta takes a revelatory look at modernism in India, exploring art's role in decolonization and aesthetic discourse across the Global South. Modernism's peak in the interwar and postwar decades coincided with the eruption of antifascist and decolonization movements globally, including the League against Imperialism, the Bandung Asian-African Conference, and the Non-Aligned Movement. Viewing artistic practices through the lens of the radical intellectual possibilities that these epoch-making events prompted, Atreyee Gupta (History of Art) uncovers a modernist internationalism incongruous with Westernist cultural hegemonies. Modernism, she shows, cannot be separated from concepts of freedom and autonomy generated by Third World political struggles. Gupta mobilizes concepts including liberation, anti-imperialism, development, and modernization as essential analytic categories for art history, reorienting our understanding of both global modernism and Indian art. Intertwining stories of art and liberation, aesthetics and decolonization, and intellectual practices and political revolution in the Third World, or what is now known as the Global South, Non-Aligned (Yale, 2025) follows the far-flung interwar and postwar networks in which Indian artists and intellectuals such as Francis N. Souza, Abanindranath and Gaganendranath Tagore, and Jagdish Swaminathan participated alongside interlocutors like W. E. B. Du Bois, Richard Wright, Octavio Paz, André Malraux, and Le Corbusier in Asia, Africa, Europe, and the Americas.

events.title: Teacher Organizing Across the Americas: Diverse Strategies for Transforming Unions, Schools, and Society
events.description: Teacher Organizing Across the Americas explores why teachers' unions in Brazil, Mexico, and the United States, representing similar constituencies and fighting for comparable goals, have embraced radically different strategies. Through an ethnographic comparison of teacher organizing in São Paulo, Oaxaca, and New York, the book focuses on three key strategies in teacher organizing—leftist party politics, autonomist politics, and interest group politics—to demonstrate how the strategic choices teachers make matter for both schools and society. In São Paulo, teachers' leftist party politics helped to elect pro-labor presidents five times, with significant social reforms; yet these same politics failed to influence education policy and led to factionalism within the union. In Oaxaca, teachers' autonomous politics led to robust cultural initiatives, an innovative pedagogical proposal, and the capacity to boycott national education reforms. Finally, in many U.S. cities in the 2000s, teachers rejected interest group politics in favor of rank-and-file caucuses that prioritized union-community coalitions and racial justice, which also created new fault lines within the unions and an ambiguous relationship with electoral politics. Teaching Organizing Across the Americas offers important lessons for both scholars and activists interested in transforming institutions like unions to promote more just schools and societies. Rebecca Tarlau is Associate Professor of Education at Stanford University and former Associate Professor of Labor and Employment Relations at Pennsylvania State University, where she was the co-founder of the Consortium for Social Movements and Education Research and Practice. Her ethnographic research focuses on theories of the state and state-society relations; social movements and popular education; Latin American education and development; and labor movements and teachers' work. She is the author of the award-winning Occupying School, Occupying Land: How the Landless Workers Movement Transformed Brazilian Education (OUP, 2019).

events.title: Condensed Matter Seminar with Harold Hwang: Superconductivity in layered nickelates
events.description: Superconductivity in layered nickelates Unconventional superconductivity in proximity to various strongly correlated phases has been a recurring theme in materials as diverse as heavy fermion compounds, cuprates, pnictides, and twisted bilayer graphene. Here we will discuss a growing family of layered nickelate superconductors. The initial discovery of superconductivity in infinite-layer nickelates was motivated by looking for an electronic analog of the cuprates. Notable aspects are a doping-dependent superconducting dome, strong magnetic fluctuations, and a landscape of unusual normal state properties from which superconductivity emerges. The subsequent discovery of superconductivity in bulk La3Ni2O7 under high pressure is quite intriguing, in that the d-electron configuration is a priori quite different. Recently, we have used epitaxial strain in (La,Pr)3Ni2O7 thin films to stabilize superconductivity at ambient pressure, which has enabled their extend experimental study and development.Bio: Harold Y. Hwang is the Shadi and Omid Farokhzad Professor in the School of Humanities and Sciences, of Applied Physics (Stanford University), of Photon Science (SLAC National Accelerator Laboratory), Senior Fellow of the Precourt Institute for Energy, and Director of the Stanford Institute for Materials and Energy Sciences. He received a BS in Physics, BS and MS in Electrical Engineering from MIT (1993), and a PhD in Physics from Princeton University (1997). He was formerly a Member of Technical Staff at Bell Laboratories (1996-2003) and on the faculty at the University of Tokyo (2003-2010). His research is in condensed matter and materials physics, with a focus on correlated electrons and emergent phenomena in quantum materials, and heterostructures for energy applications and devices. He is a fellow of the American Physical Society, the American Academy of Arts and Sciences, and member of the National Academy of Sciences. Recognitions include the MRS Outstanding Young Investigator Award (2005), the IBM Japan Science Prize (Physics, 2008), the Ho-Am Prize (Science, 2013), the Europhysics Prize (2014, with Jochen Mannhart and Jean-Marc Triscone), and the McGroddy Prize (2024).

events.title: Physics Colloquium with Wallace Marshall: Learning without a brain - how a single cell processes information
events.description: Learning without a brain - how a single cell processes information Abstract: Cells show a range of complex behaviors which might normally associated with cognition, including basic forms of learning such as habituation. The giant single-celled ciliate Stentor coeruleus is a pond-dwelling organism that attaches to substrates like pond plants and filter feeds by means of a ring of cilia at one end of the cell. Stentor cells can contract in response to mechanical stimulation, an effective escape mechanism but energetically costly. To avoid contracting due to random collision with non-threatening things like algae or pond plants, but still allow contraction when a large predator attacks, Stentor cells use a simple form of learning: when a cell is mechanically stimulated over and over again, it will gradually stop responding, representing a case of habituation. Our goal is to understand how a single cell learns, without a nervous system. We have developed automated devices for applying series of mechanical stimuli under computer control, which we are now using to test predictions of computational models for learning based on known or plausible biochemical mechanisms. Using this approach we have formulated a simplified biochemical model invoking known or suspected processes, which can account for all prior observations as well as new experiments designed to test the model. Based on this framework, we have investigated the molecular pathways involved in learning in Stentor, which suggests a role for CamKII kinase signaling in the learning process. Currently we are using a frequency domain analysis to probe the learning process, and find that the cell acts like a low pass filter with a fractional order transfer function, which provides us with a new way to discriminate among potential learning mechanisms. Biography: Wallace Marshall is Professor of Biochemistry and Biophysics at the University of California San Francisco. A native Long‐Islander, he received his bachelor's degrees in Electrical Engineering and Biochemistry from the State University of New York at Stony Brook, and his Ph.D. in Biochemistry from UC San Francisco, where he studied organization of chromosomes within the nucleus with John Sedat. He then moved to Yale University for postdoctoral studies with Joel Rosenbaum, where he became interested in questions of organelle size control and cell organization, using cilia, flagella, and centrioles as model systems. In 2003, he joined the faculty at UCSF where he continues to study questions of cellular organization in a variety of model organisms including green algae, yeast, ciliates, and mammalian cells. In recent years, his research program has expanded to include cellular engineering and the study of learning and computation in single cells. Dr. Marshall is an elected Fellow of the American Society for Cell Biology, former co‐director of the Physiology summer course at the Marine Biological Laboratory in Woods Hole, Massachusetts, and he currently is Director of the Center for Cellular Construction, an NSF Science and Technology Center (STC) devoted to engineering cells and tissues.

events.title: The Bomb in/and/out of the Archive. feat. Zoé Samudzi
events.description: An Art, Technology, & Culture Colloquium lecture with Zoé Samudzi Postdoctoral scholar in the Department of African American and Africana Studies at Ohio State University - Monday, November 9, 2026 5:00 — 6:30 PM Eugene Jarvis Auditorium,Grimes Engineering Center (http://engineering.berkeley.edu/about/facilities/grimes-engineering-center/) RSVP here (https://docs.google.com/forms/d/e/1FAIpQLSeykJAzTsXRPcjwOetCQvBjTYgUR_hNZbyFZzKTNKnwucsB-Q/viewform?usp=publish-editor)! Save the event to your bCal here (https://calendar.google.com/calendar/event?action=TEMPLATE&tmeid=MHRhNmwwNmJwZGxrMGFvZjlkZ3M5MG1xc2IgZDV1NWVrN2o4aXBvZDBvOGlxNDE1ZTFhdnNAZw&tmsrc=d5u5ek7j8ipod0o8iq415e1avs%40group.calendar.google.com)! - Begun during her 2026 residency at La Becque in Switzerland, Zoé Samudzi presents the inaugural project of the research constellation "Can the African Steal?" Through archival photographs of the Belgian Congo (c. 1929-30) at Photo Elysée in Lausanne, Samudzi stitches together a variegated visual forensic through image absence through the deployment of the black planetary (after Canham and Seedat) as an onto-epistemic and transnational geographic frame. The negative spaces in the Swiss archive enable a positively articulated materiality of the atomic bomb. Her tracing of uranium extraction and/as warcraft conjoins King Leopold's free state and the Katangese mines in the Belgian Congo, the Trinity test in Los Alamos and Operation Crossroads in the Marshall Islands, and the bombings of Hiroshima and Nagasaki and nuclear afterlives in Japan. About Zoé Samudzi Zoé Samudzi is a postdoctoral scholar in the Department of African American and Africana Studies at The Ohio State University. She holds a PhD in Medical Sociology from the University of California, San Francisco. Her research contends with genocide memory and the multiplicity of denialisms, political mythologies of the postcolonial African state, visuality and the ethics of photographic seeing and witnessing, and the spatialities of racecraft and dispossession. An art critic and writer, Samudzi is an associate editor with Parapraxis Magazine, a popular magazine dedicated to psychoanalytic thinking. She is a 2026 Public Parking editorial resident, a 2026 Andy Warhol Foundation Arts Writers Grant grantee for her project, "The Citizen and the Anthropophage: Postwar/Postcolonial Italian Memory and the Cannibal Boom," a 2026 resident at La Becque's Principal Residency Program, and an awardee of the 2026 Fire Station Studios' International Curator Residency.

events.title: Organic Chemistry Seminar
events.description: Marc Hillmyer, McKnight Presidential Endowed Chair, University of Minnesota Telechelic polymers for sustainable polyolefins Polyolefins are ubiquitous. They are lightweight, strong, and stable. These features render them useful in countless applications. Unfortunately, these attributes also contribute to the accumulation of persistent plastic waste in the environment. While polyolefins can be mechanically recycled, often this results in an inferior product and is in part the reason that only a small percentage of polyolefin products are effectively recycled. We have embarked on an effort to prepare polyolefins with functional groups at their chain ends. These telechelic polyolefins can be stitched together to form high molar mass plastics and thermosets. By virtue of the synthetic pathway used to make these materials, we generate products that include weak links along the backbones of the polymer chains. These links can be chemically cleaved to quantitatively deconstruct the material and allow for efficient chemical recycling back to the starting telechelic polymers that can be subsequently repolymerized. Our approach takes advantage of a tandem catalysis strategy that is perfectly atom economic and readily scalable. In this lecture I will discuss the preparation of the telechelic polyolefins and their use in the preparation of degradable polyolefin-based plastics and thermosets. I will also report on their materials properties, scalability, and recyclability.The Organic Seminar Series is sponsored by the William G. Dauben lecture fund

events.title: Ilyas Chattha | Citizens to Traitors: Bengali Internment in Pakistan, 1971–1974
events.description: A talk by Ilyas Chattha (https://lums.edu.pk/lums_employee/6934), Associate Professor of History at the Lahore University of Management Sciences (LUMS), on his new book, Citizens to Traitors: Bengali Internment in Pakistan, 1971–1974 (https://www.cambridge.org/us/universitypress/subjects/history/south-asian-history/citizens-traitors-bengali-internment-pakistan-19711974?format=HB&isbn=9781009568241) (Cambridge University Press, 2025). Drawing on previously untapped sources, the book examines Pakistan's internment of thousands of Bengalis after the 1971 war and explains why this history has largely been overlooked.Sadia Saeed (https://www.usfca.edu/faculty/sadia-saeed), Associate Professor of Sociology at the University of San Francisco will serve as discussant. Event moderated by Elora Shehabuddin (https://gws.berkeley.edu/people/elora-shehabuddin), Professor of Gender & Women's Studies and Global Studies; Faculty Director, Subir and Malini Chowdhury Center for Bangladesh Studies; Faculty Director, Global Studies and Global Poverty and Practice (https://blumcenter.berkeley.edu/academics/gppminor/), UC Berkeley. This event will be live streamed on the Chowdhury Center's FB page: ChowdhuryCenter@UCBerkeley (https://www.facebook.com/ChowdhuryCenter). ————–DATE: Tue, November 10, 2026 TIME: 5-6:30 pm PST VENUE: 10 Stephens Hall LIVESTREAM: ChowdhuryCenter@UCBerkeley (https://www.facebook.com/ChowdhuryCenter) ————– ABOUT THE BOOKThe breakup of Pakistan in 1971—following a brutal civil war and military defeat by India—remains shrouded in layers of silence, myth, and contested memory. When the war ended, more than 90,000 Pakistani prisoners of war captured in East Pakistan, now Bangladesh, were transferred to Indian custody. In response, Pakistan interned a comparable number of Bengalis living in West Pakistan, treating them as leverage in negotiations for the prisoners' return. Neither group was allowed to go home immediately, creating what became one of the largest episodes of reciprocal mass internment since 1945. Drawing on a wide range of previously untapped sources, this book reconstructs the resulting crisis of captivity. It traces how Bengalis in West Pakistan were stripped of meaningful citizenship and recast as "traitors" and "enemies" in the aftermath of the Bangladesh War. More than half a century later, their internment remains largely absent from accounts of the most consequential political crisis in Pakistan's history. By recovering this neglected history, the book not only reveals the human and political consequences of mass detention but also explains how—and why—the experience of interned Bengalis was erased from the historical record. SPEAKER BIOIlyas Chattha (https://lums.edu.pk/lums_employee/6934) is Associate Professor of History at Lahore University of Management Sciences (LUMS) and a historian of modern South Asia. Educated at the universities of Warwick and Southampton in the United Kingdom, he has previously been affiliated with the Centre for Imperial and Post-Colonial Studies at the University of Southampton, the University of Warwick, and SOAS University of London. Dr Chattha's research focuses on late colonial Punjab, Partition, migration, borders and borderlands, collective violence, and the formation of the early postcolonial Pakistani state. He has written extensively on the long-term consequences of the partitions of 1947 and 1971, with particular attention to displacement, citizenship, internment, property, and state-building. He is the author of Citizens to Traitors: Bengali Internment in Pakistan, 1971–1974 (Cambridge University Press, 2025), which examines the wartime and postwar experiences of Bengalis interned in West Pakistan; The Punjab Borderland: Mobility, Materiality and Militancy, 1947–1987 (Cambridge University Press, 2022); and Partition and Locality: Violence, Migration and Development in Gujranwala and Sialkot, 1947–1961 (Oxford University Press, 2012). His current book project explores the history of evacuee and enemy property in Pakistan.EVENT POSTER TBA _____________ Established in 2013 with a generous gift from the Subir & Malini Chowdhury Foundation (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Subir_Chowdhury), The Subir & Malini Chowdhury Center for Bangladesh Studies (https://chowdhurycenter.berkeley.edu/) at UC Berkeley champions the study of Bangladesh's cultures, peoples and history. The first of its kind in the US, the Center's mission is to create an innovative model combining research, scholarships, the promotion of art and culture, and the building of ties between institutions in Bangladesh and the University of California. Like us on FACEBOOK (https://www.facebook.com/The-Subir-Malini-Chowdhury-Center-for-Bangladesh-Studies-752426458213022/?ref=hl) For DIRECTIONS to the Institute please enter "Institute for South Asia Studies" in your google maps or click this GOOGLE MAPS LINK (https://www.google.com/maps/dir//Institute+for+South+Asia+Studies,+10+Stephens+Hall,+Berkeley,+CA+94720/@37.8710692,-122.2585002,19z/data=!4m16!1m7!3m6!1s0x80857c25babcc33d:0xe2ff7d5c1483db5a!2sInstitute+for+South+Asia+Studies!3b1!8m2!3d37.8710952!4d-122.2576645!4m7!1m0!1m5!1m1!1s0x80857c25babcc33d:0xe2ff7d5c1483db5a!2m2!1d-122.2576645!2d37.8710952).PARKING INFORMATION (http://southasia.berkeley.edu/parking-around-campus)Please note that parking is not always easily available in Berkeley. Faruqui (https://sseas.berkeley.edu/people/munis-d-faruqui/), Director, Institute for South Asia Studies; Director, Global, International & Area Studies (GIAS); Sarah Kailath Chair of India Studies; Professor, South & Southeast Asian Studies, UC Berkeley. ————–DATE: Thu, November 12, 2026 TIME: 5-6:30 pm PST VENUE: 10 Stephens Hall —————-About the Speaker:Rahul Parson (https://sseas.berkeley.edu/people/rahul-parson) received an MA and PhD in the Department of South & Southeast Asian Studies, UC Berkeley, with a specialization in Modern Hindi literature. Before returning to the Berkeley in 2021, he served as an Assistant Professor of Hindi and Urdu at the University of Colorado, Boulder (2016-2020) and a Wissenschaftlicher Mitarbeiter (Postdoctoral Researcher) at Max-Weber-Kolleg, Universität Erfurt, Germany (2014-2016). Rahul Parson's area of specialization is Hindi literature and literary history, with a particular emphasis on Hindi movements in Bengal. His book project, Confluences at the End of the Ganges: Modernity, Migration and Hindi Literature in Kolkata, fills in the Bengal portion of the map of Hindi studies. The monograph reveals the dynamism and syncretism of the hitherto overlooked world of Hindi literature in Bengal and the affective archives and narratives of migrants. It inaugurates research on the literatures of displaced and migrant peoples in South Asia by using cultural texts to explore the articulations of life-worlds of women and migrants. Additionally, he researches early-modern Jain poetry and philosophy, particularly the Jain adhyātma (spiritual or mystical) poetry. Dr. Parson participated as a core member of a research group based at the Max-Weber-Kolleg. In this capacity, he worked as a co-editor of a four-volume series entitled: Religious Individualisations: Historical Dimensions and Comparative Perspectives (Berlin: de Gruyter, 2020).Event Poster TBA ————��— Event is FREE and OPEN to the public. events.title: The Narrowing Sea: Three Portraits of a Region
events.location: Institute of East Asian Studies, Conference Room, 2111 Bancroft Way, 5th Floor, Berkeley, CA 94720
events.description: Speaker: Hannah Shepherd (Yale University) In Person Event | RSVP Required RSVP for In Person Attendance at Bottom of Page Note: This event will begin on "Berkeley Time" at 5:10 PM. Talk Summary: This talk will introduce Hannah Shepherd's new book, The Narrowing Sea, via vignettes of the imperial region that developed across the Tsushima Straits between Pusan and Fukuoka in the seven decades from 1876 to 1953. It will offer the imperial region as a useful scale of analysis and connection between other imperial histories, and connect the urbanization of the imperial era with contemporary Japan's urban issues, before ending with a glimpse of new work that continues some of the histories and legacies discussed in The Narrowing Sea. Speaker Bio: Hannah Shepherd is Assistant Professor in the Department of History at Yale University. She received her Ph.D. in History from Harvard University. Before joining the Yale faculty, she was Junior Research Fellow in History at Trinity College, University of Cambridge. At Yale, Shepherd teaches courses on modern Japanese history, Korea and the Japanese Empire, and the history of colonial and imperial cities. Her book, The Narrowing Sea: Fukuoka, Pusan, and the Rise and Fall of an Imperial Region, came out in December 2025, from University of California Press. With Amy Stanley, she is currently working on co-translating and co-editing an English memoir of a former comfort woman, with the working title, The Life of Mun Ok Chu: a Korean woman's story of war and empire.
